A conflict on one key refuses even when the other agrees or is absent |
| `--approve-plan <token>` | the fingerprint of the plan the arm builds | the ordinary §8 comparison, unchanged; presenting a token neither waives a trigger conflict (the row above is non-waivable, exactly as I20 is) nor waives rank 4.5/rank 3 |

Three consequences are binding: (i) **matching or flagless `--continue` resumes** — the recovery arm
runs, and no flag is required to reach it; (ii) **a conflicting trigger yields the exact I20
sentence**, so an operator sees the same words whether the run's route was learned from a payload,
from a legacy state or from a sentinel, and §22.28e (vii) asserts the byte identity against the
shipped gate's own output; (iii) **the check is on all three verbs**, so `tws sync <f> --only x
--abort` over this document refuses with the I20 sentence and clears nothing, rather than
discarding a backup under a flag the run never accepted. `--continue --abort` together is refused
above all of this by the deferred half of I7, at its shipped position, with its shipped sentence
(§13.6 rule 4b).

**The three verbs (total over `verdict: valid`).**

| Verb | Arm | Output and exit |
|---|---|---|
| `--continue` | the **recovery arm** of §12.3: reclaim the guard the interrupted setup had already claimed — dead by construction, because the process that claimed it is the one that died, and a **live** guard (foreign or self-recorded) refused above this table — or claim it where an operator removed `.sync-run.lock` by hand; then write the v3 payload from the intent block and the verified prior state, then the guarded legacy continuation | the shipped legacy resume prose and tail; `0` on success |
| `--abort` | the shipped cell-4 removals, in the shipped order — the shipped `scoped sync state appeared at %s while aborting; re-run: tws sync %s --abort` refusal where a payload appeared under it, then `DeleteSyncState`, then `ReleaseSyncRunGuard` — with **one** changed byte-sequence: the line it prints | `Sync state cleared; the interrupted guarded setup's backup of the previous sync state was discarded.`, exit `0` |
| plain `tws sync <f>` | no removal, no write | `a guarded sync was interrupted while recording state for %q; the previous sync state is preserved inside %s — use --continue to resume it, or --abort to discard it`, exit `1` |

**`--abort` discards on purpose, and says so.** It is a **clear** verb, never a restore verb
(§12.8a): it does not put the backed-up document back, it does not resume, and it does not offer to.
What it owes the operator is honesty, which is why it MUST NOT print the bare shipped
`Sync state cleared.` — that sentence would hide the destruction of a recoverable document — and
MUST NOT print §12.8's or §12.8a's guard-only lines, which claim something else happened. Its line
is not a `plan-guard:` marker either (§6.4). An operator who wanted the backup had `--continue`.

**Every other *guarded* verdict fails closed, for every verb, removing nothing.** `symlink`, `unreadable`,
`unsupported-version`, `corrupt`, `foreign` and `hash-mismatch` take their sentences from §13.6
rule 2c's outcome table at exit `1`, leaving `.sync-state.yaml`, the guard and every ref
byte-identical: a document the inspector could not verify is never resumed *and* never cleared by
an automatic arm, because both would act on bytes tws cannot vouch for. The operator's remedies —
inspect, and remove manually — are named in each sentence, and **no** sentence names
`tws sync <f> --abort` or `--continue`: `--abort` is itself one of the three verbs that refuse over
these verdicts, so naming it would send the operator to a command that answers with the same
sentence. Each verdict's sentence is **byte-identical across plain, `--continue` and `--abort`**
(§13.6 rule 2c binding 6, §22.28e (v)).

**The plan route projects these sentences; it never invents one.** A `--plan` over the same cell
publishes gate `external-a` with the sentence its **executing** twin would raise — §12.8b's plain
sentence for a `valid` sentinel, that verdict's fail-closed sentence for every other guarded
verdict, and the **shipped** cell-4 sentence for a plain one — as a rank 3 `state-refused` blocker
inside a document at exit `0`, and it writes nothing at all: no claim, no reclaim, no payload, no
removal (§13.7a step 5, §18.1, §3.6 row 2). The **flag check** above is projected the same way and
at the same gate: `--plan --continue --only x` over a valid backup sentinel publishes the shipped
I20 sentence as that gate's `detail`, exactly as the executing twin would raise it, rather than
publishing a resumable plan; `--plan --continue` with a **conflicting** limit publishes the rank 7
`guard-limit-mismatch` row and the `guard.limit_conflicts[]` entry of §13.2, with the persisted
value effective. `--plan --continue` with a matching or absent limit publishes the
persisted intent's limits with their `origin` and likewise upgrades, resumes and removes nothing.
A `--plan` whose sentinel **vanished** between the classifier and the projection takes the same
vanished-state row as its executing twin: it re-classifies once and projects the cell it then finds
— for the ordinary cell-1 outcome, a document with no backup-sentinel gate at all, whose surviving
`.sync-run.lock` is published only through the shipped `state.files.external_run_guard` evidence and,
where that guard is a **live foreign** owner, through the ordinary §11.2 cause 3 suppression and the
`live-owner-concurrency` machinery §12.5 rule 4 already owns — and it publishes
**no** `state-refused` blocker naming a backup that is no longer there (§12.8b's vanished-state row,
§25.97).

**Ownership and call sites.** `internal.InspectGuardedLegacySentinel` decides; package `cli` composes
every sentence, at the **one** interception site declared above — in `internal/cli/sync.go`'s
external `RunE`, below `syncCellLiveGuardRefusal` and above `syncCellRefusal` — which owns all three
verbs, passes each of them to the extraction as its `verb` argument, and threads the verdict into
whichever arm it selects (§19.2). `syncCellRefusal` is unchanged
apart from calling the extraction above as its first statement, with the verb it was itself given; `handleSyncAbortCell`'s cell-4 arm,
the plain-verb path's previous-incomplete refusal and every continuation handler are unchanged and
consult no sentinel of their own; cells 1, 2, 5, 7 and every unreadable cell keep their shipped arms
byte-for-byte, and §12.8's and §12.8a's arms are untouched.

**Declared compatibility.** Like §12.8 and §12.8a this is reachable **without** a control flag —
the residue is guarded, but the invocation meeting it need not be — so it is declared in §17.2 and
§19.4, asserted in §22.28e, and named in the `CHANGELOG.md` entry of §20. An older `v1.2.15` binary
meeting the same residue behaves exactly as it does today (§13.6 rule 5): it refuses plain and
`--continue` with the shipped cell-4 sentence and clears the file with its shipped `--abort`,
discarding the backup without mentioning it. Nothing about that is made worse by these arms; the new
binary simply resumes what it can prove, and states what it destroys.

## 13. Checkout transaction, stages and remaining work

### 13.1 Additive transaction and payload fields

Add these keys — and no others — to `CheckoutTransaction` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:63-100`) and
to `SyncRunState` (`internal/sync_run_state.go:38-63`). Every one is `omitempty`, so an unguarded
run's on-disk bytes are unchanged:

```go
// both structs
MaxReplayPerEntry *int   `yaml:"max_replay_per_entry,omitempty"`
MaxReplayTotal    *int   `yaml:"max_replay_total,omitempty"`
Route             string `yaml:"route,omitempty"` // "legacy" | "new-mode"; absent ⇒ derived (§13.6)

// internal/rebase_plan.go — the two spellings, declared once and shared by both
// structs, both route derivations (§13.6 rule 4) and the document's `route` key
const (
    RouteLegacy  = "legacy"
    RouteNewMode = "new-mode"
)
```

Binding:

1. The two limits are pointer-backed (or explicitly presence-flagged) so `0` is persisted and
   distinguishable from absent; a scalar `int` with `omitempty` MUST NOT be used.
2. **No approval token, no `guard_enabled` field, and no validation-digest key** is added. The
   digest stays **derived** from the command each route already persists
   (`SyncRunState.TestCommand`/`ValidationSource`, `CheckoutTransaction.TestCommand`), which the
   guarded legacy external envelope now also carries (§13.6, §15, §25.3).
3. `Route` exists because a `state_version: 3` envelope can describe **either** route, and the
   continuation dispatch is state-derived. It is written only by a guarded run; absent, it is
   derived exactly as shipped code derives it today (§13.6 rule 4), so every v1/v2 document keeps
   its shipped meaning.
4. **The fields alone do not decide the version.** `state_version` is decided at the run's birth by
   whether the run is guarded (§13.6): an unguarded new-mode run keeps `2`, an unguarded no-flag
   checkout run keeps the omitted version, and a guarded run of any route writes `3`. The one
   declared later transition is the armed-continuation upgrade of §13.2a (§13.6 rule 2b), which
   promotes a pre-guarded subject to `3` with an **inherited** route and writes no other key.
   Round-trip fidelity, including a persisted `0`, is asserted on disk for every cell of §13.6's
   matrix.

### 13.2 Limit persistence and per-key continuation resolution

| Route | Persistence |
|---|---|
| Fresh new-mode external run, **guarded** | persist both effective values in the `state_version: 3` payload |
| Fresh new-mode external run, unguarded | nothing to persist (no limits exist); payload stays `state_version: 2` |
| Fresh new-mode checkout run, **guarded** | persist in the `state_version: 3` `CheckoutTransaction` |
| Fresh **legacy** checkout run, **guarded** | persist in the `state_version: 3` `CheckoutTransaction` (it exists before the first checkout) |
| Fresh **legacy external** run, **guarded** | persist in the guarded legacy envelope — the backup sentinel of §13.6 rule 2c (with `prior_legacy_present: false` on a fresh run) plus a `state_version: 3` payload carrying `route: legacy`. The analysis's "nothing can persist here" is refined in §25.9 |
| Any unguarded run, any route | persists exactly the shipped shape; no limit key is written |
| Any continuation that arms a limit over a pre-guarded subject | **the §13.2a upgrade**: below the guard seam and before the invocation's next Git mutation, the subject is rewritten as a `state_version: 3` envelope carrying the inherited route, the effective limits and the frozen validation command. The earlier rule — "do **not** write the armed value back into payload/transaction, and do **not** upgrade the run's `state_version`" — is **withdrawn**: it left a guarded resume's limits alive for one invocation only, so a re-interruption plus a flagless `--continue` silently finished the run unguarded |

Per-key resolution (`max_replay_per_entry` and `max_replay_total` are independent):

| Case | Persisted | Supplied | Effective | `origin` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| inherit | present (incl. `0`) | absent | persisted | `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` |
| confirm | present | equal | persisted | `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction` |
| conflict | present | different | persisted stays effective | rank 7 `guard-limit-mismatch`, row in `guard.limit_conflicts[]` |
| arm | absent | present (incl. `0`) | supplied | `flags-persisted-continuation`; legacy external `.sync-state.yaml` `flags-legacy-continuation` |
| unguarded | absent | absent | `null` | `none` |

A conflict on one key refuses even when the other agrees or is absent; values are never silently
merged; the conflict is not waivable by any token; the document stays complete and mints a token
over the **persisted effective** values. Limits are scoped to **this invocation's** work and are
never accumulated across resumes. A guarded legacy-envelope continuation resolves its limits
through exactly this table with `origin: persisted-payload`. The `arm` row's two flag origins are
the labels of the invocation that *arms* a key over a subject that had none — the label describes
where **this** document's effective value came from, and it stays `flags-persisted-continuation` /
`flags-legacy-continuation` even though the same invocation, once it passes its guard seam, makes
those values persistent through §13.2a; the **next** continuation of that run therefore reads them
back as `persisted-payload` / `persisted-transaction`.

### 13.2a The armed-continuation upgrade — persist the guard before the first mutation

A limit armed on a `--continue` used to live for exactly one invocation. That is unsound in the one
cell the guard exists for: the operator arms `--max-replay-total 20` on a resume, the resume
rebases two entries and is interrupted again, and the next `tws sync <f> --continue` — the natural
flagless one — finishes the run **unguarded**, because nothing on disk records that a limit was
ever armed. A guarded run must be guarded for its whole life, not for one invocation of it.

**Trigger (four conjuncts, all required, evaluated in this order):**

1. the invocation is a **continuation** on a controlled executing route — the external scoped arm
   (`handleGuardedScopedSyncContinue`), the cell-5 or cell-7 arm of
   `handleGuardedLegacySyncContinue`, or `ContinueCheckoutSync`'s guarded arm. Its **cell-4
   recovery arm** is deliberately outside this trigger: that subject is already a guarded document
   (§13.6 rule 2c), so the arm is not upgrading anything — it is *completing* a birth whose payload
   write never landed, with the reduced step-9 form of the position table below, and it runs
   whether or not this invocation arms a flag;
2. the persisted subject is **not yet guarded**: an external payload whose `state_version` is `2`,
   a checkout transaction whose `state_version` is absent, `1` or `2`, or a real
   `.sync-state.yaml` (which carries no version at all and no guarded extension — a **backup
   sentinel** is not a member, per conjunct 1);
3. **at least one limit is effective** after §13.2's per-key resolution — which on this cell means
   at least one limit was supplied by **this** invocation, since the subject persisted none. An
   invocation that supplies only `--approve-plan` and resolves to two absent limits is rank 7.5
   `approval-without-limits` and upgrades **nothing**: there is no guard to preserve;
4. the **guard seam passed** — `EvaluatePlanGuard` returned `nil`, so no refusal of any rank stops
   this invocation — and the route is proceeding into work that can mutate Git.

**Effect — one write, before the next Git mutation.** The route persists the guarded envelope
through the **shipped atomic writer** for that state, setting these four things and nothing else:

| Field | Value | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `state_version` | `SyncRunStateGuardedVersion` / `CheckoutTransactionGuardedVersion` — `3` | the one declared transition of §13.6 rule 2b |
| `route` | the **inherited** derived route — literally `internal.PayloadNewMode(payload)` / `internal.TransactionNewMode(tx)` evaluated on the subject **as loaded**, spelled `new-mode` or `legacy` (§13.6 rule 4) | the upgrade never *decides* a route: every v2 payload and every v2 transaction inherits `new-mode`, a version-less/`1` checkout transaction inherits `legacy`, and a real `.sync-state.yaml` is `legacy` by construction. No run changes semantics by being upgraded |
| `max_replay_per_entry`, `max_replay_total` | this invocation's **effective** values (§13.2), pointer-backed so a persisted `0` survives | a key that is effectively absent stays **absent**; the two keys are independent |
| the frozen validation command | the value this invocation froze (§15) — which on every one of these arms **is** the subject's own persisted `TestCommand`/`ValidationSource`, written back byte-identically, except on the `.sync-state.yaml` arm, which has none and persists the command it resolved for itself | the upgrade never substitutes a freshly read command, and it persists **no digest**: the digest stays derived (§13.1 rule 2, §25.3) |

Everything else is written back **byte-identically** on the two arms that *re-version* an existing
subject (the external v2 payload and the checkout transaction): identity, `marker`, `owner_token`,
the policy
axes, `Selected`/`Pending`/`Completed`/`Pushed`/`FailedBranch`/`Repos` on a payload, and the whole
plan/progress block (`Plan`, `CurrentIndex`, `Stage`, `CompletedIndices`, `OriginalBranch`,
`OriginalHEAD`, the frozen new-mode decision) on a transaction. The upgrade is a version-and-guard-
keys write over the value the route already holds, never a re-derivation of the run and never a
re-planning of it. The third arm — a real `.sync-state.yaml`, which has no payload to re-version —
*creates* the already-specified guarded legacy envelope instead, and its member rules are stated
below. On **all three**, **no approval token is persisted**, and no `guard_enabled` key and no
digest key
is added (§13.1 rule 2): an approval authorizes one fingerprint of one invocation (§8.5), so
persisting it would let a later invocation inherit a waiver it never presented.

The four fields are set on the **in-memory** payload/transaction the route is already carrying, and
only then saved. Every later shipped save of that same value — a stage update, `saveScopedSyncFailure`,
`persist progress` — therefore preserves them, which is what makes a *re-interruption* inherit the
guard rather than lose it (§13.6 rule 3 already forbids `SaveSyncRunState` from re-forcing the
constant).

**Position (exact, per route; there is no discretion and no second site):**

| Route | Where the upgrade write happens | The mutation it precedes |
|---|---|---|
| external scoped, v2 payload (`handleGuardedScopedSyncContinue`) | **step 10a** — immediately after `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` (step 10, the continuation's first write) and before the header/prose of step 11 | the first `git rebase` of steps 12–13, or the push tail where the remaining set is rows-less |
| external legacy, real `.sync-state.yaml` (cell 7) | **step 9** — after the guard seam of step 8 and before the guarded executor call of step 10 (`syncWithStackScoped` with the run context that carries the payload it just wrote). On this arm the upgrade **is** the guarded legacy envelope creation of §12.3/§13.6, performed by `setupGuardedLegacyRunState` over the four-step order below, because there is no payload to re-version | the first `git rebase` of steps 10–11 |
| external legacy, valid backup sentinel (cell 4 recovery arm) | **step 9**, in its reduced form — the sentinel already exists, so the arm performs only §13.2a's step 2 (guard claim/reclaim) and step 4 (the v3 payload), skipping the replacement of step 3, at the same position | the first `git rebase` of steps 10–11 |
| checkout, version-less/`1`/`2` transaction (`ContinueCheckoutSync`'s guarded arm) | immediately after the guard seam that sits below `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` (§12.2d, §12.4) and before `resumeTransaction` | the first `git checkout`/`git rebase`/`git push`/`restoreOriginal` the resumed stage performs |
| external legacy, `state_version: 3` envelope | **not performed** — the subject is already the envelope (conjunct 2 fails) | — |

**The `.sync-state.yaml` arm, stated exactly, because it creates state rather than re-versioning
it.** `setupGuardedLegacyRunState` (declared in `internal/cli/sync_modes.go`, §13.6 rule 2a)
performs the four-step order below — capture → `ClaimSyncRunGuard` → **backup sentinel** → payload
— with the shipped sentences, and the continuation arm supplies four carried members so the
resumed run survives the transition:
`Selected` = the full-stack legacy universe in this invocation's one `TopoSort` order,
`Pending` = the remaining set of §13.3 in that order, `Completed` = the legacy state's `Completed`
verbatim, `FailedBranch` = the legacy state's `FailedBranch` verbatim. Every other member is
written exactly as the guarded legacy **fresh** route writes it — one owner, one writer, no second
shape. Three consequences are declared rather than discovered:

- the legacy state's `Skipped` list has no payload counterpart and is **not** carried into the
  payload. It was never resume-bearing: the shipped `handleSyncContinue` builds `done` from
  `Completed ∪ {FailedBranch}` alone (`internal/cli/sync.go:335-342`), so the resumed universe is
  unchanged by dropping it. It is nevertheless **not lost**: it survives verbatim inside the
  sentinel's byte-exact backup of the document it replaced;
- the sentinel write **replaces** `.sync-state.yaml`, so the arm reads that file's bytes before
  writing anything and puts them **inside the replacement**. The backup sentinel of §13.6 rule 2c
  is one document carrying three things at once: the marker an old binary fails closed on, this
  run's whole intent, and the prior document byte-for-byte with its SHA-256. That is what makes the
  ordering below safe: there is no instant at which the prior bytes exist nowhere;
- the guard claim keeps the shipped **first** position (`ClaimSyncRunGuard` → sentinel → payload),
  exactly as `setupSyncRunState` orders it. This arm's one structural difference from the shipped
  new-mode writer is *which kind of write* installs the sentinel: the new-mode writer **creates** a
  file nobody owns, while this one **replaces** the operator's own recovery document, so its
  sentinel write is a conditional compare-and-swap over the captured bytes rather than a plain
  atomic write. The shipped `setupSyncRunState` keeps its order, its sentences and its bytes
  (§13.6 rule 2a); nothing about the unguarded new-mode path moves. An earlier revision put the
  claim **below** the sentinel to shorten the window in which the prior bytes were only inside the
  sentinel; that reading is **withdrawn** (§25.80), because it let two new binaries both reach the
  replacement before either had claimed anything — a race the compare-and-swap can only turn into a
  refusal *after* one of them has already rewritten the operator's file.

**The exact order (crash-safe, four numbered steps plus a return).** This arm is the only place in
the specification where a *pre-existing* file is replaced rather than created, so its order, its
atomicity, its conditionality and its hooks are fixed here and nowhere else. `prior` is the
captured byte slice (`nil` on the fresh route, where the file does not exist), `sentinel` is the
exact byte slice step 3 installed, and every write is the shipped atomic writer (`atomicWriteFile`:
temp file in the same directory → `chmod` → write → `fsync` → `rename`), so each file is replaced
whole or left untouched:

| # | Step | Hook | On failure |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | **capture**: one `os.ReadFile` of `.sync-state.yaml` into `prior` (the bytes the classifier already decoded are **not** reused — restoration needs the file's bytes, not a re-marshalled struct). `fs.ErrNotExist` is the **fresh** cell: `prior = nil`, `prior_legacy_present = false`. A captured document that is empty, undecodable, or itself a marker sentinel is refused **here**, before any write, with the fail-closed sentence of §13.6 rule 2c | `syncStepHook(SyncStageInitializing, 3)` — the one new index this feature adds beside §12.2c's `SyncStageRebasing, -1` | return the read error wrapped as `read sync state: %w`, marker-free (or rule 2c's refusal for a non-resumable capture). Nothing has been written, nothing has been claimed; the legacy state is untouched and the run is exactly as found |
| 2 | **claim**: `internal.ClaimSyncRunGuard(featurePath, token)` — the shipped `O_EXCL` create with its shipped live/stale ladder and its shipped sentences. It is this arm's **first** write and the invocation's mutual-exclusion point: two new binaries racing over the same feature cannot both pass it, so at most one of them ever reaches step 3. On the **cell-7 continuation** arm it is also the **only** place a guard beside the subject is judged at all, because nothing above it judges one (§25.103) | `syncStepHook(SyncStageInitializing, 0)` (the shipped **artefact** index: "the guard now exists") | nothing else was created, so there is nothing to roll back: return `ClaimSyncRunGuard`'s own shipped error verbatim, marker-free, at exit `1`, with `.sync-state.yaml` byte-identical and no Git mutation issued. The four shipped cells are named exactly: a **live** PID — foreign **or** self-recorded, since `syncProcessAlive` has no self conjunct — yields `a scoped sync is already running for %q (pid %d, started %s); wait for it or use --continue/--abort after it exits`; `PID <= 0` yields `sync guard is being initialized or is invalid; retry or inspect %s`; an undecodable guard yields `invalid sync guard; inspect %s and use --abort to recover: %w`; and a provably **dead** guard is reclaimed through the shipped compare-and-swap (the `HasSyncRunState` arm cannot fire on cell 7 or on the fresh route, neither of which has a payload), with a failed swap yielding `reclaim stale sync guard: %w` |
| 3 | **backup sentinel**: `internal.SaveGuardedLegacySentinel(featurePath, sentinel, prior)` — **one conditional atomic replacement of the same path**: an `O_EXCL`-style *create* when `prior == nil`, and a compare-and-swap over the exact captured bytes when it is not, so the file is either the old bytes/absent or the complete backup sentinel and never anything else. A changed or unexpectedly present file is refused, writing nothing | `syncStepHook(SyncStageInitializing, 1)` (the shipped artefact index: "the sentinel now exists") | `rollbackGuardedLegacyRunState(...)` — release the claimed guard (`RemoveSyncRunGuard`) and nothing else, because the sentinel step wrote nothing (`guardedLegacySetupProgress{Guard: true}`) — and return `write sync sentinel: %w`, or — where the conditional write found the path changed — rule 2c's `sync state at %s changed while starting a guarded resume; re-run: tws sync %s --continue`, marker-free |
| 4 | **payload**: `internal.SaveSyncRunState(featurePath, payload)` — the `state_version: 3`, `route: legacy` envelope | `syncStepHook(SyncStageInitializing, 2)` (the shipped artefact index: "the payload now exists") | `rollbackGuardedLegacyRunState(...)`: remove the payload, then undo the sentinel replacement conditionally (`RestoreSyncStateBytes(featurePath, prior, sentinel)` where bytes were captured, `RemoveSyncStateIfUnchanged(featurePath, sentinel)` where `prior == nil`), then release the claimed guard — in that order, so the guard is still held while the prior document is put back. Then return `write scoped sync state: %w` |
| — | **return** the payload to the caller, which attaches it to the run context of §12.3 step 10 | — | — |

**Why the claim comes first, and what the conditional write still adds.** The mutual-exclusion
question and the never-lose-the-bytes question are separate, and each has its own mechanism:

- **the claim answers concurrency.** `ClaimSyncRunGuard` is an `O_EXCL` create, so of two new
  binaries starting a guarded legacy setup over the same feature exactly one passes step 2; the
  loser refuses with the shipped claim sentence having written **nothing at all**, and never
  reaches the replacement. A claim below the replacement would have let both binaries rewrite the
  operator's `.sync-state.yaml` before either learned it had lost — the compare-and-swap would then
  refuse the second one, but only *after* the first had already replaced the file, and the loser's
  own conditional undo would be racing the winner's payload write. Ordering the claim first removes
  that window instead of narrowing it;
- **the backup sentinel answers loss.** The replacement carries the captured document byte-for-byte
  with its SHA-256 (§13.6 rule 2c), so from step 3 onward the prior bytes are inside the file, and
  before step 3 they *are* the file. There is no instant, in any window, at which they exist
  nowhere;
- **the conditional write answers everything the guard cannot see.** The guard binds new binaries
  only. `SaveGuardedLegacySentinel` still refuses — writing nothing — when the path is not what
  `expect` says it is, and `RestoreSyncStateBytes`/`RemoveSyncStateIfUnchanged` still refuse unless
  the file is exactly the sentinel this invocation installed **and** no payload sits beside it
  (§13.6 rule 2c). So a foreign writer that changed the file under this arm produces a refusal, never
  a clobber, and no rollback of this arm can place a real legacy state next to a payload — classifier
  cell 8 is unreachable from every path of this arm **under this binary**.

**The one boundary this ordering does not close, stated plainly (binding).** Between step 2 and
step 3 the guard exists and `.sync-state.yaml` is still the operator's real legacy document. A
**concurrently running `v1.2.15` binary** does not consult `.sync-run.lock` at all on that path — the
shipped classifier reads the guard only under `AlwaysReadGuard` (§12.5) — so it can start, run and
later fail into its own `saveIncompleteSync` write inside or after that window. Three consequences
are declared rather than glossed:

- where the old binary's write lands **before** step 3, the compare-and-swap refuses, this arm rolls
  back to `{}` and returns rule 2c's changed-file sentence: no bytes are lost and nothing is
  clobbered;
- where it lands **after** step 3 but before this run finishes, the result is a **real**
  `.sync-state.yaml` beside this run's payload — classifier **cell 8** — which no code path of this
  binary can produce and no arm of this feature can repair automatically. The next new-binary
  invocation meets the shipped cell-8 refusal (`two unfinished syncs are recorded`) and the operator
  resolves it by hand;
- from step 3 onward an old binary that *starts* fresh fails closed instead: it decodes the backup
  sentinel into its shipped `SyncState`, sees the marker in `failed_branch`, and takes the shipped
  cell-4 refusal for a plain run and for `--continue`, moving no ref (its `--abort` still clears,
  discarding the backup — the same choice §12.8b's `--abort` makes deliberately).

**Running two different tws versions concurrently over one feature is therefore an unsupported
downgrade-concurrency boundary**, not a safety property this arm provides. No text in this
specification may claim that the guard, the compare-and-swap or the ordering makes it safe; what
they provide is that **this** binary never loses the captured bytes, never clobbers a document it
did not write, and never itself creates cell 8. §22.24j (v) asserts the new-binary half (two
concurrent guarded legacy setups: exactly one winner, the loser writing nothing) and §22.24i (ix-c)
asserts the declared boundary itself, as a *documented* outcome rather than a prevented one.

**Hooks are at every boundary, and a returned hook error is a setup failure, not a residue
(binding).** The three shipped `SyncStageInitializing` indices are bound to **artefacts**, not to
positions — `0` = guard, `1` = sentinel, `2` = payload — plus the new `3` = capture, so this arm
fires them in the order `3 → 0 → 1 → 2` while a test injecting at any index still names the same
boundary in both setups. Every one of the four boundaries is injectable, and:

- a hook (or writer, or claim) that **returns an error** at any boundary is handled exactly like
  that step's own failure in the table above: the arm rolls back everything it created, restores
  the captured bytes and returns the error. A returned error therefore **never leaks** a sentinel,
  a guard or a payload, and the invocation's own §22.24i (ix) assertions are "nothing survives"
  assertions;
- a **residue** exists only where no code of this arm ran to completion — a process crash, a
  `SIGKILL`, a power loss, or a test hook that terminates the process rather than returning — which
  is precisely the crash-window table below. This is the one behavioural difference from the
  shipped `setupSyncRunState`, whose hook returns leave the artefacts they follow in place
  (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:389-391`, `:402-404`); that shipped body is **unchanged** by this
  feature, and the difference is declared here rather than harmonised (§25.73).

**Rollback is error-returning, ordered, and never best-effort.** It uses the error-returning
removers of §12.2c rule 2 plus one additive **conditional** restorer, and it reports what it could
not undo:

```go
// internal/syncstate.go — additive, beside RemoveSyncState
//
// ErrSyncStateChanged and ErrSyncStateHasPayload are the two distinguished
// "restored nothing" outcomes; both mean the file on disk was left exactly as
// found.
var ErrSyncStateChanged error
var ErrSyncStateHasPayload error

// RestoreSyncStateBytes writes prior back over .sync-state.yaml through the
// shipped atomic writer, but ONLY when both preconditions hold:
//
//   1. the file's current bytes are byte-identical to `expect` — the exact
//      sentinel this invocation installed — so a restore can never clobber a
//      document another party wrote (ErrSyncStateChanged otherwise); and
//   2. no scoped payload exists beside it (HasSyncRunState is false), so a
//      restore can never place a REAL legacy state next to a live payload,
//      which would be classifier cell 8 (ErrSyncStateHasPayload otherwise).
//
// The result is therefore either the captured bytes or the value the file had
// before the attempt — never a partial document and never a cell-8 pair.
// len(prior) == 0 is a programming error and returns an error rather than
// truncating the file; the caller uses RemoveSyncStateIfUnchanged(featurePath,
// sentinel) for the fresh cell, where there were no prior bytes at all. The
// guarded legacy rollback NEVER calls the unconditional RemoveSyncState.
func RestoreSyncStateBytes(featurePath string, prior, expect []byte) error

// internal/cli/sync_modes.go — beside rollbackGuardedRunState (§12.2c rule 2)
//
// guardedLegacySetupProgress records exactly what setupGuardedLegacyRunState
// created, so the rollback undoes what happened rather than what it assumes.
type guardedLegacySetupProgress struct {
    Guard    bool // step 2 claimed the run guard
    Sentinel bool // step 3 installed the backup sentinel
    Payload  bool // step 4 wrote the v3 payload
}

// rollbackGuardedLegacyRunState undoes steps 4, 3 and 2 of the table above in
// REVERSE CREATION ORDER — payload, then the sentinel replacement, then the
// guard — stopping at the first failure and returning the residue actually left
// on disk. Releasing the guard LAST is load-bearing: the prior document is put
// back while this invocation still holds the run guard, so no other new binary
// can claim it and start writing over a half-undone directory. The sentinel step
// is ALWAYS conditional and never an unconditional removal:
// RestoreSyncStateBytes(featurePath, prior, sentinel) where prior bytes were
// captured, and RemoveSyncStateIfUnchanged(featurePath, sentinel) where there
// were none (the fresh route), so it can only ever undo the exact bytes THIS
// invocation installed. It never aborts a rebase, never touches a pre-existing
// artefact it did not create, and never re-attempts a step it has already
// failed. Its intermediate on-disk shapes are the crash-window shapes below, so
// an interruption inside the rollback is itself recoverable.
func rollbackGuardedLegacyRunState(featurePath string, prior, sentinel []byte,
    made guardedLegacySetupProgress) (syncStateResidue, error)
```

**The sentinel step of this rollback is conditional in both branches (binding).** It takes the
`sentinel` bytes step 3 installed as its `expect` argument in **both** cases, and it is the only
rollback in this specification that ever *restores* `.sync-state.yaml` — and the only one that
removes it **conditionally**:

| Capture cell | Undo call | Refuses (writing/removing nothing) when |
|---|---|---|
| `prior != nil` (a real `.sync-state.yaml` was replaced — the cell-7 continuation arm) | `RestoreSyncStateBytes(featurePath, prior, sentinel)` | the file is no longer byte-identical to `sentinel` (`ErrSyncStateChanged`) or a payload sits beside it (`ErrSyncStateHasPayload`) |
| `prior == nil` (the fresh route; `prior_legacy_present: false`) | `RemoveSyncStateIfUnchanged(featurePath, sentinel)` | the same two conditions, with the same two distinguished errors |

So a fresh rollback removes **only its own sentinel** and never a document another party wrote, and
a continuation rollback restores the original **only** while the sentinel it installed is still
exactly what is on disk. `RemoveSyncState` — the unconditional remover of §12.2c rule 2 — is used by
the shipped teardown and by `rollbackGuardedRunState` (which removes a sentinel written over a path
that held nothing) and by **no** guarded legacy setup rollback; a call to it from
`rollbackGuardedLegacyRunState` fails §22.24i (ix-a).

- **A successful rollback leaves the pre-attempt directory** — on the continuation arm the original
  bytes are restored byte-for-byte, asserted by hash rather than by
  re-decode, and on the fresh arm the sentinel this invocation installed is gone with nothing put in
  its place — and it leaves no payload, no sentinel and no run guard: `syncStateResidue.Empty()` is
  `true`, the feature directory is indistinguishable from the pre-attempt one, and the invocation
  returns the failing step's **shipped** sentence, marker-free, at exit `1` (§13.2a save-failure
  rule 3). No `state-preserved: ` prefix is emitted, because nothing this invocation created
  survives.
- **A failed rollback is reported, never swallowed.** Where `RemoveSyncRunState`,
  `RemoveSyncRunGuard`, `RestoreSyncStateBytes` or `RemoveSyncStateIfUnchanged` itself fails — the
  four calls this rollback makes, and the only four — the invocation
  returns one sentence composed in `cli`, at exit `1`, marker-free (the guard did not refuse — a
  write failed, and §6.4's anchored marker names guard verdicts only):

  ```text
  <the failing writer's shipped sentence>; recovery state preserved: <residue> — clear it with: tws sync <f> --abort
  ```

  `<residue>` is `syncStateResidue.String()` over the measured artefacts — `{payload, sentinel,
  guard}` when the payload removal failed, `{sentinel, guard}` when the conditional sentinel undo
  failed (the restore on the continuation arm, the conditional removal on the fresh one), and
  `{guard}` when only the guard release failed, in which case `.sync-state.yaml` is already back to
  the captured bytes (continuation arm) or already gone (fresh arm) — and `<f>` is the feature
  name. It MUST NOT retry,
  MUST NOT force-remove a later artefact, and MUST NOT claim the state was restored. All three
  residues are recoverable and **none loses the prior document**: `{payload, sentinel, guard}` is
  classifier cell 5 and is cleared by the shipped cell-5 `--abort` arm; `{sentinel, guard}` is
  cell 4 over a **valid backup sentinel**, which `tws sync <f> --continue` resumes
  through the recovery arm of §12.3 and `tws sync <f> --abort` clears through §12.8b; and `{guard}`
  is a guard-only residue beside a **restored** `.sync-state.yaml` on the continuation arm — the
  cell-7-plus-guard shape §12.8a's `--abort` clears — or beside nothing at all on the fresh arm,
  which is the cell-1-plus-guard shape §12.8's `--abort` clears.
- **No Git mutation has run at any point above**, so no ref, index or working tree is touched by a
  failed setup on this arm, and the `--continue` that follows resumes either the pre-attempt state
  (successful rollback, and the `{guard}` residue, where the subject itself is intact) or the
  sentinel's own recovery (the `{sentinel, guard}` residue) — never nothing.

**Crash windows (total; three reachable shapes, each with its recovery cell).** A crash — power
loss, `SIGKILL`, a hook that terminates the process — between two of the steps above leaves exactly
one of the three shapes below. A **returned** error at any of those boundaries leaves none of them
(the rollback rule above), which is why this table names crashes only. A crash at the **capture**
boundary is not a window at all: nothing has been written or claimed, so the directory is exactly
as found — the operator's `.sync-state.yaml` on the continuation arm (cell 7, no guard), and
nothing on the fresh route (cell 1, no guard):

| Crash point | On-disk shape | Classifier cell | Recovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| after step 2, before step 3 | `{guard}` **plus the untouched subject** — the operator's real `.sync-state.yaml` on the continuation arm, nothing at all on the fresh route. No sentinel, no payload; the prior document has not been replaced yet, so it is still the file | **cell 7** beside a guard (continuation arm); **cell 1** beside a guard (fresh route) | `tws sync <f> --abort` clears **both** artefacts: §12.8a's cell-7 arm (`Sync state cleared; stale sync guard from PID <pid> cleared.`) on the continuation arm, §12.8's cell-1 arm (`Stale sync guard from PID <pid> cleared; no sync state was present.`) on the fresh one. A plain `tws sync <f>` and a `--continue` meet the shipped cell-7/cell-1 answers for that cell — the legacy state is intact and resumable, flagless or armed — with the shipped live-guard refusal where the guard is still live |
| after step 3, before step 4 | `{backup sentinel, guard}` — the prior document is inside the sentinel, byte-for-byte, with its SHA-256; **no** payload | **cell 4** (the guard is not a cell axis) | `tws sync <f> --continue` takes the **recovery arm** of §12.3, **reclaiming** the guard (`checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable` → `ReclaimSyncRunGuard`, §12.4) — which is the ordinary case here, because the claimer is the process that died — or **claiming** it where an operator removed `.sync-run.lock` by hand, and refusing with the shipped live sentence where the guard is **live**, foreign or self-recorded alike (§12.8b's extraction table), then writing the v3 payload from the sentinel's intent block and the verified prior state and resuming the guarded legacy continuation. `tws sync <f> --abort` clears sentinel **and** guard and **discards** the backup, saying so (§12.8b). A plain `tws sync <f>` gets §12.8b's fail-closed sentence |
| after step 4 | `{payload, backup sentinel, guard}` | **cell 5** | the shipped cell-5 sentences, `--continue` (dispatched to the envelope arm, limits inherited) and the shipped cell-5 `--abort` arm — the state the setup exists to create, exactly as ledger row 9 declares |

**No window loses the prior bytes, and no window is cell 8.** Before step 3 the prior document is
the file; from step 3 onward it is inside the file; after a successful teardown neither exists,
which is the same end state the shipped flagless resume reaches. A **real** legacy state and a
payload are never both on disk at any instant of this arm — the sentinel replaces the legacy
document in one rename **before** any payload is written, the restore refuses while a payload
exists, and the executor persists failures into the payload rather than through `saveIncompleteSync`
(§12.3) — so classifier cell 8 is unreachable from every one of these paths **under this binary**.
The one way to reach it is the declared downgrade-concurrency boundary above, where a concurrently
running `v1.2.15` binary writes its own `.sync-state.yaml` beside this run's payload; that outcome
is documented, not prevented, and no text may claim otherwise.

**An older binary meeting each window is declared, not discovered, and never moves a ref.**
A `v1.2.15` binary ignores the extension keys it does not know and decodes `.sync-state.yaml` into
its shipped `SyncState`, where `failed_branch` is the **marker** (§13.6 rule 2c), so:

| Window | Old-binary `tws sync <f>` | Old-binary `--continue` | Old-binary `--abort` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — `{guard}` + the untouched subject | it does **not** fail closed, and this is the declared boundary above: the guard is invisible to it, so on the continuation arm it meets its own cell-7 `previous sync incomplete (failed on: %s); use --continue or --abort` refusal (exit `1`, **no ref moved**) and on the fresh route it meets cell 1 and **runs an ordinary unguarded legacy sync**, which can later write its own `.sync-state.yaml` | on the continuation arm, the shipped flagless legacy resume — it really rebases, because the subject is a real legacy state it is entitled to resume; on the fresh route, `nothing to continue — no sync in progress` | the shipped cell-7 arm (clears `.sync-state.yaml`, prints `Sync state cleared.`, leaves the guard) on the continuation arm; the shipped `Nothing to abort — no sync in progress.` on the fresh route, leaving the guard |
| 2 — `{backup sentinel, guard}` | classifier cell 4 ⇒ the shipped `a scoped sync left partial state for %q: …; Inspect the worktrees, then run: tws sync %s --abort`, exit `1`, **no ref moved**; plus the shipped live-guard refusal where that guard is live | the same cell-4 sentence, exit `1`, **no ref moved** | the shipped cell-4 arm: deletes the sentinel, releases the guard, prints `Sync state cleared.`, exit `0`. It **discards** the embedded backup, which is the same choice the new binary's `--abort` makes deliberately (§12.8b) and moves no ref |
| 3 — `{payload, backup sentinel, guard}` | payload `state_version: 3` ⇒ cell 6 ⇒ the shipped unsupported-version sentence, exit `1` | the same sentence | the same sentence — the old binary can neither resume nor abort, and says so (§13.6 rule 5) |

**Window 1 is the honest exception, and it is stated rather than smoothed.** In windows 2 and 3 an
old binary refuses or deletes state files and never rebases. In window 1 there is no marker for it
to fail closed on — the file is still the operator's own legacy state, or nothing — so it behaves
exactly as it does today over that same subject, which for a *fresh* residue means it may start a
whole unguarded sync while a stale guard sits beside it. That is not made worse by this feature (the
same shape is already reachable from a killed shipped `setupSyncRunState`, §12.8), it moves no ref
that the operator did not ask for, and the new binary's `--abort` clears both artefacts through
§12.8/§12.8a. The transition from "an old binary may still run" to "an old binary refuses every
running verb" happens at exactly one atomic rename — step 3's — and never mid-file; the transition
from "it may still clear this" to "it can do nothing at all" happens at step 4's, likewise.

**Every step is hook-reachable, and the hooks are the existing seam.** Steps 1–4 fire
`syncStepHook(SyncStageInitializing, 3|0|1|2)` in that order — index `3` is new, indices `0`–`2`
are the shipped ones, bound to the artefact each announces rather than to a position — so a test
can inject a failure or a crash at every boundary: capture, claim, sentinel, payload, and (through
the existing removers/restorer seam of §23.1 item 4) inside each rollback step. §12.2c rule 5's
"exactly one new hook site" is superseded by "exactly **two**": `syncStepHook(SyncStageRebasing,
-1)` before the first post-claim revalidation probe, and `syncStepHook(SyncStageInitializing, 3)`
after this arm's capture and above its guard claim. No new hook type, variable or stage is
introduced.

**Cells that do not upgrade (total):**

1. **Plan-only.** `--plan --continue` writes nothing at all, at any version, on any route: it never
   reaches an executing handler (§3.3 step 6, §18.1). Its document publishes the flag-origin limits
   of §13.2 and says so; a plan that persisted an upgrade would mutate state while claiming not to.
2. **A refusal before the first mutation need not upgrade — and a proceeding guarded route must.**
   Any refusal at or above the declared position leaves the subject exactly as found: the trigger's
   conjunct 4 is not satisfied, so nothing is written, and every "nothing was written" claim in
   §12.3, §22.14b, §22.14c and §22.28 stands unchanged. A refusal **below** the position — a JIT
   `revalidation-mismatch`, a rebase conflict, a validation failure — legitimately leaves the
   **upgraded** v3 state, which is precisely the state the next continuation must see.
3. **An already-guarded subject.** A `state_version: 3` payload/transaction is not rewritten by
   this rule; a conflicting supplied limit is rank 7 `guard-limit-mismatch` with the persisted
   value still effective (§13.2), and no key is touched.
4. **An unarmed continuation of a pre-guarded subject.** It never reaches a guarded route at all,
   writes no upgrade, and keeps the shipped bytes of §17.1.

**Consequences (binding):**

a. **The next flagless continuation is guarded, and cannot drop the limits.** After the upgrade the
   subject satisfies `state.Payload.StateVersion >= internal.SyncRunStateGuardedVersion` /
   `internal.TransactionGuarded(tx)`, so a later `tws sync <f> --continue` with **no** flag
   dispatches to `handleGuardedScopedSyncContinue`, to `handleGuardedLegacySyncContinue`'s envelope
   arm, or to `ContinueCheckoutSync`'s guarded arm (§19.2, §13.6 rule 4d), resolves both limits as
   `persisted-payload`/`persisted-transaction`, and refuses over them exactly as the arming
   invocation would have. A resume that completes over a persisted limit is the defect this rule
   exists to prevent.
b. **Route and verb semantics are unchanged by the upgrade.** Because `route` is inherited rather
   than decided, every route-derived answer is the answer the subject already gave: I20 refuses the
   same trigger flags, the deferred half of I7 gives the same verdict (a legacy subject still lets
   `--abort` win, §13.6 rules 4a/4b/4c), the continuation gates are the same gates, and the
   executor is the same executor.
c. **The upgraded run's next invocation sees the cell the envelope implies.** For the
   `.sync-state.yaml` arm that is the shipped **cell-5** sentence set and the shipped cell-5
   `--abort` arm rather than the legacy ones — shipped bytes, shipped verbs, reachable only after a
   control flag was used, exactly as for a guarded legacy fresh run (§13.6 rule 4, ledger row 9).
   Where the setup itself was interrupted, the next invocation sees whichever crash window it
   stopped in: **cell 7 (or cell 1) beside a stale guard**, where the subject is untouched and
   `--abort` clears both artefacts through §12.8a/§12.8, or **cell 4 over a valid backup sentinel**,
   whose three verbs are the recovery arm (`--continue`), the discarding clear
   (`--abort`) and the fail-closed refusal (plain) of §12.8b — reachable only after a control flag
   was used, and each declared in §17.2.
d. **Downgrade fails closed, and that is the declared cost.** A `v1.2.15` binary meeting the
   upgraded state refuses with the exact shipped sentences of §13.6 rule 5 — including for a run
   that *started* unguarded. Arming a limit on a continuation is therefore what makes that run's
   state v3, and it is declared in §17.2 and in §13.6 rule 8 rows 16–19.
e. **No stream byte, argv, exit code or gate sentence changes.** The upgrade writes a state file;
   it prints nothing, runs no process, and takes no lock beyond the one its route already holds.

**Save failure (exact: handling, preservation, message).** Every writer named above is atomic —
the shipped `SaveSyncRunState`/`SaveCheckoutTransaction`, and `setupGuardedLegacyRunState`'s
conditional sentinel write plus its payload write — so each file is either replaced whole or left
untouched; no partial state exists. When a write, a claim or a boundary hook returns an error the
invocation:

1. **performs no Git mutation.** It returns at the declared position, above the executor call, so
   no ref, index or working tree is touched by this invocation;
2. **preserves the state it found.** The pre-upgrade payload/transaction is still on disk,
   byte-identical, and is still resumable — by this binary (unguarded, exactly as before the
   attempt) and by an older one. On the `.sync-state.yaml` arm the rollback of the four-step table
   above removes the payload it wrote, undoes its own sentinel replacement conditionally —
   restoring the captured bytes over it, or removing exactly those sentinel bytes on the fresh
   route — and only then releases the guard it claimed, so a **successful** rollback leaves a
   byte-identical `.sync-state.yaml` and no payload, sentinel or guard; a **failed** rollback leaves
   the measured residue (`{payload, sentinel, guard}`, `{sentinel, guard}` or `{guard}`) — none of
   which loses the prior document — and says so in the sentence of rule 3;
3. **returns the shipped sentence of that step, marker-free**, at exit `1` — `write scoped sync
   state: %w` on the external scoped arm, `persist transaction: %w` on the checkout arm, and
   `read sync state: %w` (the one **new** sentence in this rule, because no shipped path performs
   that read) / `ClaimSyncRunGuard`'s own error /
   `write sync sentinel: %w` (or §13.6 rule 2c's changed-file sentence) /
   `write scoped sync state: %w` on the `.sync-state.yaml` arm, in that order of occurrence. Where
   that arm's rollback itself failed, the sentence gains exactly the suffix declared above —
   `; recovery state preserved: <residue> — clear it with: tws sync <f> --abort` — and nothing
   else. In every cell it is **not** a `*PlanGuardRefusalError` and carries **no** `plan-guard: `
   line: the guard did not refuse, a write failed, and §6.4's anchored marker names guard verdicts
   only. The suffix is deliberately spelled `recovery state preserved: ` and is **not** the 17-byte
   `state-preserved: ` marker prefix of §6.4, which no writer failure may emit;
4. **declares its residue honestly.** On the external scoped arm `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` has already
   run, so `.sync-run.lock` names this now-exited process — exactly the residue any crash between
   the reclaim and the first rebase leaves. The next `--continue` reclaims it through the shipped
   `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable`/`ReclaimSyncRunGuard` pair (§12.4) and `tws sync <f> --abort`
   clears it (§12.8); nothing new is required to recover. On the checkout arm the run holds
   `.checkout-sync.lock`, which its shipped failure path releases exactly as it does today. On the
   `.sync-state.yaml` arm a successful rollback leaves nothing at all; a failed one leaves
   `{payload, sentinel, guard}` (cell 5, shipped `--abort` arm), `{sentinel, guard}` (cell 4 over a
   valid backup sentinel: resumable through §12.3's recovery arm, clearable through §12.8b) or
   `{guard}` beside the restored subject (cell 7 with a guard on the continuation arm, cell 1 with a
   guard on the fresh route: clearable through §12.8a and §12.8 respectively), and the sentence
   names which.

### 13.3 `RemainingRebaseEntries` (normative, the only producer of a continuation's rows)

External:

```text
universe  := order                                   // the invocation's SINGLE TopoSort result,
                                                     // which its caller derived NOW from the
                                                     // current stack.yaml — never the persisted
                                                     // Pending list, and never a second sort
                                                     // (§9.1a rule 3)
selected  := run.selects(name)                       // scoped: rebuilt from payload.Selected;
                                                     // legacy: every entry — run == nil, or a
                                                     // run whose Route is legacy (§12.3), whose
                                                     // persisted Selected is provenance only
done      := set(Completed) ∪ {FailedBranch}          // read from the payload on a scoped or
                                                     // envelope arm, and from the legacy
                                                     // `.sync-state.yaml` on the cell-7 arm
                                                     // (§12.3); never from CompletedIndices
remaining := [e ∈ universe | selected(e) ∧ e ∉ done]  // in that order
```

The "re-derived now" property is a property of the **caller**: the stack is loaded and sorted at
§13.7a step 4 (external plan), at the guarded routes' subject-read step (§12.2b, §12.3) or inside
`InspectCheckoutPlan` (§13.7), always in this invocation, and the resulting `order` is what arrives
here. A `RemainingRebaseEntries` that loaded or sorted for itself would be the invocation's second
sort and could disagree with the document's own row order.

Persisted `Pending` is informational only and MUST NOT drive the row set. `--local-only` anchors
remain rows as `skipped-anchor`. A push-stage interruption yields `remaining == []` and is still
work when `push.targets[]` is non-empty — which it is exactly when the payload records entries in
`Completed`/`FailedBranch` that are absent from `Pushed` (§14.1a rule 10).

Checkout stage table (exact):

| `tx.Stage` | Current index | Later indices |
|---|---|---|
| `planned` | included | included |
| `switched` | included — as the pinned-destination arm of §13.3a | included |
| `rebasing` | included | included |
| `conflict` | excluded | included |
| `rebased` | excluded | included |
| `validating` | excluded | included |
| `restoring` | none | none — the restore itself is the remaining work |
| `completed` | none | none — the finalize work (push retry, transaction delete, lock release) is the remaining work |

**The two rows-less stages still carry restore work, and `restore.applies` says so.** Neither
`restoring` nor `completed` contributes a rebase row, but both describe a checkout run with real
remaining lifecycle work, so both publish `restore.applies: true` (§14.4's lifecycle definition):
`restoring` resumes through `restoreOriginal` **then** `finalizeCleanup`, while `completed` resumes
through `finalizeCleanup` **alone** (`internal/checkout_sync.go`'s `StageCompleted` arm), which is
why the latter publishes `will_switch_head: false`, carries none of the three restore-target tokens,
and still publishes `deletes_transaction: true` and `releases_lock: true`. A `completed`-stage
document publishing `restore.applies: false` fails §22.33e.

**Additional projections, and the `restoring` arm's push cell is a conjunct, not a constant.**
`restoring` keeps `intent.push` **exactly as the transaction persisted it**, and its push
projection is therefore conditional on that value: the shipped arm can only drop a push the run was
going to perform. The two cells are total and neither may be spelled the other way:

| persisted `intent.push` | `push.targets[]` | `push.executable` | `push.blocked_by[]` | `push.scope` | `push-dropped-restoring` warning | `restore.push_dropped` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `true` | `[]` | `false` | `["push-dropped-restoring"]` | the §14.1 checkout rule (`transaction-plan`) | emitted | `true` |
| `false` | `[]` | **`null`** | `[]` | **`none`** | **not emitted** | **`false`** |

The second row is **not an exception to §14.3** — it *is* §14.3's `intent.push: false` cell,
reached on this stage like on any other: a transaction that never intended to push has no push for
the restore to displace, so `executable: false` would publish a known negative for a question the
route never asked (§4.7), the `push-dropped-restoring` token and warning would name a dropped push
that never existed, and `restore.push_dropped: true` would claim the restore displaced it (§14.4).
`push.targets[]` is `[]` in **both** rows — a known-empty set, because the `restoring` arm projects
no target either way — and only `executable`, `blocked_by[]`, `scope`, the warning and
`push_dropped` move with the conjunct. Both rows remain approvable restore work under an effective
limit. `completed` projects real push-retry targets and may mint a real token; its `restore` object
is the `finalizeCleanup`-only cell of §14.4 (`applies: true`, `will_switch_head: false`,
`deletes_transaction`/`releases_lock` `true`, `push_dropped: false` — that arm **performs** the
pending push rather than dropping it). `CompletedIndices`
MUST NOT be used as the remaining-work source.

Plan, guard seam and JIT seam consume the **same** `RemainingRebaseEntries` result, so the document,
the seams and the token cannot disagree.

### 13.3a The `switched` stage is a pinned-destination arm (exactness rule)

`resumeFromSwitched` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:933-939`) calls `doRebase` **directly**. Unlike
`processBranch` (`:1024-1030`) it does **not** re-resolve the base: it consumes
`tx.Plan[tx.CurrentIndex]` exactly as persisted. The continuation planner, the guard seam and the
JIT seam MUST model that arm as it is, not as `processBranch` would have behaved:

| Fact | `Stage: switched` (`resumeFromSwitched` → `doRebase`) | `Stage: planned`/`rebasing` (`processBranch` → `doRebase`) |
|---|---|---|
| Commands run for this row | `git rebase` only — **no** `git checkout` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:933-939`) | `git checkout <entry.Branch>` (`:1041`), then `git rebase` |
| Arm predicate | `entry.LastBaseSHA != "" && entry.LastBaseSHA != entry.NewBaseSHA`, evaluated over the **persisted** `NewBaseSHA` | the same predicate, evaluated after `entry.NewBaseSHA = gitResolveRef(opts.RepoDir, entry.Base)` |
| `onto` arm argv | `git rebase --no-fork-point --onto <persisted NewBaseSHA> <LastBaseSHA>` | `git rebase --no-fork-point --onto <freshly resolved NewBaseSHA> <LastBaseSHA>` |
| `plain` arm argv | `git rebase --no-fork-point <entry.Base>` — Git resolves the ref **at command time** | identical shape, same late resolution |
| `destination.sha` | the persisted `NewBaseSHA`, published verbatim; the planner MUST NOT call `gitResolveRef(entry.Base)` to produce it | the value the executor just resolved |
| `replay.upstream_*` / `range` | the **`onto` arm's upstream is the persisted `LastBaseSHA`** — the recorded cutoff — exactly as on any `onto` row (§10.1 rule 1); the persisted `NewBaseSHA` is the *destination*, never the upstream. The plain arm's upstream is the current resolution of `entry.Base` (`determinacy: snapshot` absent a usable cutoff) | identical rule; only the destination differs, being re-resolved |
| `mutation.will_switch_head` | `false` — nothing switches; HEAD is already where the interrupted run left it | `true` |
| Drift check | compares the **persisted** `NewBaseSHA` against itself (it cannot move) plus the row's real mutable facts: current HEAD identity (rule 5), head tip, candidate identity and digest, holders, dirt, in-progress rebase | compares the freshly resolvable base ref, head tip, candidates, holders, dirt |

Binding consequences:

1. **No re-resolution before `doRebase` on the `switched` arm.** A planner or JIT probe that
   resolves `entry.Base` and then refuses because it now points elsewhere raises a *spurious*
   `revalidation-mismatch` (§10.3): the executor will never read that resolution. The base ref
   moving is, on this arm, simply not a fact of the run.
2. **The plain arm is genuinely late-bound.** Because the argv carries `entry.Base` and Git
   resolves it when the process starts, the row publishes `destination.sha` as a **snapshot** of
   the current resolution, `replay.determinacy: snapshot` when no usable cutoff pins the range, and
   the JIT seam re-probes that ref — the one fact the executor really re-reads.
3. **The document, the destination, the argv and the fingerprint all reflect the arm actually
   selected**, computed from persisted `LastBaseSHA`/`NewBaseSHA` for `switched` and from the
   re-resolved pair for `planned`/`rebasing`. Two continuations of the same transaction at
   different stages may therefore legitimately publish different destinations and different
   fingerprints; that is the executor's own behaviour, published.
4. `RemainingRebaseEntries` row **membership** is unchanged by this rule — `switched` includes the
   current index (§13.3); this rule fixes only what that row *says*.
5. **HEAD identity is a precondition of this arm, and the plan/guard route enforces it.** Because
   `resumeFromSwitched` issues no `git checkout`, `git rebase` acts on **whatever branch HEAD is
   on**, not necessarily `tx.Plan[tx.CurrentIndex].Branch`. The shipped executor neither checks nor
   publishes that; a run resumed from a different branch silently rebases the wrong branch onto the
   persisted destination.
   - **The plan reads current HEAD.** A `--plan --continue` over a `switched` transaction resolves
     the current branch with the shipped detached-safe probe (`gitCurrentBranch`,
     `internal/checkout_sync.go:330-338`) and publishes it: the row's facts are computed for
     `entry.Branch`, and `state.head` carries the measured `{detached, branch}` pair (§4.5).
   - **Mismatch is rank 4 `preflight-refused`**, on that row, with `runnable: false` and a detail
     naming the persisted entry branch, the measured HEAD (or `detached`) and the two real exits —
     check out the persisted branch, or `tws sync <f> --abort`. A detached HEAD is the same
     refusal. On the **guarded** route the same fact refuses at the continuation guard seam, before
     `resumeTransaction`, marker-carrying (§6.4, §7.1 rank 4), and moves no ref.
   - **The unguarded shipped path is unchanged**: no probe is added, no sentence changes, and a
     no-control `tws sync <f> --continue` behaves exactly as it ships. The check is a
     guard-introduced preflight, reachable only with a control flag or `--plan`.
   - The JIT seam of `resumeFromSwitched` re-asserts the same identity immediately before
     `doRebase`, because HEAD is a mutable fact the very next command reads.
6. **The persisted destination must still exist, and that is the only probe this arm performs on
   it.** `--onto <persisted NewBaseSHA>` fails outright if the object is gone — a pruned,
   garbage-collected, re-cloned or manually rewritten repository can lose it while the transaction
   survives — so the plan and the JIT seam run exactly one existence probe:

   ```text
   git -C <opts.RepoDir> rev-parse --verify <persisted NewBaseSHA>^{commit}
   ```

   - **It resolves the persisted SHA, never `entry.Base`.** Rule 1 is untouched: no ref is
     re-resolved, the destination is not recomputed, and a moved `entry.Base` remains a non-fact of
     this arm. The probe asks one question — "does the commit this run is pinned to still exist?" —
     and its answer cannot change the destination, only whether the run can proceed.
   - **A missing or unpeelable object is the existing rank 5.7 `base-ref-missing` hard blocker**
     on that row, with `runnable: false`, `strategy: unknown`, `argv: null` and
     `replay.reason: base-ref-missing` per §4.2. **No new refusal kind and no new rank is
     introduced**; §7.1 is unchanged. The `detail` names the persisted SHA and the transaction
     entry, and the two real exits: `tws sync <f> --abort`, or restore the object.
   - **The upstream is unaffected.** The cutoff stays the persisted `LastBaseSHA` on the `onto`
     arm (rule 1's table), and this probe never becomes an upstream source; a document that
     published the destination SHA as `replay.upstream_sha` would be describing a different run.
   - **It runs on the plan and guarded routes only**, once per invocation per `switched` row, and
     again at the JIT seam immediately before `doRebase` for the same reason HEAD identity is
     re-asserted there. The **unguarded** resume is unchanged: it adds no probe and keeps Git's own
     failure sentence if the object is gone.
   - The plain arm has no twin of this rule: it carries `entry.Base` in the argv and Git resolves
     it at command time (rule 2), so its late binding is the fact, and its `revalidation-mismatch`
     behaviour is unchanged.

**Tests (§22.25b, §22.25c, §23).** A transaction parked at `switched` whose `entry.Base` has since been moved to a
different commit: the plan publishes the persisted `NewBaseSHA` as the destination and the persisted
`LastBaseSHA` as the upstream, the guarded resume performs
`--onto <persisted NewBaseSHA> <LastBaseSHA>` (argv sidecar), no `revalidation-mismatch` is raised,
and the executed result matches the unguarded control byte for byte. The plain-arm twin
(`LastBaseSHA` empty) publishes the snapshot destination, passes `entry.Base` in the argv, and
*does* raise `revalidation-mismatch` when the approved snapshot has moved. A `planned`-stage control
asserts the re-resolving behaviour is unchanged. HEAD identity is covered in both directions: with
HEAD on the persisted `entry.Branch` the plan is `runnable: true` and the guarded resume proceeds;
with HEAD on another branch, and again with a detached HEAD, the plan publishes rank 4
`preflight-refused` at exit `0`, the guarded resume exits `1` with one marker line and no ref
movement, and the **unguarded** control still performs the shipped (wrong-branch) rebase, proving
the shipped path was not changed.
The persisted-destination rule 6 is covered in both directions: with the object present, the argv
sidecar shows **exactly one** `rev-parse --verify <persisted NewBaseSHA>^{commit}` and **zero**
`rev-parse` of `entry.Base`, and the run proceeds; with the object destroyed (a fixture that
rewrites the branch and expires the reflog, then prunes) the plan publishes rank 5.7
`base-ref-missing` on that row with `runnable: false` at exit `0`, the guarded resume refuses at
exit `1` before any rebase with one marker line, `replay.upstream_sha` still equals the persisted
`LastBaseSHA` in both cells, and the unguarded control still runs and fails with Git's own
sentence, unchanged.

### 13.3b Checkout continuation commands, tracked dirt and autostash, per stage

A checkout continuation's hazard profile is decided by **which command runs next**, not by the fact
that the run is a checkout run. The shipped resume dispatch (`resumeTransaction`,
`internal/checkout_sync.go:866-931`) issues a different command per stage, and neither
`ContinueCheckoutSync` nor any resume arm re-checks dirtiness. The plan models exactly this:

| `tx.Stage` | Commands the resume runs for the **current** index | Dirt consequence for that row |
|---|---|---|
| `planned` | the shipped `StagePlanned, StageRebasing` arm: **if a rebase is in progress** it reclassifies to `conflict`, persists, and refuses with `rebase in progress; resolve conflicts then --continue` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:912-921`); otherwise `processBranch`: base re-resolve, `git checkout <entry.Branch>`, then `git rebase …` | the standalone checkout may fail on an overlapping dirty path, and — if it succeeds — the rebase then reads the same dirty tree |
| `switched` | `resumeFromSwitched` → `doRebase` only: **no checkout** (§13.3a) | the `git rebase` is the next command that reads the tree |
| `rebasing` | the same shipped arm as `planned`, sentence included; otherwise `executeTransaction` re-enters `processBranch`, i.e. checkout then rebase | as `planned` |
| `conflict` | no checkout and no rebase: the rebase-in-progress short-circuit (`internal/checkout_sync.go:869-872`), then the **ancestry gate** `gitIsAncestor(opts.RepoDir, entry.NewBaseSHA, entry.Branch)` (`:875-881`), then `gitResolveRef`, the post-SHA write and the fall-through into `resumeFromRebased` | none for this row; later rows are `processBranch` rows |
| `rebased` | `resumeFromRebased` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:941-953`): the **ancestry gate** `gitIsAncestor(opts.RepoDir, entry.NewBaseSHA, entry.Branch)` **first**, then validation, then the next index — never validation alone | none for this row |
| `validating` | `resumeFromValidating`: re-runs validation, then the next index | none for this row |
| `restoring` | `resumeFromRestoring` → `restoreOriginal`: `git checkout <tx.OriginalBranch>` (plus the `OriginalHEAD` equality check when the branch was not in the plan), then `finalizeCleanup` | the restore checkout may fail on an overlapping dirty path — rank 4.5 `restore-blocked` covers the *probed* cells (§7.4); dirt itself is the `checkout-dirty-present` warning |
| `completed` | `finalizeCleanup`: the push retry loop when `opts.Push`, then transaction delete + lock release | none |

Binding consequences, all row-scoped and all published:

1. **Where the next command for the row is a `git rebase`** — stages `planned`, `switched` and
   `rebasing`, plus every later index of any stage, which is always a `processBranch` row — tracked
   dirt is decided by the rebase's own precondition:
   - effective `rebase.autoStash` **false/unset** ⇒ the rebase refuses, so the row carries rank 5.5
     `context-dirty`, `runnable: false` (§7.1). This is **not** softened to a warning merely because
     the mode is checkout;
   - effective `rebase.autoStash` **true** ⇒ `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm: true`, the
     `autostash-across-switch` warning (the closed eight-kind enum's autostash member, §4.6), and
     `context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict: true`. The `detail` states precisely whether the stash
     is applied in place (`switched`, no checkout intervenes) or across the arm's own checkout;
   - effective `rebase.autoStash` **unknown** (probe failed) ⇒ the two autostash fields are `null`
     and the dirt fact is published without a verdict, per §4.7.
2. **Where the arm additionally runs a standalone `git checkout` first** — `planned`, `rebasing`,
   `restoring` and every later index — tracked dirt keeps its **residual** non-blocking
   `checkout-dirty-present` warning even when autostash applies, because `rebase.autoStash` cannot
   reach a standalone checkout and a checkout fails only where a dirty path overlaps the
   HEAD-to-target difference, which is not decidable at plan time. **The admission predicate
   therefore promises nothing about that checkout** (§4.6): `runnable: true` here means "the guard
   admits this resume", never "the checkout will succeed".
3. **No rescue is ever published.** No text, warning `detail` or document field may say autostash
   "rescues", "protects" or "restores" the tree, and `runnable: true` beside an applicable
   autostash never implies clean completion (§18.4).
4. **Fresh checkout runs are untouched.** `RunCheckoutSync` refuses a dirty tree before any lock,
   fetch or rebase (`working tree is dirty; commit or stash changes before checkout sync`), which is
   the shipped rank 3 `state-refused` fact projected by §13.7 — so no fresh checkout row is ever
   an autostash row.
5. The warning enum stays **closed at eight** (§4.6): this subsection reuses `checkout-dirty-present`
   and `autostash-across-switch` and adds no kind.

**Tests (§22.13e, §23).** For each of the eight stages, with a tracked-dirty tree and with
`rebase.autoStash` true, false and unreadable: the projected row's `context.dirty`,
`context.autostash`, `context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm`,
`context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict`, its blocker/warning set and its `runnable`, each asserted
against the **real** resumed behaviour of the same fixture (the `switched` dirt case really is
refused by `git rebase` with autostash off, and really is stashed with it on; the `planned` case
really can fail in `git checkout` on an overlapping path and really can succeed on a
non-overlapping one). The unguarded control's exit code, sentence and process count are unchanged
in every cell.

### 13.4 Continuation approval scope

A continuation document always publishes `approval.scope: remaining-work` and mints a **fresh**
remaining-work token. The original full-run token never authorizes a continuation: presenting it
yields `approval-mismatch`. No approval is ever persisted, so an interrupted run is re-approved
against live remaining work rather than a stored verdict.

### 13.5 Continuation gate projection

Every shipped continuation gate is projected on the `--plan` route as a `blockers[]` row with
`runnable: false`, `refusal.kind: state-refused`, the **exact shipped sentence** as `detail`, and
exit `0`. On the executing route the shipped check fires unchanged, marker-free, exit `1`. The
projected set includes (sentences byte-identical): the external and checkout v2 axis mismatch
`cannot change %s on --continue: the run was started with %s=%s and this invocation requests %s`;
`nothing to continue — no sync in progress`; `no transaction to continue: %w`;
`rebase still in progress in %s; resolve conflicts, run git add . && git rebase --continue, then
retry`; `rebase still in progress; finish resolving conflicts then run --continue again` (the
checkout `conflict` stage, `internal/checkout_sync.go:871`);
**`rebase in progress; resolve conflicts then --continue`** (the checkout `planned`/`rebasing`
stages, `internal/checkout_sync.go:920` — a different sentence from the `conflict` arm's, projected
verbatim and never merged with it; on the plan route it is projected **without** the shipped
stage/`FailureKind` reclassification and without the shipped `SaveCheckoutTransaction`, per §13.7
rule 8a);
`failed branch %q no longer exists in stack`;
`resolved branch %s still does not contain its configured parent %s`;
**`after conflict resolution, %s is not descended from base %s`** (the checkout `conflict` stage's
own ancestry gate, `internal/checkout_sync.go:875-881`, reached **only** where the rebase-in-progress
short-circuit above it did not fire, evaluated through **exactly one**
`git merge-base --is-ancestor` process over the persisted pair
`gitIsAncestor(opts.RepoDir, entry.NewBaseSHA, entry.Branch)`, published **document-level**
(`entry: null`) because §13.3's stage table publishes no row for a `conflict` current index, rank 3
`state-refused` where that probe answers `false` and rank 5.9 `probe-failed` where the probe itself
fails, per §13.7 gate e);
**`%s not descended from %s after rebase`** (the checkout `rebased` stage's own ancestry gate,
`internal/checkout_sync.go:950`, projected at **rank 4** `preflight-refused` and evaluated
without the shipped `FailureKind`/`FailureMsg` assignment and without the shipped
`SaveCheckoutTransaction`, per §13.7 gate e and rule 8a);
the `syncCellRefusal` sentences;
`checkout sync transaction state version %d is newer than %d; upgrade tws or remove %s`;
`selected stack entry %q no longer exists in stack; use --abort`;
`sync guard %s does not belong to the recorded scoped run; inspect it and remove it manually`;
`sync guard held by live process %d; cannot reclaim`; I20's sentence; and
`cannot add --push to an existing transaction that was started without it; persisted push=%v wins`.
One exception: an unreadable stack on resume is rank 1 `plan-unavailable`, not `state-refused`.
A second: the checkout `rebased`-stage ancestry gate above is rank 4 `preflight-refused`, not
`state-refused` — it asks a question of **live Git ancestry** for a specific transaction row, the
same class as the `switched`-stage HEAD-identity preflight of §13.3a rule 5, rather than of a
recovery-state artefact, which is what rank 3 denotes (§7.1). It is otherwise projected like every
other gate here: `runnable: false`, the shipped sentence byte-identical as `detail`, exit `0`.
A third: **either** ancestry gate's *probe-failure* cell — `gitIsAncestor` returning an error rather
than a verdict — is rank 5.9 `probe-failed`, document-level, with the error sanitized, because an
unreadable answer is neither a state refusal nor a satisfied gate (§13.7 gate e, §7.1 rank 5.9).

**The five ancestry-shaped facts are distinct, and together they are total (binding).** Nothing in
this specification may merge them, and every ancestry question a controlled route can ask lands in
exactly one row:

| Fact | Mode / cell | When the shipped code evaluates it | Plan treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
