      `unavailable`, so `PlanPushFacts.Applies` is **true** (rule 7: `intent.push` plus a decoded
      payload), both fact halves are measured, and every row carries a real `plan-point`,
      `possibly-stale` lease — a continuation never fetches (§11.2 cause 1). An empty
      `push.targets` on that cell fails §22.33h.
   e. **Contexts follow the admitted entries, not the rebase rows.** The distinct push contexts
      `InspectExternalPlan` step 4.7 enumerates — and therefore the contexts
      `MeasurePushRemoteFacts`/`RefreshPushTrackingRefs` measure exactly once each — are the
      contexts of the entries `(Expected \ AlreadyPushed)` admits, resolved through
      `ResolvePushContext` (`entry.Repo` else the materialized worktree), **including** entries
      this invocation will push but not rebase. Where such an entry's context appears in no
      `entries[]` row — the rows-less push-only cell has no `entries[]` rows at all — the
      `context_id` join of rule 2 is **vacuous**, not violated: the id still comes from the one
      measured `PlanContextIdentities` table, and §22.33h (ii) asserts the join only over rows the
      document really publishes.
   f. **Fresh-run behaviour is unchanged by this rule.** On a fresh run `payload.Completed`,
      `payload.Pushed` and `payload.FailedBranch` are all empty, so `Expected` collapses to `E_run`
      and the membership is exactly what §14.1's fresh row already said.

### 14.2 Implicit lease baselines

`lease` = `{mode, expectation, expected_ref, expected_sha, expected_sha_freshness}` with
`mode: implicit-remote-tracking` and `expectation` ∈ `sha` \| `absent` \| `unknown`. The shipped
argv is
`git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>` with **no** explicit expectation, so the baseline is
whatever Git's own compare-and-swap resolution produces for that ref, and this section mirrors that
resolution exactly — it never models a stricter or a looser one. `unknown` is not a Git outcome at
all: it is the one cell where this projection could not read the configuration Git would resolve,
and it is published as such rather than guessed into one of Git's two answers (§14.1a rule 5a).

**Git's resolution, in the two steps it really has.** With a bare `--force-with-lease`, Git maps the
pushed ref through the remote's **fetch** refspecs and then reads the resulting remote-tracking ref;
if either step fails it expects the **null OID**, i.e. "this ref must not exist". Both steps
presuppose that this projection could **read** the configuration — where it could not, neither step
is modelled at all and the row is the `unknown` cell below:

1. **Mapping.** The destination is the first matching **non-negative** fetch refspec, in configured
   order. **Negative refspecs (`^…`) are skipped by this mapping, not applied to it**: they
   constrain what a *fetch* transfers, and Git's refspec query ignores them when asking "where does
   `refs/heads/<branch>` land?". A negative entry therefore **never** removes the mapping and is
   **never**, on its own, a reason to publish `expectation: absent`.
2. **Reading.** If the mapping exists, Git reads that remote-tracking ref. A ref that exists yields
   `expectation: sha` with its **current** value; a mapping that does not exist, or a mapped ref
   that is absent or unreadable, yields the null OID — `expectation: absent`.

The published cell is exactly that, plus the one cell Git never reaches because the projection
could not read its inputs, and nothing else:

| Cell | `expectation` | `expected_ref` | `expected_sha` | `expected_sha_freshness` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| positive mapping exists, mapped tracking ref **exists** | `sha` | the mapped ref | its current value, full 40/64-hex | `fresh` **only** where the row's facts carry `TrackingPhase: post-fetch`, `MappingReadOK: true`, `TrackingReadOK: true` **and** `FetchedThisRun: true` (§14.1a rules 7–8); `possibly-stale` in every other cell — **and `possibly-stale` unconditionally where a negative refspec also matches the branch**, per the rule below, which overrides even that cell |
| positive mapping exists, mapped tracking ref **absent**, inventory read (`TrackingPhase` ∈ `post-fetch` \| `plan-point`) | `absent` | the mapped ref (it is known; it is the ref that must not exist) | `null` | `fresh` — the absence was read by this invocation, after its own fetch decision was carried out |
| positive mapping exists, inventory **unreadable** (`TrackingReadOK: false`, `TrackingPhase: unread`) | `absent` | the mapped ref | `null` | `possibly-stale` — nothing was read, so nothing may be called fresh (§14.1a rule 5) |
| mapping **read**, and **no** positive mapping (no refspec covers the branch, or no remote named `origin` is configured) | `absent` | `null` | `null` | `fresh` — the configuration really was read, and it really maps nothing |
| mapping **unreadable** (`MappingReadOK: false`) — the identity or config read failed | `unknown` | `null` | `null` | `possibly-stale` — and the document carries that context's rank 5.9 `probe-failed` blocker (§14.1a rule 5a) |

`expectation: absent` is **stricter** than a SHA expectation, not an unprotected force: it makes
Git refuse the push if the remote ref exists at all. An explicit lease is never claimed and never
added.

**The baseline is read after the fetch, and that is what makes `fresh` mean anything.** The whole
inventory — the existence of the mapped ref and its value — is read by the single
`RefreshPushTrackingRefs` call of §14.1a rule 7, placed after this route's fetch decision has been
carried out and before `BuildRebasePlan`. Two consequences are binding and neither may be softened:

- a route that fetched publishes a baseline measured **after** its own fetch, so the `sha` cell's
  value is the value the projected `git push` would really compare against, and the `absent` cell
  is not an artefact of having looked too early. Because the lease's expectation, ref and SHA are
  approval-tuple members (§8.3), a pre-fetch baseline would also bind a token to refs the same
  invocation then moved;
- a route that did **not** fetch — `--no-fetch`, any `--continue` (§11.2 cause 1), a suppressed
  fetch of causes 4–6, or any refusing pre-fetch gate — publishes the current tracking ref with
  `TrackingPhase: plan-point`, and therefore `possibly-stale` on every `sha` row. That is the
  honest label: the value is real and current, and nothing refreshed it.

**A negative refspec makes a resolved baseline unrefreshable, and that is a freshness fact.**
Where the configured refspec set contains a negative entry matching the pushed branch **and** a
positive entry maps it, the mapping and the tracking ref both survive — so the row stays
`expectation: sha` with the tracking ref's current value — but **no fetch of this configuration can
ever update that value**, because the negative entry excludes the ref from every transfer. The
baseline is therefore stale the moment the remote moves, and it stays stale however many times the
operator fetches. Such a row publishes `expected_sha_freshness: possibly-stale` **unconditionally**,
including immediately after a successful fetch of that context, and the accompanying human/JSON
reading is "this lease compares against a ref your fetch configuration will never refresh".

Two earlier readings are **withdrawn**, and no text may restore either:

- "a negative refspec breaks the mapping, so the cell is `{absent, null, null, fresh}`" — false:
  Git's mapping skips negative refspecs, so a branch with a covering positive refspec keeps its
  tracking destination and its SHA expectation. Publishing `absent` there would describe a
  *stricter* baseline than Git sends and would tell an operator their push is protected by a
  null-OID check that Git never performs;
- "a negative refspec is irrelevant to freshness" — also false: it is precisely the fact that makes
  the resolved value permanently, unavoidably stale.

`possibly-stale` therefore has one meaning with four sources: a resolved baseline this invocation
did not or could not refresh (no fetch, a suppressed fetch, a failed fetch child, a successful
fetch that contacted a remote other than `origin`, or a successful `origin` fetch of a **different**
common dir), a baseline that could not be read at all (`TrackingPhase: unread`), a resolved
baseline no fetch could ever refresh (a covering negative refspec), **and** a mapping that could
not be read at all (`MappingReadOK: false`, the `unknown` row). `expected_sha_freshness`
remains never-`null` in every cell (§4.4a, §22.33f).

**The producer, stated as a function of the measured facts (§14.1a).** `ResolvePushLease(gitBranch,
facts)` is the only implementation of this subsection, and it reads exactly seven members of
`PlanPushRemoteFacts`, in this order:

| Step | Reads | Yields |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `MappingReadOK` | `unknown` + `expected_ref: null` + `expected_sha: null` + `possibly-stale`, and **stops**: steps 1–4 are not evaluated, because there is no configuration to evaluate them over (§14.1a rule 5a) |
| 1 | `RemoteExists`, `FetchRefspecs` — the first matching **non-negative** entry, in configured order | the mapped destination ref, or "no mapping" |
| 2 | `TrackingRefs[dst]`, `TrackingReadOK` | `sha` + the current value where the key exists and the read succeeded; `absent` otherwise |
| 3 | `TrackingPhase` and `FetchedThisRun` — **only for an `expectation: sha` row**; an `absent` row is `fresh` when the inventory was read (`post-fetch` or `plan-point`) and `possibly-stale` when it was not (`unread`), per the cell table above | `fresh` **iff** `TrackingPhase == post-fetch && FetchedThisRun`; `possibly-stale` otherwise |
| 4 | `FetchRefspecs` again — any **negative** entry matching the branch, again only on an `expectation: sha` row | `possibly-stale` **unconditionally**, overriding step 3's `fresh` |

Steps 3 and 4 never revisit steps 0–2: neither the phase, the refresh verdict nor a negative entry
changes the *mapping* or the *expectation* — only the freshness label (the withdrawn readings
above). `FetchedThisRun` itself is decided **outside** this function, by §14.1a rule 8's
both-halves-read + common-dir + `origin` predicate, so `ResolvePushLease` never inspects a
`PlanFetchOutcome` and
never learns what a fetch did. The function is pure and total over those inputs, so every cell of
the table is reachable in a unit test with no repository at all, and the three real
`--force-with-lease` controls of §22.33f pin the same cells against Git itself.

### 14.3 Reachability

`push.executable` is `true` when the corresponding controlled invocation reaches the push, `false`
when a projected gate blocks it or the shipped arm drops it, and `null` in exactly the two cells
where the question was never asked:

| Cell | `intent.push` | `push.targets[]` | `push.executable` | `push.blocked_by[]` | `push.scope` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the route performs no push at all | `false` | `[]` | **`null`** | `[]` | `none` |
| nothing about the run was established (`summary.plannability: unavailable`) | either | `[]` | **`null`** | `[]` | `none` where `intent.push` is false, else the §14.1 rule |
| the described invocation reaches its push | `true` | the projected rows (legitimately `[]` when no entry is eligible) | `true` | `[]` | the §14.1 rule |
| a projected gate stops it, or the shipped arm drops it | `true` | the projected rows — the blast radius is still published | `false` | the blocking tokens | the §14.1 rule |

**Every `false` cell requires `intent.push: true`; the table's fourth row is a conjunct, not a
route.** "The shipped arm drops it" names the checkout `restoring` stage (§13.3), and that stage
reaches row 4 **only** when the transaction persisted `intent.push: true`. A `restoring` document
whose persisted `intent.push` is `false` takes row **1** — `push.targets: []`,
`push.executable: null`, `push.blocked_by: []`, `push.scope: none` — carries no
`push-dropped-restoring` token and no such warning, and publishes `restore.push_dropped: false`
(§13.3's two-cell table, §14.4). Publishing `false` there would describe a push the run never
intended.

**`intent.push: false` publishes `null`, never `false`.** `false` is a claim about a push the route
would otherwise perform — "this run wants to push and would not get there" — and a `--continue` or
a fresh run without `--push` makes no such attempt, so `false` would be an unknown published as a
known negative, which §4.7 forbids. The same reasoning gives `push.blocked_by: []`: nothing blocks
a push nobody attempts, and a document that listed the invocation's blockers there would be copying
`blockers[]`, which rule 1 of §7.5 forbids. `push.targets[]` is still `[]` — a known-empty set,
because the §14.1 rule admits nothing when the route pushes nothing — and `push.scope` is still
`none`, because that member names the projection rule, not a reachability answer.

`push.blocked_by[]` is a sorted, de-duplicated token list drawn from the closed
compositional domain of §7.5 — the effective unwaived `RefusalKind`s that stop the invocation
before the push, plus the warning-only `push-dropped-restoring`, which the `restoring` stage
contributes **only** under a persisted `intent.push: true` — and is `[]` whenever
push is executable or the answer is `null`. It is **not** a copy of `blockers[]`. `push.targets[]`
remains the projected blast radius even when `push.executable` is `false`.

`--plan --push` is legal, projects all of the above, and pushes nothing. `--plan` never pushes on
any route. Shipped push behaviour, argv and ordering are otherwise unchanged.

### 14.4 Restore

```text
restore = {applies, will_switch_head, target_branch, target_sha, target_source, executable,
           blocked_by[], deletes_transaction, releases_lock, push_dropped}
```

**`restore` (10 members, closed)** — the normative field table; the §4.1 key-set test descends into
it exactly as it does into `fetch` and `push` (§4.4a):

| Field | Type | Nullability | Domain / rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| `restore.applies` | bool | never | `true` **iff checkout restore/finalize lifecycle work remains** on the described route — that is, iff the route will call `restoreOriginal`, or `finalizeCleanup`, or both. It is **not** "the route will move HEAD"; that question is `will_switch_head`. `true` for a fresh checkout run with a non-empty built plan, for every checkout continuation that reaches `restoreOriginal` (including the `restoring` stage, whose remaining work *is* the restore), **and** for a `completed`-stage continuation, whose `finalizeCleanup`-only resume still performs the push retry, the transaction delete and the lock release. `false` for **every** external document and for a fresh checkout run whose built plan is empty, which releases the lock and returns without writing a transaction, without `restoreOriginal` and without `finalizeCleanup`. It is a fact about the described route, never derived from `blocked_by[]` emptiness |
| `restore.will_switch_head` | bool | nullable | `true` when the restore really moves HEAD, `false` when it provably does not, `null` when `applies` is `true` but HEAD could not be resolved (the accompanying rank 5.9 `probe-failed` blocker disambiguates it). The comparison is **`restore.target_branch` against the branch HEAD will be on immediately before `restoreOriginal`** — the branch the route's last rebased row leaves HEAD on — and **never** against the post-run HEAD, which is the restore's own output and would make the field trivially `false` on every successful run. Always `false` — a known negative, not a `null` — where `applies` is `false`, and always `false` on a route that calls **only** `finalizeCleanup` (the `completed` stage), because that route runs no `git checkout` at all |
| `restore.target_branch` | string | nullable | the logical Git branch the restore checks out — on a `completed`-stage document, the branch the transaction recorded and would have restored to; `null` iff `applies` is `false` or the target could not be established |
| `restore.target_sha` | string | nullable | full 40/64-hex object id of that branch at snapshot time; `null` when unresolved, when the branch is missing (rank 4.5 `restore-target-missing`), or when `applies` is `false`. It is a snapshot fact, never re-read at a seam |
| `restore.target_source` | enum | nullable | `transaction` (the persisted `OriginalBranch` of the checkout transaction — the only source on **any** continuation, `completed` and `restoring` included) \| `probed-head` (the fresh run's `gitCurrentBranch` snapshot fact, §12.5a). `null` iff `applies` is `false`. It never takes a third value, and a fresh run never publishes `transaction` |
| `restore.executable` | bool | nullable | `true` when the corresponding controlled invocation reaches and can perform the remaining restore/finalize work; `false` when a projected gate stops it or a probed restore cell fails; `null` in the **three** cells where the question was never asked or never established — `restore.applies: false` (every external document, and a fresh checkout run whose built plan is empty), `summary.plannability: unavailable`, or an `applies: true` document whose target probe failed — in each of which `blocked_by[]` is legitimately `[]` (§4.7 declared exception). On a **`completed`-stage** document the value is decided by the **finalize** preconditions alone — the projected `.checkout-sync.lock` ladder, the transaction's decodability and the push-retry cell of `finalizeCleanup` — and by no restore-target question, since that route runs no `git checkout` (see the cell table). Never derived from `blockers[]`, and never `false` where `applies` is `false` |
| `restore.blocked_by[]` | array of tokens | never null | sorted, de-duplicated members of the closed compositional `RestoreBlockedKind` domain of §7.5: every effective unwaived `RefusalKind` that stops or fails the remaining restore/finalize work under the §14.3 control-flow projection, plus exactly `restore-target-missing`, `restore-target-held` and `restore-head-moved`. Those three are emitted **only** where the route really calls `restoreOriginal`, so a `completed`-stage document never carries one. `push-dropped-restoring` is **never** a member. `[]` when the work is executable, when `applies` is `false`, or when the answer is unknown |
| `restore.deletes_transaction` | bool | never | on-success effect: the run will remove `.checkout-sync.tx.yaml` through `finalizeCleanup`. `true` on **every** `applies: true` document whose route reaches `finalizeCleanup`, the `completed`-stage resume included. `false` whenever `applies` is `false` |
| `restore.releases_lock` | bool | never | on-success effect: the run will release `.checkout-sync.lock`. `true` on the same population as `deletes_transaction`, the `completed`-stage resume included. `false` whenever `applies` is `false`. Both effect fields describe the **success** path only and are never re-used to describe a refusal's cleanup (§12.7) |
| `restore.push_dropped` | bool | never | `true` **iff** the shipped `restoring` arm really drops a push it would otherwise have performed — the checkout `restoring` stage **and** a persisted `intent.push: true` (§13.3, §24.5) — which is exactly the cell that emits the `push-dropped-restoring` warning and puts that token in `push.blocked_by[]`. `false` on every other route, including a `restoring` stage whose persisted `intent.push` is `false` (which publishes `push.executable: null`, `push.blocked_by: []`, `push.scope: none` and no such warning), including the `completed` stage — whose `finalizeCleanup` **performs** the pending push rather than dropping it — and including every external document |

**Why `applies` is a lifecycle question and not a HEAD question (binding).** An earlier revision
defined `applies` as "the run will execute `restoreOriginal` **+** `finalizeCleanup`", which left the
`completed` stage — a real, reachable continuation whose remaining work is exactly the push retry,
the transaction delete and the lock release (`internal/checkout_sync.go`'s `StageCompleted` arm calls
`finalizeCleanup` and nothing else) — describable by **no** cell: it is not a fresh empty plan, it is
not external, and it does restore-adjacent lifecycle work, so publishing `applies: false` there would
have claimed a run with no restore object at all while `restore.deletes_transaction` and
`restore.releases_lock` were both really `true`. The definition is therefore the **disjunction**
(`restoreOriginal` **or** `finalizeCleanup`), and the "does HEAD move" half — which is what the old
conjunction was really reaching for — is carried by the already-declared `will_switch_head`, which
is `false` on that stage. **No member is added: `restore` still has exactly ten fields, in the same
order, and the schema version is unchanged** (§4.1, §13.3, §22.33e, §25.90).

`applies` is `true` for a checkout run with remaining restore/finalize lifecycle work, and
`false` for external and for a fresh checkout run whose built plan is empty. `target_source` ∈
`transaction` \| `probed-head`. `deletes_transaction` and `releases_lock` are on-success effects.

**`applies: false` publishes `executable: null`, never `false` — the same rule §14.3 applies to
`push.executable`, for the same reason.** `false` is a claim about restore/finalize work the route
would otherwise perform ("this run has that work and would not get there"); an external document and
an empty-plan fresh checkout run have none at all, so `false` would publish an unknown as a
known negative, which §4.7 forbids. The row is total and closed:

| Cell | `applies` | `will_switch_head` | `executable` | `blocked_by[]` | Disambiguated by |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| every **external** document, in both plan and guarded-twin fixtures | `false` | `false` | **`null`** | `[]` | `applies: false` itself, plus `target_source: null` |
| fresh **checkout** run whose built plan is empty | `false` | `false` | **`null`** | `[]` | `applies: false`, `target_branch: null` |
| nothing about the run was established (`summary.plannability: unavailable`) | `false` | `false` | **`null`** | `[]` | `summary.plannability` |
| `applies: true`, target probe failed | `true` | `true`/`false`/**`null`** | **`null`** | `[]` | the accompanying rank 5.9 `probe-failed` blocker |
| `applies: true`, restore/finalize reachable | `true` | per the field rule | `true` | `[]` | — |
| `applies: true`, a projected gate or probed restore cell stops it | `true` | per the field rule | `false` | the blocking tokens, non-empty | the tokens themselves |
| **`completed` stage** (`finalizeCleanup` only), finalize preconditions met | `true` | **`false`** | `true` | `[]` | `will_switch_head: false` beside `deletes_transaction`/`releases_lock` `true` |
| **`completed` stage**, a projected gate or the finalize preconditions stop it | `true` | **`false`** | `false` | the blocking `RefusalKind` tokens, non-empty; **never** one of the three restore-target tokens | the tokens themselves |

The `completed`-stage rows are the reason `applies` is the lifecycle disjunction: that route calls
`finalizeCleanup` and no `git checkout`, so it has real on-success effects
(`deletes_transaction: true`, `releases_lock: true`) and a real reachability question, but no HEAD
move and no restore target to be missing, held or moved. Its `target_*` members still describe the
transaction's recorded original branch (`target_source: transaction`), because that is what the
persisted document says the run was going to restore to — publishing `null` there would hide a fact
the transaction really carries. Its `executable` is decided by the finalize preconditions alone:
the projected `.checkout-sync.lock` ladder of §13.7 gate j, the transaction's decodability, and the
push-retry cell of `finalizeCleanup` (`tx.Stage == completed && opts.Push`), whose own failure is
already projected through `push` (§14.3) and contributes its `RefusalKind` here through §14.3's
control-flow projection like any other gate.

The other members keep their declared `applies: false` values and are **not** nulled with it:
`will_switch_head`, `deletes_transaction`, `releases_lock` and `push_dropped` are `false` — known
negatives about work that will not happen — while `target_branch`, `target_sha` and
`target_source` are `null`, because they name facts about a restore target that does not exist. A
document publishing `executable: false` beside `applies: false`, or `blocked_by[]` non-empty there,
fails §22.33e.

`blocked_by[]` is drawn from the closed compositional domain of §7.5: the effective `RefusalKind`s
that stop or fail the remaining restore/finalize work, plus exactly `restore-target-missing`,
`restore-target-held` and `restore-head-moved`, which are rank 4.5 `restore-blocked` and
non-waivable on **every** `applies: true` document **whose route really calls `restoreOriginal`** —
fresh **and** continuation alike (the probe-scope table below) — and are emitted on **no**
`completed`-stage document, which calls only `finalizeCleanup`.
`push-dropped-restoring` is **never** a member — it describes
the push the restore displaces, not a reason the restore cannot run — and on a `restoring` stage
that never intended to push it exists nowhere in the document at all (§13.3). The fresh-run hazard
is the `restore-head-collateral-risk` warning of §7.4.

**The three probed cells have producers, and `restore-target-held` has exactly one (normative).**
Each is evaluated on **every** document whose `restore.applies` is `true` **and whose route really
calls `restoreOriginal`** — i.e. on every fresh checkout run with a non-empty plan and every
continuation whose stage reaches the restore, fresh **and** continuation alike, never
only on a continuation, and on **no** `completed`-stage document, where the question does not arise
because no `git checkout` runs — and each is document-level (`entry: null`), rank 4.5
`restore-blocked`, non-waivable, contributing its own token to `restore.blocked_by[]` and setting
`restore.executable: false`:

| Cell | Producer | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| `restore-target-missing` | `VerifyGitRef` over `refs/heads/<restore.target_branch>` in the checkout repository, from the same snapshot that filled `restore.target_sha` | the branch the restore will check out does not exist. `restore.target_sha` is `null` beside it |
| **`restore-target-held`** | the rule below, over that context's entry in the **one** holder index the checkout snapshot already built (§14.4's index rule, §19.1) | that branch is held by a **foreign** worktree — checked out, or held mid merge-rebase, apply-rebase or bisect — so `git checkout` will refuse it |
| `restore-head-moved` | the transaction's persisted `OriginalHEAD` compared against the snapshot tip of `restore.target_branch`, in the one cell the shipped `restoreOriginal` performs that equality check (`internal/checkout_sync.go`'s `restoring` arm, §13.3b) | the recorded original HEAD is no longer that branch's tip, so restoring would move the operator's branch |

**Probe scope is the same on a fresh run; only the reachable values differ (normative, total).**
An earlier revision called these "the three probed **continuation** cells", which left a fresh
`applies: true` document with three unanswered questions and made `restore.executable` untotal
there. They are answered on both arms, from the same snapshot, by the same producers — what changes
is what the answers *can* be, because a fresh run's `restore.target_branch` is its own
`probed-head` value (§14.4's `target_source`), i.e. the branch HEAD was on when the run started:

| Cell | Fresh run (`target_source: probed-head`) | Continuation (`target_source: transaction`) |
|---|---|---|
| `restore-target-missing` | evaluated; normally **`false`** — the target *is* the branch the snapshot just resolved HEAD to, so the ref exists by construction. It can still be `true` in the one honest cell where the probe itself could not establish the ref, which is **not** this token but §14.4's probe-failure cell (`executable: null`) | evaluated; may be **`true`** — the persisted `OriginalBranch` can have been deleted since the interrupted run recorded it |
| `restore-target-held` | evaluated; normally **`false`** by **self-exclusion**, not by omission — the run's own checkout holds the target, and clause 1 excludes exactly that holder. A **foreign** holder is not evaluated away: where the index really reports one (a foreign detached `rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply`/`bisect` record naming the same branch), the token is emitted on a fresh run exactly as on a continuation | evaluated; may be **`true`** by any of the four mechanisms |
| `restore-head-moved` | evaluated; **`false`**, and it is a *known* negative rather than an unknown: there is no persisted `OriginalHEAD` on a fresh run, so nothing can have moved away from it, and the run has not yet moved a ref at the snapshot point. The fresh-run hazard that resembles it — a restore target inside the projected collateral upper bound — is the `restore-head-collateral-risk` **warning** of §7.4, `runnable: true`, and it is **not** this token | evaluated; may be **`true`** — the recorded original HEAD is no longer the target's tip |

Binding consequences: (i) `restore.blocked_by[]` on a fresh `applies: true` document is `[]`
**because all three were evaluated and none held**, never because they were skipped — and a fresh
document that carries `restore-target-held` from a real foreign holder is correct, not a bug;
(ii) §7.4 fixes their **rank**, which is the same on both arms, and says so explicitly; its earlier
"three probed **continuation** cells" wording is withdrawn there and MUST NOT be reintroduced as a
scope restriction anywhere; (iii) the
`restore.executable` cell table above is therefore **total** for every `applies: true` document on
both arms — `true` when all three are false and no projected gate stops the work, `false` with a
non-empty `blocked_by[]` when any of them holds or a gate stops it, and `null` with `blocked_by: []`
only in the declared probe-failure cell; there is no fourth cell and no unanswered one; (iv) the
**`completed` stage** is `applies: true` with **no** restore-target question at all — it calls only
`finalizeCleanup` — so all three cells are *inapplicable* rather than evaluated-and-false there, none
of the three tokens may appear, and its `executable` is total over the same three values decided by
the finalize preconditions alone (§14.4's cell table, §13.3).

**The holder producer, stated exactly (one function, one process per repository, four
mechanisms).** The shipped
`BuildWorktreeInventory` cannot answer this question on its own: its `ByBranch` map is keyed by the
**short** branch name (`internal/agent_status.go`'s `flush`), it routes a **prunable** record into
`Prunable` instead of `ByBranch` — silently exempting exactly the holder `git checkout` still
refuses on — and it discovers no **detached** holder at all. One additive, read-only producer closes
all three gaps, and it is the only holder producer this feature adds:

```go
// internal/rebase_plan_probe.go — package internal; read-only, no write, no
// lock, no fetch, no refusal.

// BranchHoldMechanism names the FOUR ways a worktree holds a branch, all of
// which make `git checkout <branch>` refuse. The count is four everywhere in
// this specification — one attached mechanism and three detached ones — and no
// text may say three.
type BranchHoldMechanism string

const (
    HoldCheckedOut  BranchHoldMechanism = "checked-out"  // porcelain `branch refs/heads/<name>`
    HoldRebaseMerge BranchHoldMechanism = "rebase-merge" // detached, <gitdir>/rebase-merge/head-name
    HoldRebaseApply BranchHoldMechanism = "rebase-apply" // detached, <gitdir>/rebase-apply/head-name
    HoldBisect      BranchHoldMechanism = "bisect"       // detached, <gitdir>/BISECT_START
)

// BranchHolderRecord is one holder of one branch. Path is CANONICAL by the
// §18.3 rule (EvalSymlinks plus the macOS /private spelling), which is what
// makes the self-exclusion below comparable at all.
type BranchHolderRecord struct {
    Path      string
    Mechanism BranchHoldMechanism
    Prunable  bool // a LABEL, never an exemption (clause 1)
    Detached  bool // true for every mechanism but HoldCheckedOut
}

// BranchHolderInventory is keyed by SHORT branch name — `feature/x`, never
// `refs/heads/feature/x` — matching the shipped map's key form. Values are
// sorted by canonical path, then mechanism, and are never nil for a present
// key. Available == false means "not measured": callers MUST take §14.4's
// probe-failure cell rather than reading an empty map as "not held".
type BranchHolderInventory struct {
    Available bool
    ByBranch  map[string][]BranchHolderRecord
    Err       error
}

func BuildBranchHolderInventory(repoRoot string) BranchHolderInventory
```

Producer rules, all binding:

- **One process per call, and one call per repository.** `BuildBranchHolderInventory` performs
  exactly one
  `BuildWorktreeInventory(repoRoot)` — one `git worktree list --porcelain`, the shipped parser
  consumed verbatim (§9.1a) — and derives everything else from that result plus plain filesystem
  reads. It issues **no** second Git process, and it never shells out to resolve a branch. How many
  times an invocation calls it is decided by the index rule below, never by the number of rows,
  targets or questions.
- **Every record contributes, including a prunable one.** The index is built from
  `inv.Records`, not from `inv.ByBranch`: a record carrying `branch refs/heads/<name>` yields a
  `checked-out` holder keyed by `<name>` with `Prunable` copied from the record.
- **Detached holders are discovered, safely.** For every record the porcelain marked `detached`,
  the producer resolves that worktree's own Git directory exactly as the shipped `probeActiveGitOp`
  does (`.git` directory, else the `gitdir:` pointer, rejecting a malformed pointer, a vanished
  target and a non-directory target), then reads at most three files with a bounded read, following
  no symlink and executing nothing: `rebase-merge/head-name` and `rebase-apply/head-name` — whose
  first trimmed line must be `refs/heads/<name>`, anything else contributing **no** holder — and
  `BISECT_START`, whose first trimmed line is taken as a short branch name and contributes nothing
  when it is empty or is a raw object id. `fs.ErrNotExist` is the ordinary "no operation in
  progress" answer, never a failure.
- **Fail closed, whole-inventory, per repository.** An empty `repoRoot`, an unavailable
  `BuildWorktreeInventory`
  (Git failure or malformed porcelain, which it already fails closed on) or a non-`ErrNotExist`
  failure while resolving or reading a detached record's Git directory yields
  `Available: false, ByBranch: {}` with `Err` set **for that repository's inventory only**. A
  partially populated inventory is never published,
  because a missing holder reads as "not held" — the one error direction that would let the plan
  claim an executable restore that Git refuses — and one repository's failure never nulls another
  repository's measured holder facts.

**The holder index — one inventory per repository, not one per invocation and not one per
question (normative).** An external run spans as many repositories as its rows do (§4.2's
`base_context`/`execution_context` split, §11.7's per-context reads), so "one
`git worktree list --porcelain` for the whole invocation" is wrong in exactly the direction that
loses facts: rows in a second repository would be answered from the first repository's inventory,
which cannot see their holders at all. The invocation therefore builds an **index**, once, inside
the same inspection that owns the context-identity table:

```go
// internal/rebase_plan_probe.go — package internal

// PlanHolderIndex is this invocation's holder facts. It is keyed by context_id —
// the document's only join key (§4.2) — so every consumer looks its inventory up
// by the same id it already publishes, while MEASUREMENT is de-duplicated by
// canonical --git-common-dir: `git worktree list --porcelain` enumerates the
// worktrees of a REPOSITORY, so two contexts sharing one common dir share one
// measured value and one process. It is the same join §14.1a rule 8 uses for
// FetchedThisRun, and for the same reason.
//
// ByContext is total over the contexts that NEEDED a holder fact and over no
// others: a context nothing asked about is absent, not zero-valued. Absent and
// `Available: false` are different answers and no caller may conflate them —
// absent means "not needed", unavailable means "needed and not measured", which
// is §14.4's probe-failure cell.
type PlanHolderIndex struct {
    ByContext map[string]BranchHolderInventory // key: context_id
}

// BuildPlanHolderIndex measures one BranchHolderInventory per DISTINCT canonical
// common dir among `need`, then maps every requested context_id onto the value
// its common dir produced. `ids` is the one PlanContextIdentities table of
// §14.1a — the only source of a context_id and of a canonical common dir, keyed
// by context_id — so `need` is a list of context_ids, every lookup is the direct
// `ids[id]`, and no second identity measurement happens here. A requested id
// that is ABSENT from `ids` (identity never established) or present with
// `CommonDir == ""` (identity established, store not measured) yields an
// `Available: false` entry with Err set, never a lookup into another
// repository's inventory and never a silent "not held".
func BuildPlanHolderIndex(ids PlanContextIdentities, need []string) PlanHolderIndex
```

Index rules, all binding:

1. **Measured once per repository at the snapshot point.** The number of
   `git worktree list --porcelain` processes an invocation issues for holder facts **at the snapshot
   point** equals the
   number of **distinct canonical common dirs** among the contexts that need one — never the number
   of rows, never the number of push targets, and never a fixed `1`. Two linked worktrees of one
   repository are one process and one measured value published under both `context_id`s; two
   genuinely different repositories are two processes and two values. Checkout mode has exactly one
   context, so it issues **at most** one process at that point — one on every checkout document that
   asks a holder question at all (which includes a rows-less `restoring` continuation), and **zero**
   on the two checkout documents that ask none: an empty-plan fresh run and a `completed`-stage
   resume (§9.0, §14.1's checkout rule, rule 2 below), which is
   why every checkout assertion in §22.33i counts one there and the two rows-less cells of
   §22.33i (v-d) count one and zero respectively. Executing routes add the JIT
   refreshes of rule 4 **below** the snapshot point; a plan-only route adds none, because it has no
   seam.
2. **Built only where a holder fact is really needed, and never speculatively.** The `need` set is
   the union of the contexts of the three consumer families that ask holder questions:

   | Family | Contexts contributed | Facts served |
   |---|---|---|
   | `entries[]` | each published row's **execution context** (§4.2), plus its **base context** where that is a different directory the row's own facts are measured in | the row-level `branch_checked_out_at` fact (§4.2), the rank 5.4 `branch-checked-out-elsewhere` question on a planned switch (§7.1), and §11.8's "minus every ref checked out in any worktree of that repository" collateral exclusion |
   | `fetch` | each **fetch context** whose refspecs cover `refs/heads/**` (§11.6) | `fetch_effect.local_branch_destinations.held[]` and the rank 5.06 `fetch-local-branch-checked-out` predicate, whose own `hold` domain (`head` \| `rebase` \| `bisect` \| `update-ref`) is a **publication** vocabulary and is projected from these records plus the refspec inventory — it is not a second measurement and adds no `BranchHoldMechanism` member |
   | `push` / `restore` | each **push context** of an applicable `PlanPushFacts` that asks a holder question, and — checkout only — the repository the document-level restore runs in, on **every** document whose `restore.applies` is `true` and whose route reaches `restoreOriginal` (§14.4) | `restore-target-held`, and any push-surface holder question. **In v1 the push projection asks none**: `PushTargets`/`ResolvePushLease` are pure over `PlanPushFacts` (§14.1a) and consume no holder record, so a **push-only** context contributes **no** entry and costs **no** process. The family is named here so that the rule is the same one when a push question does arise: it is answered from this index, by `context_id`, and never by a new probe |

   A context that appears in more than one family contributes one entry, measured once.

   **The trigger is the union, not the row count (binding).** An index entry is built for a
   repository when **any** published row needs a holder fact for it, **or** when the fetch family
   asks about it, **or** when the push/restore family does — and `restore` is a **document-level**
   consumer, so it contributes its context whether or not the document has rows. Three cells fix
   the rule, and none may be collapsed into another:

   | Document | `need` | Snapshot-point `worktree list --porcelain` processes |
   |---|---|---|
   | a **rows-less `restoring` checkout continuation** whose `restore.applies` is `true` (its remaining work *is* the restore) | the one checkout context | **one** — the restore question is real work and must be answered from a measured inventory, never from an empty index read as "not held" |
   | a rows-less document with **no** restore work — every external rows-less document (`restore.applies: false` on every external route, §14.4), a fresh checkout run whose built plan is empty, and a rows-less push-only continuation | `{}` | **zero**, and an **empty** index |
   | a `completed`-stage checkout continuation, which calls only `finalizeCleanup` and asks **no** holder question, despite `restore.applies: true` | `{}` | **zero** — the lifecycle disjunction of §14.4 makes `applies` true there, but the *question* is what builds the index, and that arm asks none |

   The earlier blanket sentence "a rows-less document … builds an empty index" is **withdrawn**: it
   was true of every rows-less document that asks nothing and false of the one that asks about its
   own restore target, which is exactly the document whose whole remaining work is a restore
   (§22.33i (v-d), §25.98).
3. **One value per context, reused by every consumer of that context.** Within a repository the
   inventory is measured once and read many times: the row-level fact, the rank 5.4 question,
   §11.8's collateral exclusion and (in checkout) the restore question all read the **same**
   `BranchHolderInventory` value for their context. `BuildBranchHolderInventory` has exactly
   **three** callers and no fourth: `BuildPlanHolderIndex`, the §10.3 JIT seam (rule 4) and the one
   pre-`restoreOriginal` restore refresh (rule 4 clause 6). A *consumer* that calls it directly, or
   that reaches into `BuildWorktreeInventory` itself, fails §22.33i (v).
4. **JIT refresh is per common dir, per seam, and is required wherever the next command reads a
   holder — including for collateral (exact).** §10.3's JIT seam re-probes "branch/worktree
   holders" for the row it is about to mutate. That re-probe is at most one
   `BuildBranchHolderInventory` call per **canonical common dir** the seam needs, issued at that
   row's seam, replacing every index entry whose `context_id` resolves to that common dir for every
   consumer that reads it **below** the seam. Six clauses close it:
   - **a seam refreshes only the common dir(s) its own next command reads.** It never refreshes
     another repository's entry, never refreshes the whole index, and never re-measures a common dir
     whose rows it is not about to touch;
   - **N rows in one repository re-probe N times**, once per seam, because the question is "is it
     held *now*, immediately before this command" — the run's own earlier rows can have created and
     released holders. Sharing one refreshed value across a repository's rows would answer a
     later row with an older fact and is forbidden;
   - **the two holder-reading classes are enumerated, both are total, and collateral is one of
     them.** A seam re-probes when its row's next command is a **planned switch**, **and** when that
     row's own published
     `entries[].argv` can invoke `--update-refs`, because §11.8's collateral set is defined as the
     candidate-range refs of that repository *minus every ref checked out in any worktree of it* —
     a holder fact, read by the very command about to run.

     | Class | Membership test | Rows in it |
     |---|---|---|
     | **switch** | the row publishes `mutation.will_switch_head: true` (§4.2) — the same field the document already publishes, so the class is derived from the plan and not from a route name | every checkout row whose arm runs a standalone `git checkout` (`processBranch`, and `resumeFromSwitched` where it switches), **and every external pass-2 row**, which permanently moves the repository's HEAD onto the branch it is about to rebase |
     | **collateral** | the row's published `entries[].argv` contains `--update-refs` | external **pass 1**, whose unscoped argv is `["rebase", "--update-refs", <base>]` (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:123-126`), and any row an operator's configuration puts in the same shape under `effective_backend: merge` (§11.7) |

     **External pass 2 is in the switch class, and the earlier text excluding it is withdrawn.** A
     pass-2 row checks the branch out in the execution context's repository and rebases it there, so
     the very next command reads holders: a foreign worktree that took that branch — or any of the
     four `BranchHoldMechanism` holders — between the plan point and this seam is exactly the
     condition rank 5.4 exists to catch, and a stale snapshot would let the run try to check out a
     branch another worktree holds. Such a row therefore re-runs `BuildBranchHolderInventory` for
     its **execution** common dir immediately before the rebase, re-evaluates the row's holder
     facts over it, and a **foreign** holder that appeared or disappeared is a rank 9
     `revalidation-mismatch` raised **before** the rebase and before the checkout, exactly as for
     the collateral class. The run's **own** holder is excluded by the same canonicalised
     self-exclusion the snapshot uses, so a row that merely re-observes its own checkout does not
     mismatch (§7.1, §22.33i (v-e), §25.99). A row in **neither** class — every `skipped-*` row, an
     anchor no-op, and a **scoped** pass-1 row, which neither switches HEAD nor carries
     `--update-refs` (§9.3, §11.8) — performs
     no holder re-probe and adds no process. No sentence in
     this specification, in a test name or in a comment may claim that external pass 1 makes no JIT
     holder probe (§25.89), nor that external pass 2 makes none (§25.99);
   - **the refresh is compared as a whole, not merely stored, and the collateral comparison is
     total.** Immediately after it, the seam recomputes that
     row's `collateral_refs` and `collateral_exposed` from the refreshed inventory and the row's
     re-probed candidate range, and compares them against the approved/planned values through the
     same `RevalidatePlanGuardEntry` fingerprint comparison every other JIT fact uses. On a
     **collateral**-class row the refresh is not the holder inventory alone: it is the four inputs of
     §25.102 — holders for the row's **execution** common dir, one `BuildBranchRefInventory`
     (`git for-each-ref`) over that repository's complete `refs/heads/*`, a safe `stack.yaml` reload
     that rebuilds only the stack-owned membership mapping (a read, never a re-sort or a
     re-selection), and the row's re-probed candidate range/digest — with an unreadable stack, an
     unavailable ref inventory or an unavailable worktree inventory taking rank 5.9 `probe-failed`
     before Git rather than being read as an empty set. The compared
     value is the row's **full canonical collateral tuple array** — the `(repo, ref)`-sorted
     sequence of `{repo, ref, sha, stack_owned}` tuples §8.3 already binds, plus
     `collateral_exposed` — and **any** difference in it is a rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` raised
     **before** the rebase: a tuple **added**, a tuple **removed**, a tuple's `sha` **changed**
     (the same ref now pointing somewhere else, including a tip-only move), a tuple's `stack_owned`
     **changed** in either direction, an element becoming or ceasing to be `null` where the member
     is nullable, the array as a whole moving between `null` and known, and a `collateral_exposed`
     that flipped. The refusal is **conservative identity drift**, not a claim about what the rebase
     would have done: the plan the operator approved described a specific set of refs in specific
     positions, and tws refuses rather than reasoning about whether the difference is benign. A
     **switch**-class row compares the holder facts *it* published in the same way — its
     `branch_checked_out_at` and the rank 5.4 answer over the refreshed inventory — so both classes
     compare exactly the facts their own next command reads, and a row in both classes compares
     both. No
     narrower spelling — "a ref **enters** the set", "a known-unexposed row becomes exposed" — is
     the rule any more; both are single cells of the total comparison and are **withdrawn** as
     statements of it (§25.100). Where the pre-run collateral facts were `null` (§11.8's unknown cell)
     the comparison follows §10.3's "approved collateral was `null`" row and re-evaluates instead of
     treating `null` as an approved empty set;
   - **one refresh per common dir per seam, cached within that seam.** A seam that asks two holder
     questions of the same common dir — the row-level `branch_checked_out_at` fact and the
     collateral exclusion, or a row whose base and execution contexts share a common dir — issues
     **one** process and reuses the value for both, and the same once-per-seam rule governs a
     collateral row's `BuildBranchRefInventory` call and its `stack.yaml` reload: one each, reused by
     every question that seam asks. Caching **across** seams is forbidden by the
     second clause; caching **within** one seam is required;
   - the **document-level** restore question is not re-probed at a row seam: it is a document fact
     measured at the snapshot point, and a row seam that refreshes the restore answer is a spurious
     `revalidation-mismatch` source and is forbidden (§10.3). It **is** re-judged where the checkout
     route reaches its own restore: immediately before `restoreOriginal`, the route issues **one**
     `BuildBranchHolderInventory` for the checkout common dir, re-evaluates `restore-target-held`
     over it by the same predicate and the same self-exclusion, and refuses rank 4.5
     `restore-blocked` there rather than letting `git checkout` fail — one process for the whole
     invocation, outside every row's ceiling (§10.3), and issued **iff** the route really calls
     `restoreOriginal`: `restore.applies: true` on any arm but the `completed` stage, which calls
     only `finalizeCleanup`, asks no holder question and issues **no** such process (§14.4). It is
     **not** keyed off `will_switch_head`, which is legitimately `false` on a route that does
     restore (target already checked out).
5. **The plan's per-invocation process budget follows the index, and is stated as a formula.**
   Holder measurement costs `D` processes at the snapshot point, where `D` is the number of distinct
   canonical common dirs in the `need` set — the **union** of rule 2's three families, so `D` is `1`
   for a rows-less checkout continuation that still asks its restore question and `0` for a rows-less
   document that asks none — plus one per **seam × distinct common dir that seam
   reads** (rule 4), plus **one** where the checkout route reaches its own `restoreOriginal`. A
   **collateral**-class seam costs one further Git process per distinct common dir it reads — the
   single `BuildBranchRefInventory`/`git for-each-ref` of §25.102 input 2 — while that seam's
   `stack.yaml` reload (input 3) is a file read and costs **none**. It is
   **not** a constant and it is **not** a function of the row count, and §10.3's per-row JIT ceilings
   (external ≤ 13, checkout ≤ 8) already
   include both per-row measurement processes a re-probing row can make; the restore refresh is
   counted once for
   the invocation and against no row. A rows-less `restoring` continuation that really restores
   therefore costs `1` at the snapshot point on a plan-only route and `1 + 1` on its executing
   guarded twin (snapshot + the pre-`restoreOriginal` refresh), with no row seam in either
   (§22.33i (v-d), §25.98, §25.102).

**`restore-target-held`, stated exactly (no second predicate, no second probe).** Let `inv :=
holders.ByContext[<the checkout context's context_id>]` be the entry the checkout inspection's
holder index of the rule above already holds for the one context a checkout-mode run has (§9.0,
§14.1) — measured at the snapshot point and **consumed** by the builder, which never probes
(§9.1a's "5 — what this invocation already measured" group),
and re-measured once by the executing route's pre-`restoreOriginal` refresh of rule 4 clause 6,
which re-evaluates this same predicate over the refreshed value and adds no second predicate —
`target :=
restore.target_branch` (a **short** branch name, exactly as the map is keyed), and `own` the
canonical path of **this run's own checkout** — the
single physical checkout a checkout-mode run operates in (`opts.RepoDir`), canonicalized by the
same rule the inventory's own `Path` uses (`EvalSymlinks` plus the `/private` spelling
normalisation of §18.3, so a symlinked or `/private`-prefixed spelling of the same directory is the
same path). Then:

```text
held := inv.Available
        && ∃ h ∈ inv.ByBranch[target] : h.Path != own
```

and `restore-target-held` is emitted **iff** `held` — that is, **iff a foreign holder exists**, by
any of the four mechanisms. Binding clauses:

1. **The run's own checkout is excluded, and it is the only exclusion.** A checkout-mode run
   necessarily has `target` checked out somewhere in its own checkout at some point in its life;
   refusing on that would refuse every restore. Every **other** holder — another worktree of the
   same repository, a worktree of another feature, an operator's ad-hoc worktree, a detached
   `rebase-merge`, `rebase-apply` or `bisect` holder the inventory reports for that branch — is
   foreign and blocks, whatever its `Mechanism`. A `prunable` holder is still a holder:
   `git checkout` refuses against it until it is pruned, so `h.Prunable` is a published **label**
   and never an exemption — which is exactly why the index is built from the porcelain records
   rather than from the shipped `ByBranch` map, whose prunable entries live elsewhere.
2. **Fail closed on an unavailable — or absent — inventory, without inventing a held claim.** Where
   `inv.Available` is `false` — an empty `repoRoot`, a Git failure, malformed porcelain (which
   `BuildWorktreeInventory` already fails closed on) or a detached record whose Git directory could
   not be resolved or read — **and** likewise where the index has **no entry** for that
   `context_id`, which on a checkout run means the context identity itself was not established, the
   plan MUST NOT emit
   `restore-target-held` — the fact was not measured — and MUST instead take §14.4's declared
   probe-failure cell: `restore.executable: null`, `restore.blocked_by: []`, and the accompanying
   document-level rank 5.9 `probe-failed` blocker that disambiguates the `null` (§4.7). Publishing
   `false`/`[]` alone there would dress an unknown as a known negative. A failure in **another**
   repository's inventory never reaches this cell: entries are per repository and one unavailable
   entry never nulls another.
3. **One inventory per repository, and the restore question reads the checkout one.** The restore
   question performs
   **no** Git process **of its own at the snapshot point**: it reads its context's entry in the
   holder index the checkout inspection already built — whose own cost on this mode is the
   **single** `git worktree list --porcelain` a one-context run needs — at that point, and no row
   seam refreshes this document-level answer. The **one** further probe it may cause is the
   executing route's restore refresh of rule 4 clause 6, issued immediately before
   `restoreOriginal` and only there. A second `git worktree list` at the snapshot point, or any
   probe on a plan-only route, fails §22.33i.
4. **It does not collide with rank 5.4.** `branch-checked-out-elsewhere` is **row-scoped** — a
   planned *switch* on a published entry — while `restore-target-held` is **document-scoped** and
   describes the run's final restore. Where the same branch is both, both are published, with their
   own ranks, scopes and tokens; neither is de-duplicated into the other, and §7.2's collapse picks
   the higher-ranked `refusal.kind` (4.5) as it does for any pair. Both read the **same** index
   entry, because in checkout mode the row's execution context and the restore's context are the
   same context.
5. **`applies: false` never emits it, and neither does a `completed` stage.** The predicate is
   evaluated **only** where `restore.applies` is `true` **and** the route really calls
   `restoreOriginal`. Every external document and every
   empty-plan fresh checkout run therefore publishes `restore.executable: null` — never `false` —
   with `restore.blocked_by: []`, `target_*: null` and the three effect booleans `false` (§14.4's
   cell table), so no external fixture and no empty-plan fixture may carry this token or any other
   `RestoreBlockedKind` member; and a **`completed`**-stage document, though `applies: true`, runs no
   `git checkout`, asks no holder question, issues **no** pre-restore holder refresh (§14.4 rule 4
   clause 6) and may carry none of the three restore-target tokens either — asserted, not assumed
   (§22.33e, §22.33i).

---

## 15. Validation identity (§19.17 resolved — the freeze is accepted)

v1 ships the guarded-route validation freeze.

1. The plan resolves the effective validation command once and publishes **only** its full 64-hex
   SHA-256 as `intent.validation.command_digest`. The raw command — including
   `internal.LoadConfig().TestCommand` and any `--test` value — is **never** published, in JSON, in
   human output, or in any `detail`.
2. On a guarded route the guard seam resolves the effective command once, digests it, and compares
   it with the approved digest. A mismatch there is rank 8 `approval-mismatch`.
3. The guarded executor consumes **that exact frozen value** for the whole invocation. It is
   **plumbed as an explicit value parameter through `runValidation`**
   (`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:401-403`), not as an ambient per-invocation config snapshot:
   a value parameter is what makes "the executor cannot re-read another command" a compile-time
   property rather than a convention.
4. The JIT seam recomputes the digest of the command **it is carrying** — the frozen value plumbed
   through the invocation, or the value persisted in the run's own state on a continuation — never
   a fresh `internal.LoadConfig()` read. A mismatch there means the carried value itself changed
   (state edited or replaced under the run); it is rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` and refuses
   **before** that entry executes. A configuration edit cannot produce it (rule 9).
5. Published stability labels:

| Route | `stability` | `guarded_stability` |
|---|---|---|
| Unguarded legacy external | `per-entry-dynamic` | `per-entry-dynamic` |
| Guarded legacy external, fresh | `per-entry-dynamic` | `frozen-at-plan` |
| Guarded legacy external, **armed** continuation of a real `.sync-state.yaml` (cell 7) | `per-entry-dynamic` | `frozen-at-plan` |
| Guarded legacy external, continuation of a `state_version: 3` envelope | `frozen` | `frozen-at-plan` |
| New-mode external (frozen in `SyncRunState` at startup) | `frozen` | `frozen-at-plan` |
| Checkout (`--test` in opts, or the persisted transaction value) | `frozen` | `frozen-at-plan` |
| Validation does not apply | `not-applicable` | `not-applicable` |

5a. **Where a guarded run's frozen command comes from, and where it goes.** Every guarded route
   resolves the effective command **once, above the plan** (§12.2b, §12.3), digests it for
   `command_digest`, and hands the *value* to the executor. A guarded run that persists state also
   persists that command — new-mode external and checkout already do
   (`SyncRunState.TestCommand`/`ValidationSource`, `CheckoutTransaction.TestCommand`), and the
   guarded **legacy external** envelope of §13.6 now does too, which is what makes its continuation
   `stability: frozen` rather than `per-entry-dynamic`. **No digest key is persisted anywhere**: the
   digest is always derived from the persisted command (§25.3), so §13.1's key list is unchanged by
   this rule. A guarded legacy continuation therefore validates with the command its own run
   started with. The `.sync-state.yaml` legacy cell has **nothing persisted at document time**, so
   its document publishes `stability: per-entry-dynamic` with `guarded_stability: frozen-at-plan`
   — the command was re-resolved by this invocation and frozen for it — exactly like the guarded
   legacy **fresh** row above. Where that invocation then proceeds past its guard seam, the §13.2a
   upgrade persists *that same frozen command* into the envelope it creates, so the run's **next**
   continuation is the envelope row and publishes `stability: frozen`. The label describes the
   document, the envelope carries the value, and no invocation validates with a command it did not
   itself publish a digest for.

5b. **On the cell-7 arm the frozen value has two carriers below the seam, and they are the same
   value.** Step 8a writes the frozen command into the envelope's `TestCommand`/`ValidationSource`,
   and step 9 attaches that envelope to the run context whose `Validation` member already holds it
   (§12.3). The executor therefore validates through `syncRunContext.validate()`'s payload arm —
   the persisted command, the `validating`/resume stage writes, and the empty-command rule that
   means "this run was started with no validation configured and must not acquire one mid-run" —
   instead of `runValidation`'s per-entry `internal.LoadConfig()` read, which is what the *flagless*
   cell-7 resume keeps (rule 7). A test asserts the two carriers are byte-equal at the seam, that
   the executor issues **zero** config reads for validation below it, and that a configuration edit
   after step 9 changes neither the command that runs nor any digest (§15.9, §22.14c (vii)).

6. The fingerprint binds `intent.validation.applies` **plus** `command_digest`, and explicitly
   **not** the descriptive `source` / `stability` / `guarded_stability` labels.
7. **Unguarded legacy external behaviour is unchanged**: `runValidation` still resolves
   `internal.LoadConfig().TestCommand` fresh, per entry, and the no-flag goldens are unmoved.
   External continues to ignore `--test` exactly as shipped, published as
   `intent.validation.cli_test_ignored`.
8. A guarded invocation publishes **no** document and **no** token; `guarded_stability` appears only
   in a plan document.

9. **The freeze is authoritative, and a later configuration edit is not drift.** Once a run is
   planned (a `--plan` document) or guarded (a guarded execution), the frozen command is the
   command, and the only question any seam asks is "is the value I am carrying still the value that
   was approved?".

   | Moment of the configuration edit | Consequence |
   |---|---|
   | After `--plan` printed a token, before the guarded executing invocation | the executing invocation re-resolves the command **once, above its own plan** (§12.2b, §12.3), digests it, and finds it differs from the approved digest ⇒ rank 8 `approval-mismatch` at the guard seam, **before** `setupSyncRunState`, nothing created. This is the intended detection point, and the remedy is a fresh `--plan` |
   | After the guarded run's state exists (between a failure and its `--continue`, or between two entries of one invocation) | **no mismatch of any kind.** The continuation loads the persisted command, the JIT seam digests that same carried value, and validation runs it. Rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` MUST NOT be raised, `approval-mismatch` MUST NOT be raised, and the edited configuration MUST NOT be read; a run bounded and approved with one command finishes with that command |
   | Never planned or guarded (unguarded legacy external) | unchanged: `runValidation` re-resolves per entry, exactly as shipped (rule 7) |

   No acceptance criterion and no test may require a configuration change to produce a
   `revalidation-mismatch`; asserting the *absence* of one is required instead (§22.24f, §23).
   Rank 9 stays reserved for the mutable Git plan facts of §10.3.
