## 16. Git capability handling (§19.27 resolved)

**No minimum supported Git is declared, assumed, or implied anywhere** — not in code, tests, docs or
skills. Instead:

1. On a plan/guard path only, probe `git --version` **at most once per invocation** (never per
   context) — exactly once where the invocation establishes a subject, and **zero** times where it
   does not (rule 1b). This is one extra process, and it is outside the frozen no-flag budget,
   which stays at zero new processes.
1a. **The probe has exactly two producers and one position in each, and no other site may call
   it.** `ProbeGitVersion()` (`internal/git_capability.go`, §19.1) is called by
   `InspectCheckoutPlan` (§13.7) and by `InspectExternalPlan` (§13.7a), each **at most once per
   controlled invocation — exactly once where that invocation establishes a subject, zero times
   where it does not (rule 1b)** — and by nothing else — not by `BuildRebasePlan`, not by either checkout
   builder, not by the probe layer, not by a guarded executing route outside its inspection. Each
   inspector stores the results on its own inspection struct as
   `Version GitVersion` and `Capabilities GitCapabilities`, and `RebasePlanRequest.Version` /
   `.Capabilities` are **copied from there** (§9.1a): the builder consumes, it never probes.
   The position is fixed by two obligations, and is the same in both modes:

   > **after this invocation's subject exists** — the loaded, sorted stack and order of §9.1a
   > rule 3 on a fresh arm, the decoded transaction/payload on a `--continue` — and **before the
   > first capability-gated read**, which is the fetch-context/effect enumeration of §11.1 and the
   > ordered configuration inventory of §11.7, whichever this route reaches first.

   The first half is what makes rule 1b's skip possible; the second is mandatory, because three of
   the six gates below change what `fetch_effect` may claim (`prune_tags`/`may_delete_tags` at
   2.17, the sole-remote fallback at 2.37, `fetch.all` at 2.44), and an effect enumerated before
   the version is known would have to be re-derived afterwards — a second truth. The ordered
   config inventory of §11.7 is bound by the same rule for a stronger reason:
   `CapConfigShowScope` decides whether that read may be issued at all, so no route may perform it
   — for `repositories[]` evidence, for the §14.1a push facts, or for anything else — before the
   probe has answered.
1b. **A rows-less, no-subject document skips the probe, and a skipped probe is not a failed one.**
   Where the described route never establishes a subject — an unreadable `stack.yaml` (rank 1
   `plan-unavailable`), a cyclic one (rank 1 `stack-unsortable`), a refused selection (rank 2), an
   absent or undecodable continuation transaction/payload, or any gate that refuses **above** the
   subject reads — the inspector stops before this probe, and:
   - `Version`/`Capabilities` stay the zero value and travel to the builder as such;
   - **no** rank 5.9 `probe-failed` blocker is published for the missing probe. The document
     already carries its own rank 1/2/3 refusal, and inventing a probe failure for a probe the
     route deliberately did not issue would publish a second, false cause;
   - every capability-dependent field publishes its **unavailable** value rather than a modelled
     one: `fetch.repos: []` (or the per-cause shape of §4.4a), `fetch_effect` absent with the row,
     `repositories[].config.*` unpopulated, `freshness` per §11.3's refusing cell, and
     `summary.plannability: unavailable`. No field derived from a capability gate may be published
     from a zero `GitCapabilities`;
   - the argv sidecar therefore records **zero** `git --version` processes for those documents,
     which §22.13b/§22.13c assert per gate.
   Zero-value `Capabilities` reaching the builder on a document that *does* publish a
   capability-dependent field is a specification violation, not an "unknown" cell: the two states
   are distinguished by `Version.Probed`, a member of `GitVersion` that is `false` only where rule
   1b skipped the probe.
2. Parse with a locked, tested parser: match `^git version (\d+)\.(\d+)(?:\.(\d+))?` on the first
   line, ignoring any vendor suffix (e.g. `git version 2.39.5 (Apple Git-154)`); compare
   `(major, minor)` numerically. Anything that does not match, or a probe that fails to run, is
   an **unknown version**. The type carries that distinction rather than encoding it in a zero
   value:

   ```go
   // internal/git_capability.go — package internal
   type GitVersion struct {
       Probed bool   // this invocation ISSUED the probe (rule 1b)
       OK     bool   // ... and the first line matched the locked pattern
       Raw    string // the first line verbatim, for the rank 5.9 detail; never a schema field
       Major  int
       Minor  int
       Patch  int
   }

   func ProbeGitVersion() (GitVersion, error)
   ```

   `Probed: false` is "not asked" (rule 1b), `Probed: true, OK: false` is "asked and unusable"
   (rule 6). No caller may conflate them, and no `GitCapabilities` field may be read where
   `OK` is false.
3. Capability-model **six** independent gates, each applied per capability rather than once for
   the feature. Two of them share the version number `2.26` and are still **two** gates, with two
   names, two model consequences and two independent tests — a shared boundary is not a shared
   property:

| Capability | Gate | Behaviour below the gate |
|---|---|---|
| `fetch.pruneTags` / `remote.<name>.pruneTags` and the `--prune-tags` shorthand | **2.17** | the keys read fine and the command ignores them: model no tag deletion from them; publishing `prune_tags: true`/`may_delete_tags: true` there would claim a deletion the run cannot perform |
| `git config --list --show-scope` (the ordered, scoped inventory of §11.7) | **2.26** | the plan/guard route **refuses**: document-level rank 5.9 `probe-failed` (`entry: null`), `runnable: false`, non-waivable, with a detail naming the capability and the observed version. There is no scope-less fallback, because `config_issues[].source`, the §11.7 occurrence rules and the `repositories[].config.*.source` slots are all defined over Git's own scope names, and inventing `unknown` for every row would publish a scope the plan never measured. **No project-wide minimum Git is declared**: an unguarded `tws sync` on Git 2.25 keeps working exactly as shipped, because it takes no config read at all (§17.1) |
| built-in default rebase backend `merge` | **2.26** | an **unset** `rebase.backend` is an **apply** arm, so `rebase.abbreviateCommands` is not read and `rebase.maxLabelLength` is unreachable; the rank 5.07 blocker for either key MUST NOT be published there |
| sole-configured-remote fallback (`8a649be7`) | **2.37** | an unset/absent `branch.<name>.remote` falls straight to `origin`; a single-remote clone whose remote has another name resolves to `origin`, and the modelled effect must say so |
| **`git rebase --update-refs` (`CapRebaseUpdateRefs`)** | **2.38** | the option does not exist, so a run whose planned argv carries it cannot execute the argv this plan publishes: where — and **only** where — at least one **actual planned `entries[].argv` row of this invocation** contains the literal `--update-refs` (§9.3: the external `scope=all` **pass-1, materialized** shapes, `plain` and `onto` alike), the plan/guard route **refuses** with a document-level rank 5.9 `probe-failed` (`entry: null`), `runnable: false`, non-waivable, whose detail names the capability and the observed version. The refusal is raised **above the route's fetch and above every mutation** (rule 3b). **No project-wide minimum Git is declared**: a scoped (`--only`/`--from`) external run, an external `scope=all` run **none of whose executed rows is a materialized pass-1 row**, every checkout run — checkout never passes `--update-refs` (§11.8) — and **every unguarded `tws sync`** are unaffected on the same host |
| `fetch.all` honoured by `git fetch` | **2.44** | a configured `fetch.all=true` is ignored by the command: model a single-remote effect, never a multi-remote one |

3a. The two `2.26` rows are `CapConfigShowScope` and `CapDefaultBackendMerge` in `GitCapabilities`,
   each with its own boolean and its own test; they MAY be derived from one shared version constant
   (`gitVersionShowScopeAndMergeBackend = (2, 26)`) but MUST NOT be collapsed into one field. One
   is a **feature gate** on a probe this feature issues (refuse), the other is a **semantic gate**
   on how a value is interpreted (model the older behaviour) — opposite consequences from the same
   number.

3b. **The two refusing gates have one position, one predicate each, and neither may be answered
   after a fetch or a mutation.** `CapConfigShowScope` and `CapRebaseUpdateRefs` are the only gates
   that refuse; both are decided **inside the inspection**, immediately after the probe of rule 1a
   — external step 4.5, checkout step 1.3a (§13.7a, §13.7) — and therefore above the
   fetch-context/effect enumeration, above the ordered config inventory, above the route's
   `git fetch` and above every claim, lock, state write, checkout, rebase and push. Their
   predicates are:

   | Gate | Predicate, evaluated from values the inspection already holds |
   |---|---|
   | `CapConfigShowScope` | the described route needs the ordered, scoped inventory at all — i.e. it would issue `git config --list --show-scope` for `repositories[]` evidence, for the §14.1a push facts, or for `effective_backend` |
   | `CapRebaseUpdateRefs` | **at least one argv row this invocation would really issue carries `--update-refs`** — the predicate is over the invocation's **actual planned argv set**, never over its scope. It is decided from the §9.3 frozen argv shapes applied to the rows this invocation will execute: mode `external`, effective scope `all`, **and** at least one executed row that is **materialized** and takes the **pass-1** arm. Never from the effective scope alone, never from a configured `rebase.updateRefs` (which is not an argv, §11.8), and never from a row the run will not execute |

   **The `--update-refs` predicate is argv-derived, and its early position is a projection that must
   agree with the published argv (binding).** The gate is decided inside the inspection, above the
   fetch, from facts the inspection already holds — the mode, the effective scope, the executed row
   set (the selection on a fresh run, `RemainingRebaseEntries` on a continuation, §13.3) and each
   of those rows' **materialization**, which is a local filesystem fact measured per entry and never
   a fetch result (§4.2). Three consequences follow, and each is separately asserted (§22.32b):

   - **scope is not the predicate.** An external `scope=all` invocation **none** of whose executed
     rows is a materialized pass-1 row publishes **no** `--update-refs` argv anywhere — every row is
     a `plain-explicit-branch`/`skipped-updated-ref` pass-2 row (`["rebase", <base.ref>,
     <git_branch>]`, §10.6), a `skipped-*` row (`argv: []`), or absent entirely on a rows-less
     push-only continuation — so the gate is **not required** and the run proceeds on Git 2.37
     exactly as an unguarded one would. A gate that fired there would refuse a run whose every
     command the host can execute;
   - **one qualifying row is enough.** A **mixed** `scope=all` run — some materialized pass-1 rows,
     some non-materialized pass-2 ones — does carry the option on at least one row, so the gate is
     required and the whole invocation refuses; the gate is a property of the invocation, never of
     a row, and it never refuses "just that row";
   - **the projection is checkable against the document it precedes.** For every controlled
     invocation, `CapRebaseUpdateRefs`-required **iff** the document that invocation would publish
     contains at least one `entries[].argv` (or `argv_alternatives` member) whose elements include
     `--update-refs`. A test asserts that biconditional over the whole fixture corpus in both
     directions; a predicate that refuses where no published argv carries the option, or that lets a
     published `--update-refs` argv through, fails §22.32b regardless of how it was derived.

   Consequences, binding:
   - the refusal is the **same** rank 5.9 `probe-failed` shape in both modes and on both the
     plan-only and guarded routes; plan-only publishes it inside a document at exit `0`, the
     guarded twin refuses at exit `1` having written nothing and moved no ref (§3.6, §18.1);
   - because it sits above the fetch, `fetch.attempted: false`, `fetch.outcome: skipped` and the
     freshness token is §11.2 **cause 2**'s `not-refreshed-no-plan-subject` — the same attribution
     every other pre-fetch gate takes; no thirteenth `freshness` value and no seventh suppression
     cause is created;
   - **no effective-backend or collateral claim may be derived from an argv the host cannot run.**
     Where the gate applies and the host is below it, the route refuses above the ordered config
     inventory, so
     `effective_backend` is `null` by §11.7 row 2 and the row's collateral facts are `null` with
     `summary.entries_with_unknown_collateral` incremented (§11.8) — never `merge` from §11.7
     row 1, never `collateral_mechanism: argv`, never a known-empty `collateral_refs: []`. §11.7
     row 1 and §11.8's `argv` mechanism are claims about **that row's own published argv**, so they
     are reachable only on a row whose argv really carries `--update-refs` and only after this gate
     has passed. Both follow the actual argv, exactly as this gate does: on a `scope=all` run's
     **pass-2** row — whose argv is `["rebase", <base.ref>, <git_branch>]` — §11.7 row 1 does not
     match and `collateral_mechanism` is `config` or `none`, never `argv`, on **every** Git version,
     gate or no gate;
   - the **unguarded** route is untouched on every version: it neither probes nor refuses, and it
     keeps passing the argv it passes today (§17.1, non-goal 14).

4. `remote.<name>.skipFetchAll` / `skipDefaultUpdate` is **ungated** (Git 1.6.6 era): every Git that
   honours `fetch.all` honours the suppression.
5. Git **2.20** — the boundary at which an unforced `refs/tags/*` update became rejected — is a
   boundary, **not** a gate: `may_clobber_tags` describes 2.20-and-later semantics, the keys exist
   either side, and it MUST NOT be counted as a **seventh** gate.
6. **An unparseable or failed probe ⇒ REFUSE the plan/guard path rather than lie.** Where the probe
   really ran and its output did not parse, or the child itself failed (`Probed: true, OK: false`),
   the document publishes a document-level rank 5.9
   `probe-failed` blocker (`entry: null`) with `runnable: false`, non-waivable, on the plan-only and
   guarded routes only, with a detail naming the probe and quoting `GitVersion.Raw` sanitized. This
   reuses the existing kind — it *is* a replay-critical probe failure with
   no more specific owner — so the closed enum of §7 gains no member and no second precedence order
   is created (see §25.1). A **skipped** probe (`Probed: false`, rule 1b) is not this cell and
   publishes no such blocker. The **unguarded** route is untouched: it neither probes the version
   nor refuses.
7. Where a capability is below its gate the plan models the **older** behaviour and publishes it as
   a known fact; it does not fall back to `fetch_effect: null`. `fetch_effect: null` remains
   reserved for effects the reads genuinely could not establish, which is what
   `freshness: unknown-fetch-effect` is computed from.
8. Every capability-dependent claim is asserted against a **real** `git fetch` / `git rebase` in the
   fixture, never against this ladder's restatement, and every such test is skipped with a recorded
   reason when the host Git is below the relevant gate.

## 17. Compatibility and the frozen path

### 17.1 What is frozen

For a no-control, no-flag `tws sync <feature>` in both modes: stdout bytes, stderr bytes, exit code,
Git argv sequence (including order, cwd and environment), process count, and state-file shape.
Enforcement is the existing suite in `internal/cli/sync_golden_test.go` over the **126** immutable
artefacts under `internal/cli/testdata/sync_noflag/`.

**No existing golden may be rebaselined.** New plan/guard coverage may add *new* artefacts only;
it may never replace, normalise or regenerate an existing one. Every claim that guarded or planned
behaviour preserves shipped behaviour is paired with an unguarded control asserting the goldens are
unmoved.

The frozen path adds **zero** Git processes: no `git --version`, no config inventory, no candidate
probe, no untracked enumeration.

State-file shape is frozen for **every unguarded route**, not only the no-flag cell: an unguarded
new-mode external run still writes a `state_version: 2` payload with no `route` and no limit key,
an unguarded new-mode checkout run still writes a `state_version: 2` transaction, an unguarded
legacy checkout run still omits the version, and an unguarded legacy external run still writes
`.sync-state.yaml` on failure and nothing else. Byte-level on-disk diffs against the shipped shape
are asserted for each of those four cells beside the guarded cells of §13.6.

### 17.2 What may change, and only on its own path

- New probes and new output exist only on `--plan` and on guarded execution.
- `--plan --json` owns stdout; that contract applies only to that flag combination.
- Guarded success adds no output and is indistinguishable on stdout from the unguarded twin.
- Guarded refusal adds only the anchored marker line, and only where the guard owns the refusal.
- The external `--onto` SHA pinning of §10.5 exists only on guarded execution.
- Under `--plan` the `Sync mode:` header and fetch prose move to stderr; on executing routes they
  are unchanged.
- **Controlled-path ordering differences (external new-mode fresh, §12.2b).** A *guarded* fresh
  new-mode run differs from its unguarded twin in three declared ways, none of which an unguarded
  invocation can reach:

  | Axis | Unguarded (frozen) | Guarded (controlled-only) |
  |---|---|---|
  | Output order | claim, then the `Sync mode:` header, then fetch prose | **header, then fetch prose — identical on stdout**; the header is hoisted above the fetch precisely to preserve that. The **only** header divergence is a failure of the claim/setup step itself: the guarded run has already printed the header there, the unguarded run has not reached it. A refusal **below** the claim (post-claim revalidation, JIT, rebase failure) creates **no** divergence — the unguarded twin claimed successfully and printed the header too |
  | Process order | claim/sentinel/payload, then `git fetch` | fetch-context reads and `git fetch`, then the plan's probes, then claim/sentinel/payload |
  | State order | payload written at `initializing`, then `fetching`, then `rebasing` | no state at all until the guard passes; payload written at `initializing`, then `rebasing`. `SyncStageFetching` is never written on this route |

  The guarded route also adds the plan's own probes (`--version`, `config --list`, `rev-list`, …)
  before the claim. All three axes are asserted in §23 with an unguarded control beside each
  guarded assertion; §22.28 pins the "a refusal at or above the guard seam creates nothing" half,
  §22.28a pins the post-claim cleanup half (§12.2c) and §22.28c pins the header cells — the
  claim/setup-failure divergence **and** the below-claim non-divergence. The only other place the
  header moves is `--plan`, where it goes to stderr by stream routing (§3.6), not by position.
- **A guarded new-mode `--continue` runs a different function, and only a guarded one does
  (§12.3, §19.2).** `handleGuardedScopedSyncContinue` is reached exactly when the persisted payload
  is `state_version: 3`, `route: new-mode` or the invocation carries a control flag; every other
  cell-5 continuation still enters the shipped `handleScopedSyncContinue`, which keeps its bytes,
  its statement order and its two `TopoSort` calls. The controlled twin differs in three declared
  ways, none observable to an unguarded invocation: it sorts **once**, it evaluates the guard seam
  **above** `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` (so a refusal there leaves the payload, the sentinel and the run
  guard byte-identical), and it builds a plan before reclaiming. Its shipped gate sentences, its
  `[~] resolved` and `Resuming sync with %d pending branch(es)` prose, its resume argv and its
  push/finalize tail are byte-identical to the unguarded control's (§22.14b). It also **consumes** the gate
  ladder its one inspection produced rather than re-running those predicates; the only re-read below the
  ladder is `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable`, whose compare-and-swap cannot be projected (§12.3, §12.4).
- **An ARMED legacy `--continue` runs a different function too, and only an armed one does (§12.3, §19.2).**
  A real `.sync-state.yaml` (cell 7) resumed **with** a limit flag reaches
  `handleGuardedLegacySyncContinue`'s legacy-state arm — one inspection, one `TopoSort`, the same full-stack
  remaining set, the guard and JIT seams, and the shared executor entered as `syncWithStackScoped(…, run{Route:
  legacy, Payload: the envelope}, guard)` over that one order, whose legacy arm keeps every shipped argv, line and
  gate — while a
  **flagless** cell-7 resume still enters the shipped `handleSyncContinue`, byte-, statement-, output- and
  sort-count-identical. The armed arm writes nothing **at or above** its guard seam, so a refusal there leaves
  `.sync-state.yaml` byte-identical; below the seam and above its first rebase it creates the guarded legacy
  envelope of §13.2a, and from that point on its failure persistence, validation and success teardown are the
  envelope's — which is what keeps the armed limit alive across a re-interruption
  (§13.6 rule 8 rows 14, 17, §22.14c, §22.24i).
- **A guarded checkout `--continue` is selected by the persisted transaction as well as by this
  invocation's flags (§13.6 rule 4d, §12.2d).** A `state_version: 3` transaction — which only a
  guarded run can have written — takes `ContinueCheckoutSync`'s guarded arm even when the resume
  supplies no flag, so the persisted limits and the frozen validation command stay load-bearing
  exactly as the external cell-5 persisted-v3 disjunct keeps them. Nothing else about that arm
  moves: the seam stays below `forceAcquireCheckoutLock`, every shipped gate keeps its sentence and
  position, and there is no second continuation executor. A `state_version` absent/`1`/`2`
  transaction resumed without a control flag still takes the shipped unguarded arms, inspects
  nothing and adds no Git process; the one added operation anywhere on that path is a **pure**
  `LoadCheckoutTransaction` read in the CLI arm, which moves no byte, no argv and no exit code
  (§22.24h).
- **The push lease baseline is read after the route's fetch on every controlled route whose push facts
  apply (§14.1a rule 7).** That is a new *probe position*, not a new behaviour: no unguarded route reads
  a remote-tracking inventory for a lease at all, the read is local and pure, and it exists so the
  published `expected_sha` — and the approval token that binds it (§8.3) — describe the refs the
  projected `git push --force-with-lease` would really compare against. A controlled invocation whose facts do
  **not** apply — `intent.push` false, or a rows-less document — reads nothing at all, and an unreadable
  mapping is published as `expectation: unknown` plus a rank 5.9 `probe-failed` blocker rather than as a
  null-OID claim (§14.1a rule 5a, §14.2).
- **Persisted state shape changes only for guarded runs (§13.6).** A guarded run writes
  `state_version: 3` plus `route` and the two limit keys; an unguarded new-mode run still writes
  `2`, an unguarded no-flag checkout run still omits the version, and an unguarded legacy external
  run still writes only `.sync-state.yaml` on failure. The consequence is deliberate and declared:
  **an older tws release (v1.2.15) refuses to resume a guarded run** with the exact shipped
  sentences of §13.6 rule 5, and — external only — refuses `--abort` on it too. A guarded legacy
  external run additionally *creates* recovery state that its unguarded twin would not have
  created until failure, and clears it on success; the run's stdout, argv and selection semantics
  are unchanged. Because that state is scoped-shaped, a **later** invocation over an interrupted
  guarded legacy run meets the shipped cell-5 sentences and the shipped cell-5 `--abort` arm rather
  than the legacy ones — shipped bytes, shipped verbs, reachable only after a control flag was used
  (§13.6 rule 4, §22.24d).
- **A limit armed on a `--continue` becomes persistent, and that is a declared state-shape change
  (§13.2a, §13.6 rule 2b).** Where a continuation arms a limit over a pre-guarded subject — a
  `state_version: 2` payload, a version-less/`1`/`2` checkout transaction, or a real
  `.sync-state.yaml` — and its guard seam passes, the run's state is rewritten as a
  `state_version: 3` envelope **before the invocation's next Git mutation**, with the route
  inherited rather than re-decided. Three consequences are declared: the next **flagless**
  `--continue` of that run is dispatched guarded and cannot drop the limits; an older `v1.2.15`
  binary refuses that state with the shipped sentences of §13.6 rule 5 even though the run started
  unguarded; and the cell-7 case additionally makes the next invocation meet the shipped **cell-5**
  sentences and `--abort` arm, exactly as a guarded legacy fresh run already does. It is reachable
  only from an invocation that supplied a control flag, it writes no approval token, it changes no
  stream byte, argv, gate sentence or exit code, and a failed write leaves the pre-upgrade state
  intact and moves no ref (§22.24i).
- **Checkout D1 (§9.2) changes two cells on a no-flag path.** D1-a turns a hard failure into a
  successful run; **D1-b silently changes the destination** where a real Git branch shares an
  in-stack parent's *logical* name. Both are declared here, in §19.4, in the `CHANGELOG.md` entry
  of §20 and in the §23 matrix. No `sync_noflag` golden is affected.
- **The checkout sort is hoisted above the lock — on controlled paths only, and observably only on
  the LEGACY arm (§13.7 step 1.3, §12.2d, §25.35).** The shipped checkout executor's pre-lock
  preflight is
  `LoadStack` → `ResolveSyncSelection` → `verifyCheckoutBasesLocally`
  (`internal/checkout_sync.go:588-607`); it contains **no** visible `TopoSort`, but
  `ResolveSyncSelection` **sorts inside itself** (`internal/sync_selection.go:166`), so the
  **new-mode** arm already sorts above the lock and above the fetch, and already refuses a cyclic
  stack there with the bare `cycle detected in stack.yaml`. The **legacy** arm has no preflight at
  all: it loads below the lock and sorts inside `BuildCheckoutPlan` (`:465`). Any earlier claim
  that checkout "already sorts inside its ladder" is **withdrawn**, and so is the round-8 claim
  that the hoist moves the **new-mode** arm's refusal. Two orders therefore exist, and only the
  legacy one changes:

  | Route | Order |
  |---|---|
  | **Unguarded** checkout (including the frozen no-flag path) | unchanged and frozen: preflight (new-mode: load → `ResolveSyncSelection`, which sorts → I14) → `AcquireCheckoutLock` → `Sync mode:` header (new-mode only) → optional `git fetch` (new-mode only) → `BuildCheckoutPlan` (which performs a **second** `TopoSort` on the new-mode arm and the **only** one on the legacy arm) → transaction |
  | **Controlled** checkout — `--plan` (§13.7) and guarded execution (§12.2d) | one `InspectCheckoutPlan` call performs the snapshot, the load, **one** sort, the selection over that order, the one `git --version` probe, I14 and the fetch-context enumeration **above** the lock and the fetch; the native ladder, the native lock and the shipped fetch then run in their shipped positions |

  The observable consequences are declared per arm. On the **legacy** arm a **cyclic** and an
  **unreadable** `stack.yaml` both refuse **earlier** — with the *same* shipped sentences
  (`build plan: cycle detected in stack.yaml`, `load stack: %w`) and the same exit `1` — having
  taken **no lock** and written **no transaction**, where the shipped run locks, then fails and
  releases; that arm never fetches, so no fetch is involved. On the **new-mode** arm both cells
  keep the shipped sentence *and* the shipped position (above the lock and the fetch); what
  changes is invisible — one sort instead of two. It is a strict reduction in side effects for a
  run that was always going to fail, it is reachable only with a control flag, and the plan
  route's twin is the rows-less `stack-unsortable` document of §10.2 at exit `0`. Ledger row 12 of
  §13.6 rule 8 records it; §22.13l asserts it **per arm**, with an unguarded control asserting each
  arm's shipped order is unmoved.
- **`tws sync <f> --abort` now recovers a guard-only cell 1 (§12.8).** Where the feature directory
  holds a `.sync-run.lock` and neither a payload nor a legacy state, `--abort` used to print
  `Nothing to abort — no sync in progress.` and leave the guard file on disk; it now removes a
  stale guard and prints `Stale sync guard from PID <pid> cleared; no sync state was present.`, or
  refuses with a specific sentence when the guard is live, self-PID, symlinked, unreadable or
  changed under it. This is reachable **without** a control flag — a shipped crash between
  `ClaimSyncRunGuard` and the sentinel write produces the same cell — which is why it is declared
  here rather than assumed, and counted as the **third** no-flag behaviour change in §19.4. Cell 1
  *without* a guard file, and every other cell, keep their shipped
  bytes; no `sync_noflag` golden covers `--abort`. Asserted by §22.28b.
- **`tws sync <f> --abort` also recovers cell 7 *with* a guard beside it (§12.8a)** — the **fourth**
  no-flag behaviour change of §19.4. Where a real
  `.sync-state.yaml` and a `.sync-run.lock` sit together — reachable from shipped paths alone, from
  §13.2a's first crash window and from the guarded legacy rollback's `{guard}` residue (§12.8a,
  §25.78) — `--abort`
  used to clear the state, print `Sync state cleared.` and leave the guard behind for the next
  invocation to meet as cell 1. It now clears both and prints
  `Sync state cleared; stale sync guard from PID <pid> cleared.` where the guard is provably stale
  **or records this very process**, and otherwise refuses with §12.8's sentence for that cell while
  leaving the legacy state and the guard byte-identical. Cell 7 *without* a guard file keeps the
  shipped arm byte-for-byte, and the self-PID divergence from §12.8's cell-1 table is deliberate
  and declared there. Asserted by §22.28d.
- **Cell 4 over a *valid guarded backup sentinel* gains three arms (§12.8b)** — the **fifth**
  no-flag behaviour change of §19.4. Where
  `.sync-state.yaml` is the backup sentinel of §13.6 rule 2c — a document only a guarded legacy
  setup can write, left by §13.2a's second crash window — `--continue` now **resumes the setup**
  instead of refusing (claim/reclaim the guard, write the v3 payload from the sentinel's intent and
  its verified prior state, then continue), `--abort` still clears but prints
  `Sync state cleared; the interrupted guarded setup's backup of the previous sync state was
  discarded.` instead of the bare shipped line, and a plain `tws sync <f>` refuses with a sentence
  that names **both** recovery verbs instead of only `--abort`. Every **plain** shipped sentinel in
  the same cell keeps every shipped byte for every verb, a live guard — foreign **or** self-recorded,
  since the shipped `GuardLive` has no self conjunct — still refuses first
  with the shipped sentence, and every unverifiable sentinel (`symlink`, `unreadable`,
  `unsupported-version`, `corrupt`, `foreign`, `hash-mismatch`) fails closed while removing nothing.
  Reachable **without** a control flag — the residue is guarded, the invocation meeting it need not
  be — which is why it is declared here. No `sync_noflag` golden covers cell 4. Asserted by
  §22.28e.
- **A guarded *continuation* pins its external `--onto` to a SHA (§10.5).** Guarded cell-5, cell-7
  and cell-4 external continuations pass the planned, JIT-revalidated full SHA where the unguarded
  twin passes the ref name. Every other argv element, the selection, the prose, the exit codes and
  the plain-rebase shape are unchanged, and every unguarded and no-flag invocation keeps its frozen
  argv. Asserted as a matched guarded/unguarded pair by §22.14b (vi) and §22.14c (vi).
- **The deferred half of I7 becomes route-derived (§13.6 rule 4b).** For every state a shipped
  binary can have written the answer is unchanged; only a `state_version: 3`, `route: legacy`
  envelope differs, where **not** refusing `--continue --abort` is what preserves legacy semantics.
- **Three shipped teardown helpers gain error-returning twins (§12.2c rule 2).**
  `DeleteSyncRunState`, `DeleteSyncState` and `ReleaseSyncRunGuard` become one-line wrappers over
  `RemoveSyncRunState`, `RemoveSyncState` and `RemoveSyncRunGuard` that discard the error exactly as
  their shipped bodies do. No caller's behaviour, output or exit code changes; only the guarded
  post-claim rollback consumes the errors.
- **A checkout plan may fetch (§13.7), and an external plan usually does (§13.7a) — but only where
  the described run would have reached its own fetch.** Both plan routes project every gate their
  executor raises above its fetch (checkout: I19 containment, an existing transaction, an
  in-progress Git operation, a dirty tree, a detached HEAD, an unreadable or unsortable stack, a
  refused selection, the I14 preflight, **the whole native `.checkout-sync.lock` ladder of
  `AcquireCheckoutLock`/`forceAcquireCheckoutLock` — read error, invalid YAML, `pid <= 0`, live
  foreign holder, a self-PID holder on the fresh arm only, and on a fresh run the
  stale-lock-with-transaction relation — each with its shipped
  sentence**, the two reachable fetch-effect facts, I20 and the
  continuation gates; external: the cell refusals, I20, the previous-incomplete refusal, the
  frozen-axis continuation mismatch, and the failed-branch and guard-ownership checks), and
  a refusing gate of **any** rank suppresses both the header and the fetch. Which §11.2 cause it is
  attributed to depends on the gate and on the effective policy, and no cell is attributed twice:
  cause 2 for a refusing gate on a route whose policy is `fetch`, cause 3 for the live-holder arm,
  causes 5–6 for the two fetch-effect facts, and **no suppression at all** — `local-only` — for
  every gate on a `no-fetch` route, which is every checkout I14 cell and every legacy checkout cell
  (§13.7 step 2). The deferred half of I7 is
  **not** projected on either plan route:
  `--plan` with `--abort` is refused at §3.4, so the gate is unreachable there and is deliberately
  absent rather than carried as dead code (§13.7a rule 7). **The external completion gate is not
  projected as a pre-fetch gate either**: it is a postcondition, and its only precondition cell is a
  rows-less push-only continuation (§13.7a rule 15). Otherwise, under `--plan --fetch` the
  checkout plan route performs exactly one `git fetch`, with the header and prose on stderr; the
  default checkout plan route and every continuation fetch nothing. The external plan route performs
  exactly one policy fetch — the legacy whole-stack loop or the new-mode selected loop — through the
  same helpers the executing routes use, and never a second one. Both executing routes' fetch
  blocks are unchanged.
- **The controlled checkout routes enumerate their fetch context and effect before fetching
  (§11.1, §13.7 step 1.5 and rule 6a).** A checkout `--plan --fetch` and a guarded checkout run measure the
  single workspace-root context's `--git-common-dir`, its `head_branch` and its full fetch effect
  **before** the `git
  fetch`, carry that effect through it, and can therefore publish `freshness: fetched` instead of
  `unknown-fetch-effect`; §11.2 causes **5 and 6** and their ranks 5.05/5.06 become reachable in
  checkout mode — and, because the row was measured first, such a document publishes that whole
  un-attempted row rather than an empty `fetch.repos[]` — while cause 4 stays unreachable there
  because a single candidate always fetches
  (§11.4). The probes are new and exist on controlled routes only; the unguarded checkout
  fetch block is byte- and process-identical.
- **The plan-only gate order differs from the executor's, deliberately and only on `--plan`
  (§13.7a).** The external plan route loads and sorts the stack and resolves the selection
  **before** it projects the state gates, so a document refused by a cell refusal, I20,
  a continuation mismatch or a live foreign guard still publishes `entries[]`.
  Every gate keeps its shipped predicate, sentence and rank; nothing is added, removed or reordered
  on any **executing external** route, guarded or unguarded, which keep the shipped ladder position
  for position (§12.2b, §12.3). The checkout half of this axis is the sort hoist above, which
  **does** reach the guarded executing route and is declared there.
- **The controlled routes take one typed pre-acquisition snapshot per mode (§12.5, §12.5a,
  §12.2d).** `InspectExternalPlanState` always `Lstat`s the guard, including on a legacy `--plan`
  where `AlwaysReadGuard` is false and neither sentinel nor payload exists, so `state.files.*` and
  the live-owner suppression are truthful there; `InspectCheckoutPlanState` is taken **above**
  `AcquireCheckoutLock` (and above `forceAcquireCheckoutLock` on a continuation) on the guarded
  checkout routes — inside the one `InspectCheckoutPlan` call both controlled checkout routes now
  share — so a guarded run and a `--plan` of the same command decide `state.*`, the row set and the
  execution order from one producer. Both are extra reads on controlled routes only: the shipped
  classifier, its options,
  I18 and every native acquisition ladder are unchanged, and neither inspector raises a refusal of
  its own.
- **The `switched` continuation arm gains one existence probe on controlled routes (§13.3a rule
  6).** `git rev-parse --verify <persisted NewBaseSHA>^{commit}` runs on the plan and guarded
  routes, and a missing object is the existing rank 5.7 `base-ref-missing` blocker. It never
  re-resolves `entry.Base`, adds no refusal kind, and the unguarded resume is unchanged.
- **Route derivation replaces the shipped version comparisons (§13.6 rules 4, 4c).**
  `txNewMode` / `TransactionNewMode` (nil-safe) and its recovery alias `checkoutRecoveryIsNewMode`,
  plus `PayloadNewMode`, decide "is this a new-mode run?" for continuation dispatch, the
  frozen-axis checks, the checkout deferred half of I7 in `AbortCheckoutSync`, I20 (§13.6 rule 4a,
  with the shipped `loadErr`/`nil` arms preserved verbatim) and the external deferred half of I7
  (rule 4b). For every state a shipped binary can have written, `route` is absent and the
  derivation reproduces the shipped comparison exactly, so no shipped state changes behaviour; the
  one declared new cell is the `state_version: 3`, `route: legacy` envelope, where an old binary
  still refuses `--continue --abort` while the new binary lets `--abort` win (§13.6 rule 4c).
- **Stream plumbing is additive in effect, single-source in structure.** The writer-taking twins of
  §3.6 rule 3 are new symbols, and each shipped printer becomes a one-line wrapper over its twin
  passing exactly the writers it used — `os.Stdout` for the two headers and the checkout fetch
  block, `os.Stdout, os.Stderr` for `fetchQuiet`, whose verbose arm wires a child's stderr. Every
  executing route's bytes, ordering, interleaving and destination stream are therefore unchanged
  while the body exists once; no golden-covered byte moves. `internal/exec.go` gains
  `RunTo`/`RunDirTo` beside untouched shipped helpers.
- **`runCheckoutSync` sets `opts.FeaturePath`/`opts.RepoDir` before the I19 containment check
  (§13.7 step 0).** The two assignments are pure and unread between the two positions, the
  containment refusal keeps its shipped predicate, sentence, position-in-order and exit code, and
  §22.13d asserts the executing route is byte- and exit-identical. It is listed in §19.4 as a
  statement reordering, not as a behaviour change.

### 17.3 What is preserved verbatim

I1–I20 semantics; the six trigger flags; `syncPresenceFlags` at seven; `CheckoutSyncOpts.Changed`
at seven keys; `syncChangedTriggerList` and the I8 message derivation; `--continue`/`--abort`
semantics — with exactly the three declared exceptions of §12.8 (guard-only cell 1), §12.8a
(cell 7 with a guard beside it) and §12.8b (cell 4 over a **valid guarded backup sentinel**, whose
`--continue` resumes, whose `--abort` clears with an honest line and whose plain run names both
verbs), all listed in §17.2 and §19.4; every sync-modes mismatch refusal; every shipped error sentence, which stays native,
verbatim and marker-free **regardless of rank**, including `BuildCheckoutPlan` head/base failures
and every native lock/guard failure; **the checkout finalizer's whole-plan ancestry postcondition —
`finalizeTransaction`'s per-`tx.Plan` `gitIsAncestor` loop, its
`final ancestry check failed: %s not descendant of %s` sentence, its position between the
`LastBaseSHA` `SaveStack` and `tx.Stage = StageRestoring`, and its residue (transaction and lock
surviving, `stack.yaml` already updated) — which is identical on guarded and unguarded executing
routes and is projected, pre-empted and re-ranked by nothing (§13.5 rule F, §12.7, §22.13n)**;
shipped execution order, persisted `Selected` ordering and
checkout transaction indexing; `TopoSort`'s non-determinism. The **unguarded** continuation handlers are preserved as bodies, not merely as behaviour: `handleScopedSyncContinue` (cell 5) and `handleSyncContinue` (cell 7) keep their statements, their prose, their sort counts and their call sites for every invocation that carries no control flag, and no guarded route calls either of them (§12.3, §19.2).

Unaffected surfaces: `tws status`, `tws doctor`, `tws stack status` — including their wording over
a `state_version: 3` envelope, which they decode through the extended loader rather than reporting
unreadable (§13.6 rule 6). Any future plan exposure elsewhere MUST consume this planner rather than
compute its own.

`--plan` over the legacy route describes the **legacy** route; `--plan --no-fetch` describes the
**new-mode** route — there is deliberately no fully-local preview of the legacy external route, and
`--no-fetch` MUST NOT be added to stabilise a round trip. Continuations never fetch. A plan fetch
follows the effective route policy, may mutate remote-tracking refs, `FETCH_HEAD`, tags and — under
covering refspecs — local branches, and MUST disclose that through `fetch.*` and `freshness`.

No new runtime file is introduced, and no runtime **path** changes: the guarded envelope of §13.6 —
including the backup sentinel of rule 2c, which is `.sync-state.yaml` itself — is a set of
*document fields* inside the shipped `.sync-state.v2.yaml`/`.sync-state.yaml`/`.sync-run.lock`
and the shipped checkout transaction path, so `isRuntimeState` in `internal/cli/importcmd.go` keeps
its exact three-name list unchanged. If a new runtime file ever were introduced, `isRuntimeState`
would have to be updated in the same change.

## 18. Safety and security

### 18.1 Plan isolation

`--plan` MUST NOT rewrite a local branch, write `stack.yaml`, write or clear runtime state, take or
reclaim a lock/guard/transaction, push, or run a probe outside the row executor's real context.
**Writing runtime state includes *mutating* it**: a projected gate whose shipped arm reclassifies and
persists a transaction — the checkout `planned`/`rebasing` active-rebase gate of §13.7 rule 8a is the only
one — is projected with its shipped sentence and **no** save, so `.checkout-sync.tx.yaml` is byte-identical
after the plan run.
Under `--no-fetch` it is fully read-only. Under an effective fetch policy it is deliberately not
Git-write-free, and says so.

The read-only probe set under `--plan --no-fetch` is exactly: `rev-parse`, `rev-list`, `merge-base`,
`for-each-ref`, `config --list …`, `status --porcelain`,
`status --porcelain --untracked-files=no --ignore-submodules=all`,
`ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z`, `ls-files --stage -z`, `worktree list --porcelain`,
`--version`. All are issued with `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0`, mirroring `probeDirty`
(`internal/stack_status.go:326-337`), so no index refresh is written.

### 18.2 Process execution

Every probe uses `exec.Command` argv. `sh -c` MUST NOT be used for any plan probe; the shipped
checkout validation's `sh -c` is explicitly not a model to copy.

### 18.3 Predicates that must not be substituted

- Row dirtiness is Git's own **rebase** precondition: tracked-only, submodule-ignoring,
  `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 git -C <execution_context.repo_root> status --porcelain
  --untracked-files=no --ignore-submodules=all`. The `diff-files`/`diff-index` pair MUST NOT be
  used — it marks stat-dirty but content-identical files as dirty. Checkout's shipped whole-repo
  `git status --porcelain` gate stays a **separate** fact, `state.worktree.dirty`.
- Untracked presence is enumerated once per canonical worktree top level with
  `ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z`. It is warning-only: `untracked_present` +
  `overwrite_risk` ∈ `none-known` \| `unknown` + the `untracked-present` warning. It is **never** a
  blocker, never a `runnable` consequence, never a fingerprint member, and no rendering may present
  it as a prediction. `context.untracked_overwrite_paths[]` MUST NOT exist. Exact dry-run simulation
  is out of scope (§24).
- Fresh external rebase-in-progress uses the **operation-directory** predicate
  (`rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply`, the shipped `gitRebaseInProgress` shape) over each row's own
  execution directory — the pass-1 worktree and the pass-2 `execution_context.repo_root`. The
  shipped `isRebaseInProgress` MUST NOT be used for this cell; its `false` at a `break` stop and on
  an unreadable context is exactly the answer that would let the hazard through. On a
  **continuation** the shipped failed-branch gate owns its own, different rank 3 question with
  `isRebaseInProgress` verbatim.
- Prunability mirrors the executor's cwd-scoped `IsPrunableWorktree` exactly, including its
  fail-open error behaviour; `prunability.probe_context` is the constant `cwd`.
- Branch holders come from `BuildBranchHolderInventory` (§14.4, §19.1) — one
  `git worktree list --porcelain` through the shipped `BuildWorktreeInventory`, indexed by **short**
  branch name, covering the **four** `BranchHoldMechanism` values (`checked-out`, `rebase-merge`,
  `rebase-apply`, `bisect`), including **prunable** records and the **detached** holders it
  discovers mid
  merge-rebase, apply-rebase or bisect by safely reading that worktree's own `rebase-merge/head-name`,
  `rebase-apply/head-name` and `BISECT_START`; a self-hold is never a blocker. Canonical path
  comparison (including symlink and macOS `/private` spellings) decides self vs foreign, and an
  unavailable inventory is a probe failure, never a "not held" answer. An invocation measures it
  **once per distinct canonical common dir** that needs a holder fact, through the
  `PlanHolderIndex` of §14.4 keyed by `context_id`, and every consumer — the row fact, rank 5.4,
  §11.8's collateral exclusion, §11.6's `held[]` and the restore question — reads that shared entry
  rather than probing again; a JIT seam refreshes exactly the canonical common dir(s) its own next
  command reads — a planned switch **or** a row whose argv carries `--update-refs`, external pass 1
  included — once per common dir within that seam, and the checkout route refreshes once more
  immediately before `restoreOriginal` (§14.4 rule 4, §25.89).

### 18.4 Autostash honesty (§19.18 resolved)

`context.autostash_applies_to_this_arm` is true exactly where this arm's own `git rebase` is the
next command that reads the dirty tree:

| Arm | Applies | Why |
|---|---|---|
| External pass 1 | yes | the rebase stashes and reapplies in place |
| External pass 2 | yes | the stash survives the rebase's own implicit switch |
| Checkout **fresh** row | no | the shipped whole-repo dirty gate refuses the run before any lock, fetch or rebase — a fresh checkout row can never be a dirty row |
| Checkout continuation, `switched` | yes | `resumeFromSwitched` issues **no** checkout; `git rebase` is the very next command, so `rebase.autoStash` reaches the tree in place (§13.3a, §13.3b) |
| Checkout continuation, `planned` / `rebasing`, and every later index | yes, **for the rebase only** | `processBranch` runs a standalone `git checkout` first, which `rebase.autoStash` cannot reach; the rebase that follows it is still an autostash arm |
| Checkout continuation, `conflict` / `rebased` / `validating` / `restoring` / `completed` (current index) | no | those arms run no rebase for that row (§13.3b) |

Consequences, all row-scoped:

- Tracked-dirty with an applicable autostash is the `autostash-across-switch` **warning** with
  `runnable: true`, unconditionally; the warning's `detail` states whether the stash is applied in
  place or across the arm's own switch, which is why no ninth warning kind is needed (§4.6).
- Tracked-dirty with autostash false/unset is rank 5.5 `context-dirty` — on external pass 1/pass 2
  **and** on every checkout continuation arm whose next command is a `git rebase`, because that
  rebase refuses (§7.1, §13.3b rule 1).
- A tracked-dirty checkout arm that *also* runs a standalone `git checkout` keeps the non-blocking
  `checkout-dirty-present` warning **even when autostash applies**, because a standalone checkout
  fails only where a dirty path overlaps the HEAD-to-target difference, which is not decidable at
  plan time. `runnable: true` there is an admission verdict, never a promise that the checkout
  succeeds (§13.3b rule 2).

`context.autostash_reapply_may_conflict` publishes the real residual: the reapply may conflict, in
which case the rebase still exits `0`, the tree is left conflicted and the stash is kept in
`refs/stash`. No text may say autostash "rescues", "protects", "restores", or that
`runnable: true` plus autostash guarantees a clean completion.

**A guarded run MUST NOT pass `--no-autostash`.** Turning the warning into a refusal by Git would
change the argv of a guarded run over a configuration the operator chose deliberately, and the only
argv difference a guarded run may carry is the §10.5 destination pinning.

### 18.5 Rendering and evidence

- `ancestrySanitize` / `ancestryCommandToken` / `ancestryDetail`
  (`internal/stack_ancestry.go:551-624`) are applied to every rendered attacker-controlled branch
  name, base ref, repository path and commit subject, with the limits of §5.11. No `detail` may
  contain a raw or unsanitized value.
- Raw configuration evidence lives **only** in `config_issues[]`; raw invalid-UTF-8 evidence lives
  **only** in `encoding_issues[]`, all six members ASCII. Neither ever reaches a `detail`, a
  warning, a human line, or a refusal string.
- `issue_id` and `context_id` are length-framed raw-byte SHA-256 identities and disclose neither a
  raw path nor a raw value.

### 18.6 Raw bytes and UTF-8

Bound identity strings are preserved as raw bytes in the TLV pre-image (§8.2). Every bound `BYTES`
value is additionally checked with `utf8.Valid` **before** hashing. Invalid bound identity ⇒
structured `encoding_issues[]` evidence, `approval.fingerprint: null`, `approval.usable: false`,
and a non-waivable rank 5.08 `identity-not-utf8` blocker **only** where the document would otherwise
mint a token or a token was supplied. A limitless plan with invalid identity publishes the evidence,
mints nothing, and stays runnable; the unguarded run is unchanged in every case.

### 18.7 Concurrency honesty

The snapshot is taken before acquisition; this invocation's own artefacts are excluded by snapshot
timing and by `self: true`. Liveness is *signalable*, with both residuals documented. Absent decoded
data or `alive: null` MUST NOT be read as "nothing is running". A checkout transaction's `lock_pid`
is never an owner signal.

### 18.8 Blast-radius honesty

Never claim a plan fetches only the selected repositories or only the listed contexts — submodule
recursion can reach further stores, and the honest statement is "the contexts listed in
`fetch.repos[]`, which may include the process cwd, plus any submodule store
`fetch_effect.submodule_recursion` names or declares unbounded". Collateral is always an upper
bound. Approval fingerprints are integrity receipts, not secrets and not authentication.

## 19. Implementation plan — real files and symbols

### 19.1 New files (package `internal`)

**`ControlledPathBlocker` is declared here, verbatim, and nowhere else (§4.6, §7.5).** The schema
uses `[]ControlledPathBlocker` for `guard.execute_blocked_by[]` — never `[]RefusalKind`, never
`[]string` — so a `RefusalKind` cannot be assigned into the array without an explicit, and
forbidden, conversion:

```go
// internal/rebase_plan.go — package internal

// ControlledPathBlocker is the closed token domain of guard.execute_blocked_by[].
// It is deliberately NOT RefusalKind (§4.6): these five tokens name controlled-
// path preconditions the guard itself owns, they are non-waivable, and three of
// them also exist as RefusalKinds with the same spelling but a different job.
type ControlledPathBlocker string

const (
    ControlledFetchContextIndeterminate ControlledPathBlocker = "fetch-context-indeterminate"
    ControlledFetchLocalBranchHeld      ControlledPathBlocker = "fetch-local-branch-checked-out"
    ControlledFetchSubmoduleReach       ControlledPathBlocker = "fetch-submodule-reach-indeterminate"
    ControlledLiveOwnerConcurrency      ControlledPathBlocker = "live-owner-concurrency"
    ControlledOwnerArtefactUndecodable  ControlledPathBlocker = "owner-artefact-undecodable"
)

// ControlledPathBlockers is the complete domain, in the SORTED order the
// document publishes (§4.8). It has exactly five members.
var ControlledPathBlockers = []ControlledPathBlocker{
    ControlledFetchContextIndeterminate,
    ControlledFetchLocalBranchHeld,
    ControlledFetchSubmoduleReach,
    ControlledLiveOwnerConcurrency,
    ControlledOwnerArtefactUndecodable,
}

// GuardBlock.ExecuteBlockedBy is the array itself: sorted, de-duplicated, never
// nil, [] when nothing blocks.
type PlanGuardBlock struct {
    // … the other §4.6 guard members …
    ExecuteBlockedBy []ControlledPathBlocker
}
```

Tests enforce the domain rather than trusting it: `len(ControlledPathBlockers) == 5`, the slice
equals the §4.6 list in sorted order, every emitted token parses back into the type, the array is
sorted/de-duplicated/`[]`-never-`null` (including on a rows-less document), `invalid-git-config`
and `identity-not-utf8` are asserted **absent** from it and **present** in `RefusalKinds`, and a
compile-level assertion shows it is a distinct type from `RefusalKind`, `PushBlockedKind` and
`RestoreBlockedKind` with no conversion function producing it (§22.33d).

### 19.4 Minimality statement

The only production **behaviour** changes on a path that a shipped invocation can reach without a
new flag are **five**: (a) `BuildCheckoutPlan` becoming an adapter, which is argv-identical by
construction
and proven by the goldens; (b) the checkout D1 fix, whose **two** declared cells are D1-a (a run
that fails today succeeds) and D1-b (a silent destination change where a real Git branch shares an
in-stack parent's logical name) — both enumerated in §9.2, §17.2, the CHANGELOG entry of §20 and
the §23 matrix; (c) the guard-only cell-1 `--abort` recovery of §12.8, which replaces
`Nothing to abort — no sync in progress.` with either a precise release sentence or a specific
refusal **exactly when** a `.sync-run.lock` exists beside no payload and no legacy state — a cell a
shipped crash between `ClaimSyncRunGuard` and the sentinel write can already produce, and the cell
§12.2c's named recovery command depends on; (c2) its sibling, the cell-7 `--abort` recovery of
§12.8a, which additionally removes a **provably stale or self-recorded** `.sync-run.lock` sitting
beside a real `.sync-state.yaml` and prints `Sync state cleared; stale sync guard from PID <pid>
cleared.` instead of the bare `Sync state cleared.`, or refuses with a specific sentence and
touches nothing; and (c3) the **third** member of that family, the cell-4 **backup-sentinel**
recovery of §12.8b, which over a `verdict: valid` guarded backup sentinel makes `--continue` resume
the interrupted setup instead of refusing, makes `--abort` print
`Sync state cleared; the interrupted guarded setup's backup of the previous sync state was
discarded.` instead of the bare `Sync state cleared.`, and makes a plain `tws sync <f>` name **both**
recovery verbs instead of only `--abort`. It belongs in this list rather than in the
control-flag-only one below for the same reason (c) and (c2) do: the *residue* can only have been
written by a guarded run, but the **invocation that meets it carries no flag**, so a shipped-shaped
`tws sync <f>`, `--continue` or `--abort` really does behave differently. All five are covered by
new tests and by the unchanged
126 goldens; (c) is additionally asserted not to move cell 1 *without* a guard file, (c2) not
to move cell 7 *without* one, and (c3) not to move cell 4 for any document the sentinel ladder does
not accept — every **plain** shipped sentinel keeps every shipped byte for every verb (§22.28e
(iv)).

**One further production behaviour change exists, and it is reachable only *with* a control flag,
so it is listed separately rather than smuggled into the list of five above:** (d) the **checkout
subject
hoist** of §13.7 step 1.3 and §12.2d, whose observable half is the **legacy** arm. On `--plan` and
on guarded execution the one `TopoSort` runs
inside `InspectCheckoutPlan`, above `AcquireCheckoutLock` and above the fetch. On the **legacy**
arm that is a real move — the shipped route loads below the lock and sorts inside
`BuildCheckoutPlan` — so a cyclic **and** an unreadable `stack.yaml` refuse with the *same shipped
sentences* (`build plan: cycle detected in stack.yaml`, `load stack: %w`) and the same exit `1`
while creating no lock and no transaction (that arm never fetches). On the **new-mode** arm nothing
moves: the shipped `ResolveSyncSelection` sorts internally at that same pre-lock position and
already raises the bare `cycle detected in stack.yaml` there, so the controlled route keeps the
sentence and the position and merely drops the second, below-lock sort. The plan twin publishes the
rows-less
`stack-unsortable` document at exit `0`. The unguarded checkout route — including the frozen
no-flag path — keeps its shipped order and its shipped **two** sorts on the new-mode arm and one on
the legacy arm (§9.1a rule 3a),
which the 126 goldens and the §22.13l per-arm unguarded controls both enforce. It is declared in
§17.2, in §13.6 rule 8 row 12 and in §25.35.

Everything else that touches a shipped file is one of **seven** non-behavioural categories, and each
is enumerated so a reviewer can check the classification rather than trust it:

| Category | Instances | Why it cannot change shipped behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Pure extraction (same body, new name) | `fetchScopedReposTo`, `fetchStackReposTo`, `syncFeatureScopedPlanned`, `fetchQuietTo`, `fetchCheckoutRepoTo`, `printSyncModeHeaderTo` (both packages), `abortLegacySyncState` (the shipped `handleSyncAbort` body minus its two `fmt.Println` calls, which stay in the wrapper — §12.8a), `buildCheckoutPlanFrom` (the shipped `BuildCheckoutPlan` body minus its opening `TopoSort`, which stays in the wrapper — §9.2), `ResolveSyncSelectionFromOrder` (the shipped `ResolveSyncSelection` body minus its opening `TopoSort`, which stays in the wrapper — §9.2a), `checkSyncRunGuardReclaimable`, `firstUnresolvedSelectedBase`, `firstUnresolvedCheckoutBase`, `syncTriggersNeedV2`, `checkoutTriggersNeedV2`, `checkoutRecoveryIsNewMode`, `syncStateRefusesContinueAbort`, `InspectCheckoutPlan` (which *calls* the shipped predicates and the shipped loaders rather than re-deriving them, §13.7 rule 1; its **position** on a guarded run is the declared change (d) above, not an extraction claim) | the original caller calls the extraction at the same point with the same arguments; no statement is added, removed or reordered on the unguarded route. | Statement reordering with no observable difference | hoisting `opts.FeaturePath = featurePath` and `opts.RepoDir = ws.RepoRoot` above the I19 containment block in `runCheckoutSync` (§13.7 step 0, §19.2) | both are assignments to a local struct copy with no side effect and no reader between the old and new positions; the containment predicate, its sentence, its exit code and its position relative to every other statement are unchanged, and §22.13d asserts the executing route's containment refusal is byte- and exit-identical |

The §12.2b/§12.3 guarded orderings, the guarded state envelope, the plan renderers, the plan-path

continuation entry points, `handleGuardedScopedSyncContinue` (cell 5) and

`handleScopedSyncContinue`, `handleSyncContinue` and
`clearSyncRunState` keep their shipped bodies and their shipped call order for every invocation

**`setupSyncRunState` is the one exception, and it is not claimed to be unchanged.** It gains the
trailing `birth syncRunStateBirth` parameter of §13.6 rule 2a and applies that value to the payload
**before** the first `SaveSyncRunState`, so its body really does change; `SaveSyncRunState` changes
with it, preserving a non-zero `StateVersion` instead of forcing the constant. What is preserved —
and asserted, not asserted-away — is the *observable* behaviour of every unguarded call:
`syncRunStateBirth{}` reproduces the shipped payload byte for byte (§22.24a), the claim → sentinel
→ payload order, the three step hooks, the two failure teardowns and every error sentence are
untouched, and every unguarded call site passes the zero value at its shipped position.
`NewSyncRunState` keeps its shipped signature and body and still writes `StateVersion: 2`; the v3
fields (`Route`, `MaxReplayPerEntry`, `MaxReplayTotal`) reach the payload only through `birth` on a
guarded run. No sentence anywhere in this specification may describe `setupSyncRunState` or
`SaveSyncRunState` as unchanged.

## 20. Documentation and skills

All eight surfaces are updated in the same change. There are exactly **three** embedded skills;
no text may say or imply two.

| File | Required content |
|---|---|
| `README.md` (sync flag table, sync-modes narrative) | the five flags with their exact semantics; `--plan` before a wide sync; candidates ≠ applied; bare `--plan` describes the no-flag run; `--plan --no-fetch` is a different route; exit contract |
| `docs/cheatsheet.md` (sync block) | the two approval workflows of §8.6 and the four-conjunct admission predicate |
| `assets/skills/claude/tesseraworkspaces/SKILL.md` | in-worktree agent workflow: plan → read document → approve → execute; marker parsing |
| `assets/skills/claude/tesseraworkspaces-orchestrator/SKILL.md` | pre-sync orchestration: plan before sync; use rows to narrow with `--only`/`--from`; broadcast the plan |
| `assets/skills/copilot/tws.prompt.md` | the same plan/guard contract for Copilot |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | one Unreleased entry that names, explicitly: the five flags; that a plan fetches where the run it describes fetches; **both** D1 cells — the fixed decoupled-parent failure (D1-a) **and** the silent checkout destination change where a real Git branch shares an in-stack parent's logical name (D1-b), with the `StackEntry.Name` vs `GitBranch()` rule that decides it; the guarded `state_version: 3` recovery state with its consequence that an older tws release refuses to resume (and, external only, to `--abort`) a guarded run, quoting the two exact sentences of §13.6 rule 5; the **third, fourth and fifth** declared behaviour changes, which are the three no-flag `--abort`/recovery cells and are each named explicitly and separately — (3) `tws sync <f> --abort` now clearing a stale guard-only `.sync-run.lock` with its own sentence instead of reporting nothing to abort (§12.8); (4) `--abort` over a real `.sync-state.yaml` that has a stale or self-recorded guard beside it now clearing both and saying so with `Sync state cleared; stale sync guard from PID <pid> cleared.` (§12.8a); and (5) **cell 4 over a guarded backup sentinel** — the document a guarded legacy setup leaves if it is interrupted — where `--continue` now **resumes** that setup, `--abort` clears it and states that **the backed-up sync state was discarded** (quoting `Sync state cleared; the interrupted guarded setup's backup of the previous sync state was discarded.`), and a plain run names **both** recovery verbs (§12.8b, §13.6 rule 2c), with the note that an older tws release refuses the same residue or silently discards the backup; and the control-flag-only one — a `--plan` or guarded checkout run reads and sorts its `stack.yaml` **before** taking its lock or fetching, so on the **legacy** checkout arm **both** an **unsortable** and an **unreadable** stack now refuse above the lock, with the same shipped sentences (`build plan: cycle detected in stack.yaml`, `load stack: %w`) and the same exit code, leaving no lock and no transaction behind, while the **new-mode** arm is unmoved (it already refused there) and every unguarded run keeps its shipped order (§17.2, §25.35). The entry states the arm split explicitly rather than claiming a blanket reordering |
| `docs/roadmap.md` | move **rebase plan guard** to shipped, in the sync-modes entry style; name the next target. **Prose, not flag reference**: it is not required to spell any flag literally (§22.33) |
| `docs/engineering-workflow.md` | the same shipped/next-target update; the destructive-action convention. **Prose, not flag reference**, same rule as the roadmap |

**After this ships the roadmap target becomes `safe reparent/restack` — update Git and metadata
atomically for a single-parent stack.** It is named in both `docs/roadmap.md` and
`docs/engineering-workflow.md`.

Every doc and every skill MUST teach, at minimum:

- the exact admission predicate
  `runnable && !guard.would_refuse && guard.execute_blocked_by == [] && refusal.kind == null`, and
  that it is an **admission** predicate, not a success oracle;
- branch on the document fields, never on a plan-only exit status (`--plan` exits `0` even for a
  refusal) — including for an unreadable or cyclic `stack.yaml`, a refused selection and every
  projected state gate, all of which publish a document (a rows-less one where the subject could
  not be read) at exit `0`. A plan-only invocation exits `1` only for a flag error, an unresolvable
  subject or a security refusal, an encoding failure or a writer failure (§3.6);
- the two-line entry grammar, the `Plan blockers:` / `Plan warnings:` blocks (every row is printed,
  in canonical order, and a warning is never hidden — §6.2a), the `Configuration issues:` block, the
  `Guarded execution blockers:` block — whose rows are **bare tokens**, `  - <token>`, with the
  detailed evidence living in `state`/`fetch`/`blockers[]` (§6.3 part 3) — and the
  `Approval fingerprint:` line including `none`;
- that the human `<range>` is `<12-char upstream>..<branch>` while JSON `replay.range` carries the
  **full** upstream SHA, so a script must read `replay.range`, never scrape the row;
- the scope vocabulary: JSON `policy.scope_kind` ∈ `all` \| `one` \| `subtree` with a separate
  `policy.selector`, human `scope=all` \| `only:<name>` \| `subtree:<name>`, and **no `from`
  token** on either surface even though `--from` is the flag that selects `subtree`;
- the **eight** warning kinds, and that `selection-hazard` is a blocker in v1, never a warning;
- candidates are an upper bound; "applied" is never published;
- that `--plan` is non-mutating for branches, working trees and tws state but **not** Git-write-free:
  a plan fetches exactly where the run it describes fetches — an external plan by default, a
  checkout plan only under `--fetch` — and `--plan --no-fetch` previews a **different**, new-mode
  route. No doc, skill or help string may make the unqualified claim (Normative vocabulary,
  §22.33a);
- a fetch-enabled plan performs network I/O and may mutate remote-tracking refs, `FETCH_HEAD`, tags
  and covered local branches; always report `freshness` beside a base SHA;
- **exactly six** plan fetch-decline causes — never four, never five;
- the token is 64 lowercase hex, bytewise compared; all three unusable-token causes; that
  `--approve-plan` requires a limit on every route, `--plan` included; limits bound **each invocation's** work and are
  never cumulative, while an armed `--continue` persists them so the run stays guarded (§13.2a); `approval.scope` ∈ `full-run` \| `remaining-work`. **Every published workflow
  passes a limit on both the `--plan` line and the executing line** (§8.6); a workflow that mints or
  presents a limitless token is a documentation bug;
- that a **guarded** run records its limits in `state_version: 3` recovery state — **including a
  run that became guarded because a limit was armed on its `--continue`** (§13.2a), after which its
  next flagless `--continue` stays guarded — that an older tws
  release therefore refuses to resume it (exact sentences in §13.6 rule 5), and that the remedy is
  to use a tws new enough to understand the run — never to delete the state blindly;
- guarded refusal parsing: exit `1` plus the anchored `^plan-guard: <kind>: <detail>` line, never a
  substring grep of arbitrary stderr; the marker is decided by origin, not rank;
  `state-preserved: ` distinguishes post-mutation from pre-mutation refusals;
- that a **guarded refusal happens after that run's own policy fetch** (the fetch sits above the
  guard seam), so "the guard refused" means "no tws state and no rebase", never "nothing happened":
  remote-tracking refs, `FETCH_HEAD`, tags and covered local branches may already have moved. Only
  a §3.4 flag error and the pre-subject refusals happen before any fetch;
- that the plan/guard path needs Git **2.26** for `git config --list --show-scope` and refuses with
  a document-level rank 5.9 `probe-failed` below it or on an unknown version, and that it likewise
  needs Git **2.38** for `git rebase --update-refs` — but **only** for the invocations whose
  published rows really carry that option, which is decided from the planned `argv` and not from the
  scope: a whole-stack external sync that will rebase a materialized entry is gated, while a scoped
  sync, an all-scope sync whose rows are all non-materialized, and every checkout sync are not —
  refusing the same way above the fetch, while unguarded
  `tws sync` keeps working unchanged on older Git in every one of those cells; tws declares **no**
  minimum supported Git;
- `context_id` is the sole join key — never `repo_root`, never the `repo` token;
- how to read `push.targets[].lease`: `expectation: sha` compares against a real ref, `absent` is Git's **stricter** null-OID check (the push fails if the remote ref exists at all), and `unknown` means this run could not read that context's remote configuration — it always arrives with a rank 5.9 `probe-failed` blocker and is never a claim about the remote; and that `expected_sha_freshness: possibly-stale` names a real hazard, including the negative-refspec cell no fetch can ever refresh (§14.2);
- `summary.plannability` (`empty` has real zeros, `unavailable` has nulls) is not a runnability
  claim, and remaining work is read from `entries` **and** `push.targets` **and** `restore.applies`;
- tracked dirt vs untracked presence, and the banned words "rescue", "safe", "restored" for
  `rebase.autoStash`;
- that an `approval-mismatch` on a re-plan normally means plan drift, and that the remedy is a fresh
  receipt, never adding `--no-fetch`;
- that a **controlled** checkout run (`--plan` or a guarded execution) reads and sorts `stack.yaml`
  before it locks or fetches, so on the **legacy** checkout arm a cyclic **or** unreadable stack is
  reported with its shipped sentence *before* any lock, fetch or transaction exists — while an
  unguarded `tws sync` keeps its shipped order in both arms (§17.2, §22.13l);
- that a **stale or divergent ancestry** on a row the run will rebase is the *work*, not a blocker:
  the plan publishes it as the row's `ancestry` and stays `runnable: true`. The completion gate
  (`Sync incomplete; stale stack edges remain:`) fires **after** the rebases, so meeting it means
  branches already moved and recovery state was written — the remedy is `--continue`/`--abort`,
  never "nothing happened" (§7.1, §13.5). The checkout twin of that honesty is the finalizer's
  whole-plan check (`final ancestry check failed: <branch> not descendant of <base>`), which fires
  **after** every rebase and after `stack.yaml` was updated, cannot be predicted at plan time
  because it catches a concurrent ref move, and leaves the transaction and the lock in place for
  `--continue`/`--abort` (§13.5 rule F, §12.7);
- that the `plan-guard:` marker belongs to **guard-owned** refusals only: a dirty tree, a held lock,
  an unresolvable base or any other refusal tws already performed keeps its own wording and carries
  no marker, so the marker's absence is never evidence of success (§6.4, §3.1a).

## 21. Dependencies

**The three declared hard parents are necessary and sufficient**, and stay as recorded in
`status.json`:

| Parent | Why |
|---|---|
| `sync-modes` | owns the axes, selection, frozen-decision persistence, scoped argv, the v2 state machine and the golden harness |
| `stack-status` | owns the versioned/null-honest projection style and `BuildBranchRefInventory`; transitively owns `StackEdge` through `stack-ancestry-doctor` |
| `amend-aware-rebase` | owns `LastBaseSHA` and the `--onto` strategy this feature describes |

`sync-modes` already pulls the relevant hard closure (`branch-name-decoupling`,
`multi-repo-workspaces`, `archive-worktree`, `checkout-stack-safety`, `fix-default-base-branch`,
`fix-sync-continue-descendants`, `push-branches`, `cobra-migration`,
`agent-work-status-dashboard`).

**Soft parents to register:**

| Parent | Kind | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `skill-distribution` | soft | this spec edits `assets/skills/claude/tesseraworkspaces/SKILL.md` and `assets/skills/copilot/tws.prompt.md`, both created by that feature |
| `tiered-skill-system` | soft | this spec edits `assets/skills/claude/tesseraworkspaces-orchestrator/SKILL.md`, created by that feature |

**Deliberately not registered:**

- `fix-missing-completions` — the analysis listed it *conditionally* ("only if a new entry-valued
  flag registers completion like `--only`/`--from`"). This spec registers **no** completion
  function: two integers and a 64-hex digest have no completable domain, and
  `internal/cli/sync.go`'s two `RegisterFlagCompletionFunc` calls are unchanged. Adding the edge
  would be DAG noise (§25.2).
- `stack-ancestry-doctor` / `agent-work-status-dashboard` — reused unchanged. `ancestrySanitize` and
  friends are unexported members of the same package `internal`, so no export and no edit is
  required; `BuildWorktreeInventory` is already exported, and `BuildBranchHolderInventory` (§14.4)
  wraps it inside package `internal`, so no new dependency edge is created.

DAG discipline: extra edges are noise and MUST NOT be added to silence historical verification
concerns. Run `tpatch feature deps --validate-all` after `define` and after `explore`, and before
implementation.

Registration commands:

```sh
tpatch feature deps rebase-plan-guard add skill-distribution:soft
tpatch feature deps rebase-plan-guard add tiered-skill-system:soft
tpatch feature deps --validate-all
```
