process), indexes by short name, keeps prunable records, adds the detached
`rebase-merge`/`rebase-apply`/`bisect` holders from bounded, symlink-free reads of each detached
worktree's own Git directory, canonicalizes every path by §18.3's rule and fails closed
whole-inventory. `restore-target-held` is then emitted **iff** a holder other than this run's own
checkout exists, by any of the **four** mechanisms (§25.86), with an unavailable inventory taking
§14.4's
`executable: null` + rank 5.9 `probe-failed` cell rather than claiming held, and rank 5.4 coexisting
rather than colliding. `restore.applies: false` can never carry it. The **quantifier** on that one
call — how many inventories an invocation builds — is fixed separately in §25.83: one per
repository, through the `PlanHolderIndex`, which this rule reads rather than probing again
(§7.1, §14.4, §22.33i, §23.2, §25.83, §25.86).

**25.78 §12.8a's residue has two provenances, and both are declared.**
§12.8a was introduced to clear `{real .sync-state.yaml, guard}`, described as
§13.2a's first crash window. Round 16 removed that window by putting the sentinel before the claim
and justified the arm by a shipped-only sequence instead; §25.80 restores the claim to first
position, so **both** provenances now hold and both are stated. The shape is reachable
without any guarded run at all — a guard-only cell 1 (§12.8's own residue) met by an unguarded
legacy sync that then fails writes exactly that pair — **and** it is §13.2a's crash window 1 on the
cell-7 continuation arm, plus that arm's `{guard}` rollback residue, where the prior document has
already been restored beside a guard whose release failed. Its scope is stated by classifier cell
rather than by provenance, §22.28d keeps the shipped-only fixture **and** gains the two
guarded-legacy ones, and its behaviour, sentences and self-PID divergence are unchanged
(§12.8a, §13.2a, §22.28d).

**25.79 `--update-refs` needs its own capability gate, because the plan publishes an argv the host
may not be able to run.** §19.27 enumerated four capability gates and §25.14 added a fifth, all of
them about facts the plan *models* — tag deletion, scope names, the default backend, remote
resolution, `fetch.all`. None covered the one option tws itself puts on the command line: the
external `scope=all` argv of §9.3 carries `--update-refs`, which Git only understands from **2.38**.
Below that version the published argv is not merely mismodelled, it is unexecutable, and two further
claims derived from it — §11.7 row 1's `effective_backend: merge` and §11.8's
`collateral_mechanism: argv` — would describe a run that cannot happen. §16 therefore adds a
**sixth** gate, `CapRebaseUpdateRefs`, and it is the **second refusing** one: where at least one
**actual planned `entries[].argv` row** of this invocation carries the option, the plan/guard route
refuses with a document-level
rank 5.9 `probe-failed` (reusing the kind per §25.1, adding no enum member and no rank), raised
inside the inspection immediately after the version probe and therefore **above** the ordered config
inventory, above the route's fetch and above every claim, lock, state write and Git mutation (§16
rule 3b). The gate is deliberately **argv-derived, not a version floor and not a scope test**: a
scoped external run, an external `scope=all` run whose executed rows are **all non-materialized**
(pass-2 `["rebase", <base>, <branch>]` argv and skips, §9.3), a rows-less push-only continuation and
every checkout run — checkout never passes `--update-refs` (§11.8) — are unaffected on the same
host, while a **mixed** all-scope run with one materialized pass-1 row is gated as a whole. The
inspection's pre-fetch evaluation is a projection of the published argv and must agree with it in
both directions (§22.32b (i-c)). The **unguarded** route neither probes nor refuses on any version,
and **no project-wide
minimum Git is introduced**. Where the gate applies and the host is below it the document publishes
`effective_backend: null` (§11.7
row 2) and `null` collateral facts with `summary.entries_with_unknown_collateral` incremented,
rather than a backend or a mechanism inferred from an option the host would reject; and §11.7 row 1
and §11.8's `argv` mechanism likewise follow each row's **own** argv, so a pass-2 row is never
`mechanism: argv` on any version
(§11.7, §11.8, §16 rules 3/3b, §22.32, §22.32b, §23.2).

**25.80 Mutual exclusion belongs to the claim, so the claim goes first; the sentinel keeps the
bytes.** Round 16 moved `ClaimSyncRunGuard` **below** the backup-sentinel replacement, reasoning
that the operator's bytes must never live only inside the sentinel. The reasoning was right about
*loss* and wrong about *concurrency*: with the claim last, two new binaries starting a guarded
legacy setup over the same feature could **both** reach the replacement, and the compare-and-swap
could only turn the second one into a refusal *after* the first had already rewritten
`.sync-state.yaml` — with the loser's own conditional undo then racing the winner's payload write.
§13.2a therefore reorders to capture → **`ClaimSyncRunGuard`** → conditional backup sentinel →
payload, restoring the shipped `setupSyncRunState` order and making the `O_EXCL` claim the single
mutual-exclusion point: of two new binaries exactly one passes it, and the loser writes nothing at
all. Loss safety is unaffected, because it never depended on the ordering — it is carried by the
**content** of the replacement (§25.74): before the sentinel the prior bytes *are* the file, from
the sentinel onward they are inside it. The rollback is reordered to match and releases the guard
**last** (payload → conditional sentinel undo → guard), so the prior document is restored under
this invocation's own claim. Three consequences are declared rather than discovered: the crash
windows become `{guard}` + untouched subject (cell 7, or cell 1 on the fresh route), `{sentinel,
guard}` (cell 4) and `{payload, sentinel, guard}` (cell 5); the failed-rollback residues become
`{payload, sentinel, guard}`, `{sentinel, guard}` and `{guard}`; and §12.8a's arm regains a
guarded-legacy provenance beside its shipped-only one (§25.78). Cell 8 stays unreachable from every
path of this arm under this binary (§12.3, §12.7, §12.8a, §12.8b, §13.2a, §13.6 rules 2a/2c, §23.1,
§23.2, §25.66, §25.67, §25.74, §22.24i (ix-a), (ix-b), §22.28d, §22.28e).

**25.81 An extraction that drops the verb cannot reproduce two sentences.** §12.8b extracted
`syncCellRefusal`'s live-guard arm as `syncCellLiveGuardRefusal(feature, st)` so the cell-4
interception could sit below it — but that arm does not emit **one** sentence: the shipped switch
emits the `--abort` spelling (`… wait for it to exit before --abort`) for `--abort` and a plain twin
for the other two verbs, and a two-parameter extraction can reproduce only one of them. The
signature gains a third parameter, `verb syncVerb` — the **shipped** `cli`-internal string type of
`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:260-265`, reused rather than redeclared (§25.88) — and
§12.8b tabulates the total mapping — `--abort` sentence, plain twin for plain and `--continue`, and
`nil` only where the classifier reports no live guard at all — with §22.28e (vi) asserting both
sentences byte-for-byte
against the pre-feature binary and asserting them **distinct**, so a collapse into one spelling
fails. `syncCellRefusal` forwards the verb it was itself given, so it stays a pure extraction
(§12.8b, §19.2, §19.4, §22.28e, §25.95).

**25.82 The interception is above I20, so I20 must not also claim to decide cell 4.** Round 16
placed the valid-backup-sentinel interception below `syncCellLiveGuardRefusal` and **above**
`syncCellRefusal` — which, since the shipped ladder is `syncCellRefusal` → I20 → previous-incomplete,
puts it above I20 too — while simultaneously giving `syncTriggersNeedV2` a `case 4:` arm fed by the
threaded sentinel view and asserting that I20 "keeps its position above it". Both cannot hold: the
arm was unreachable and the position claim was false. The cell-4 arm and the view parameter are
**removed**, `syncTriggersNeedV2(st)` returns to its three-arm shape, and the **interception** owns
this document's flag validation — refusing any mode-trigger flag with the shipped I20 sentence
composed there, byte for byte, on all three verbs, and resolving the two limit keys through §13.2's
per-key table so a matching or flagless `--continue` resumes and a differing one is rank 7
`guard-limit-mismatch`. A **malformed** or non-backup cell-4 document falls through to the shipped
`syncCellRefusal`, and ordinary I20 keeps its shipped position and its shipped behaviour for every
other cell. There is now exactly one call site that consults the view and exactly one that answers
for this document (§12.8b, §13.6 rules 4a/4b, §19.2, §22.28e (vii), §22.24j (vi)).

**25.83 One `worktree list --porcelain` per invocation was the wrong quantifier — it is one per
repository.** §14.4 declared the holder inventory "one process per invocation", which is right in
checkout mode (one context) and wrong in external mode, where rows span repositories: a second
repository's rows would have been answered from the first repository's inventory, which cannot see
their holders at all — a silent "not held" for real holders, the exact error direction the
fail-closed rule exists to prevent. The inspection now builds a `PlanHolderIndex` keyed by
`context_id`, measured once per **distinct canonical common dir** among the contexts that need a
holder fact (`entries[]` execution contexts, `fetch` contexts covering `refs/heads/**`, and the
push/restore family), and every consumer — `branch_checked_out_at`, rank 5.4, §11.8's collateral
exclusion, §11.6's `held[]` and `restore-target-held` — reads its context's entry rather than
probing again. Measurement de-duplicates on common dir while lookup keys on `context_id`, exactly as
§14.1a rule 8's `FetchedThisRun` join does; a rows-less document measures nothing **unless it still
asks a holder question — the rows-less `restoring` continuation whose whole remaining work is the
restore measures exactly one inventory for its own repository (§25.98)**; JIT refresh is
per seam and per that seam's own canonical common dir, `N` re-probing rows in one repository
re-probing `N` times and a row whose next command reads no holder re-probing none (§25.89, §25.99); and one
repository's unavailable
inventory never nulls another's (§4.2, §10.3, §11.6, §11.8, §14.4, §18.3, §19.1, §22.33i (v-a)–(v-f),
§23.2, §25.77).

**25.84 The `--update-refs` gate must follow the argv the document really publishes, not the
scope.** §16 rule 3b spelled its predicate as "external `scope=all`", which over-fires: an
all-scope run whose executed rows are **all non-materialized** publishes only pass-2
`["rebase", <base>, <branch>]` argv and skips, carries `--update-refs` nowhere, and would have been
refused on Git 2.37 for an option it never passes. The predicate becomes "**at least one actual
planned `entries[].argv` row contains `--update-refs`**", decided inside the inspection from the
mode, the effective scope **and** the executed rows' materialization — all pre-fetch facts — and
asserted as a corpus-wide biconditional against the published argv, so the early evaluation can
never drift from the document it precedes. A **mixed** run with one materialized pass-1 row is gated
as a whole; §11.7 row 1 and §11.8's `argv` mechanism follow each row's own argv for the same reason,
so a pass-2 row is never `mechanism: argv` on any version (§11.7, §11.8, §16 rule 3b, §20, §22.32b
(i-a)–(i-c), (iii-a), §23.2, §25.79).

**25.85 A fresh restore is probed too; only its answers differ.** §7.4 called
`restore-target-missing`, `restore-target-held` and `restore-head-moved` "the three probed
**continuation** cells", which left a fresh `applies: true` document with three unanswered questions
and made `restore.executable` untotal there. All three are now evaluated on **every**
`applies: true` document. On a fresh run the target is the run's own `probed-head` original branch,
so `restore-target-missing` is normally `false` by construction, `restore-target-held` is normally
`false` by **self-exclusion** — but a real **foreign** detached holder still emits the token — and
`restore-head-moved` is a known `false`, because no `OriginalHEAD` is persisted yet; the fresh-run
hazard that resembles it stays the `restore-head-collateral-risk` **warning** of §7.4. On a
continuation all three may block. §7.4's sentence is re-scoped to fix the **rank**, never the
evaluation scope, and `restore.executable` is asserted **total** over every `applies: true` document
(§7.4, §7.5, §14.4, §22.33e, §23.2, §25.71).

**25.86 `BranchHoldMechanism` has four members, and every sentence must count four.** The type
declares `checked-out`, `rebase-merge`, `rebase-apply` and `bisect`, while §14.4's doc comment,
its producer heading and its `restore-target-held` clause all said "three" — an off-by-one that
reads as though the attached `checked-out` holder were not a mechanism, which is the one holder
every fresh-run self-exclusion turns on. Every count is now **four** (one attached, three detached),
§18.3 names all four, and a table test asserts the constant set has exactly four members and that no
emitted `Mechanism` falls outside it (§4.2, §14.4, §18.3, §22.33i (iii-a), §23.2).

**25.87 The cell-4 backup-sentinel recovery is a no-flag behaviour change, and the count says so.**
§12.8b is reachable by a shipped-shaped `tws sync <f>`, `--continue` or `--abort` carrying no
control flag — only the *residue* requires a guarded run — so it belongs in §19.4's no-flag list
beside §12.8's and §12.8a's, not in the control-flag-only paragraph. The list becomes **five**
((a) the checkout adapter, (b) D1's two cells, (c) cell 1, (c2) cell 7, (c3) cell 4), "all four" is
corrected to "all five", §17.2 numbers the three recovery cells third, fourth and fifth, and §20's
`CHANGELOG.md` requirement names them as three separate disclosures. §22.33 33-i-a asserts the
entry's content per cell, with the cell-4 row — resume, honest discard, both verbs, downgrade note —
asserted **present**: a corpus disclosing only cells 1 and 7 fails, because cell 4 is the one where
`--abort` destroys a recoverable document (§12.8b, §17.2, §19.4, §20, §22.33, §23.2, §25.75).

**25.88 `syncVerb` already exists; the extraction reuses it and declares nothing.** §12.8b's
verb-aware `syncCellLiveGuardRefusal` was accompanied by a fresh `type syncVerb int` with
`iota` constants — a **redeclaration** of the shipped `cli`-internal type
(`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:260-265`), which is `type syncVerb string` with the constants
`syncVerbPlain = "plain"`, `syncVerbContinue = "continue"` and `syncVerbAbort = "abort"`. Two
declarations of one identifier in one package do not compile, and re-basing the type on `int` would
also break the two shipped table tests that name all three constants —
`TestSyncModes_CellMessages` (`internal/cli/sync_modes_test.go:436-514`), whose case table declares
a `verb syncVerb` column, and `TestSyncModes_UnreadablePayloadCellsShareOneMessage` (`:516-528`),
which iterates them as a `[]syncVerb`. The single span `:444-561` cited through round 19 was
neither symbol's range: it started inside the first test's table literal and ended inside a third
function (`TestSyncModes_MixedAndCorruptCells`, `:530-566`), so both citations are now symbol-named
with the range each symbol's body really spans (§23.1's citation rule). The declaration is **removed**: the helper's third parameter is the shipped
type, the shipped constants keep their spellings and values, `syncCellRefusal` — whose shipped
signature already takes `verb syncVerb` as its **first** parameter — forwards the verb it was given,
and this feature adds no type, no constant and no fourth value to that domain. The three-row mapping
table and the §22.28e (vi) byte-exact/distinct assertions are unchanged
(§12.8b, §19.2, §19.4, §22.28e, §25.81).

**25.89 Collateral is a holder fact, so the JIT seam must refresh holders for it — including on
external pass 1.** §14.4 rule 4 exempted "a row whose next command reads no holder" and named
external pass 1 as an example, "which rebases in place without a checkout". That is the wrong test
and the wrong example. §11.8 defines the collateral set as the candidate-range refs of the row's
repository **minus every ref checked out in any worktree of that repository**, and the executor's
unscoped pass-1 argv is `["rebase", "--update-refs", <base>]`
(`internal/cli/sync_helpers.go:123-126`) — the one shape that really moves those refs. A run planned
at T0 and executing at T1 could therefore rebase with `--update-refs` against a holder set measured
before an operator (or an earlier row of the same run) created or released a worktree, silently
moving a ref the approved plan excluded. The rule is restated: the seam refreshes
`BuildBranchHolderInventory` for **each canonical common dir its own next command reads**, which is
now two enumerated classes — a planned **switch** (every row publishing
`mutation.will_switch_head: true`, external pass 2 included, §25.99), and any row whose own published
argv can invoke
`--update-refs`, external pass 1 included — recomputes `collateral_refs`/`collateral_exposed` from
the refreshed inventory and compares the **whole** canonical tuple array through
`RevalidatePlanGuardEntry` (§25.100), so a holder change is a
rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` **before** the rebase (§10.3). Refreshes are cached **once per common
dir within a seam** and never shared across seams (holders move between rows), the budget formula
gains the per-seam term and one further probe for the checkout route's own pre-`restoreOriginal`
restore refresh, and §22.33i (v-e-1) asserts a **real** held→unheld and unheld→held transition in
both directions. No sentence, test name or comment may claim external pass 1 makes no JIT holder
probe (§10.3, §11.8, §14.4 rules 4–5, §18.3, §22.33i (v-e)–(v-e-2), §23.2, §25.83, §25.99).

**25.90 `restore.applies` is a lifecycle disjunction, so `StageCompleted` is describable.** §14.4
defined `applies` as "a checkout run that will execute `restoreOriginal` **+** `finalizeCleanup`",
which left the `completed` stage — a real, reachable continuation whose resume calls
`finalizeCleanup` **alone** (`internal/checkout_sync.go`'s `StageCompleted` arm) — in no cell at all:
`false` would have denied a run whose `deletes_transaction` and `releases_lock` are genuinely `true`
and whose remaining work is a real push retry, while `true` under the old definition would have
demanded a restore that route never performs. `applies` becomes "checkout restore/finalize lifecycle
work remains" — `restoreOriginal` **or** `finalizeCleanup` — and the HEAD question the conjunction
was reaching for stays where it already lived: `will_switch_head`, which is `false` on that stage
and whose comparison is re-anchored to the branch HEAD is on **immediately before**
`restoreOriginal` rather than to the post-run HEAD (the latter is the restore's own output and would
read `false` on every successful run). The `completed` stage therefore publishes `applies: true`,
`will_switch_head: false`, `target_*` from the transaction, `deletes_transaction`/`releases_lock`
`true`, `push_dropped: false` (that arm **performs** the pending push), an `executable` decided by
the finalize preconditions alone, and **none** of the three restore-target tokens — it runs no
`git checkout`, so it asks no holder question and issues no pre-restore holder refresh (§25.89).
**No member is added**: `restore` keeps exactly ten fields in the same order and the schema version
is unchanged, and a `will_restore_original` (or any other) eleventh member is explicitly rejected
because the existing `will_switch_head` already answers it (§13.3, §14.4, §22.33e, §23.2, §25.71,
§25.85).

**25.91 `PlanContextIdentities` is keyed by `context_id`, and the reverse direction belongs to the
measurement.** The table was declared `map[string]PlanContextIdentity` with no stated key, which left
every consumer free to assume a different one — a repo root, a common dir, a display path — and made
`BuildPlanHolderIndex`'s `need []string` and `PlanPushRemoteFacts`'s `context_id` keying join to
nothing in particular. The key is fixed as the 64-lower-hex `context_id`, so every read is the direct
`ids[id]` with no scan and no re-derivation; a context whose identity was never established is
**absent** rather than stored under `""`, so two failures cannot collide into one row and each
consumer takes its own declared unknown cell (`context_id: null` + rank 5.1, `Available: false` in
the holder index, §14.4's probe-failure cell). The `directory → context_id` direction is owned by the
**measurement** — §4.4's one generic context-identity function, run once per distinct directory of
the closed set the invocation uses and stamped onto the context value it produced — which is what
keeps `ResolvePushContext` pure under §14.1a rule 1 and makes rule 2's context-id equality hold by
construction. §22.33h (ii-a) asserts `k == v.ContextID`, the absent-on-failure rule and the
direct-index source assertion (§4.2, §4.4, §14.1a rules 1/2/2a, §14.4, §22.33h).

**25.92 The cell-4 `--abort` line depends on which sentinel the residue holds, not on the residue
shape.** §22.28b asserted one blanket literal — the shipped `Sync state cleared.` — for both the
`{payload, sentinel, guard}` and the `{sentinel, guard}` residues of §22.28a, which covers **guarded
new-mode and guarded legacy fresh runs alike**. On the legacy arm the `{sentinel, guard}` residue's
sentinel is the **backup sentinel** of §13.6 rule 2c (`verdict: valid`), whose `--abort` must print
§12.8b's discard sentence precisely because a recoverable document is being destroyed; on the
new-mode arm it is `setupSyncRunState`'s plain shipped marker (`verdict: not-guarded`), whose
`--abort` must keep the bare shipped line byte for byte. The criterion is split into a per-residue,
per-route table, and both `{sentinel, guard}` rows are asserted **in the same test** so a collapse
into either literal fails. `{payload, sentinel, guard}` keeps the single shipped cell-5 answer on
both routes, because a payload makes it cell 5 and the cell-4 interception is never consulted
(§12.8b, §22.28a, §22.28b, §22.28e, §23.2, §25.75).

**25.93 Three stale literals are corrected, and each has one true value.** (i) §12.8b's
mode-trigger example list named `--all`, which **is not a flag**: `syncTriggerFlags` is exactly
`{fetch, no-fetch, full, local-only, only, from}` (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:31`), so the row now
enumerates the six and states that no `--all` exists. (ii) §9.2 called D1 "one of the **two**
production behaviour changes" — a count §25.87 already raised to **five** — so it now cites §19.4's
(b) and restates the count, which is five everywhere. (iii) §3.4's legal-combination row called
`--plan --approve-plan` "Legal, non-mutating", an **unqualified** non-mutation claim the Normative
vocabulary reserves for an explicit new-mode `--no-fetch` plan; it becomes "Legal plan-only token
validation" with the scope named, since that invocation still performs the policy fetch of the route
it describes (§3.4, §9.2, §12.8b, §19.4, §25.87).

**25.94 One array cannot have two orders, so `route_triggers[]` is bytewise.** §4.1 said "sorted
trigger names" and §4.8 said "trigger key order" — two rules for one array, and for a legal maximal
triple they disagree (`--no-fetch --local-only --from x` is `from, local-only, no-fetch` bytewise and
`no-fetch, local-only, from` by `syncTriggerFlags` position, exactly reversed). The **bytewise
lexical** order is chosen, for the
same reason §4.8 already sorts `config_issues[]`, `guard.evaluation[]` and
`approval.covers.waived_*` bytewise: it is a property of the values, not of a Go slice literal a
future refactor could reorder, and it makes two documents comparable without knowing the source
order of a flag registration. The shipped code agrees where it renders these names for a human —
`syncChangedTriggerList` walks the slice and then `sort.Strings`es the result
(`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:143-152`) — and that sentence stays byte-identical, since this rule
governs the JSON array alone. "Trigger key order" is withdrawn, §4.1 and §4.8 now say the same
thing, §22.8b asserts the triple, mixed-triple, two-flag, legacy-empty and shell-order-independent
cells element
by element, and §8.3's exclusion is restated explicitly: the array is a fingerprint **non-member**,
so the digest never enforced either order and the conflict had to be closed in the schema
(§4.1, §4.8, §8.3, §22.8b, §23.2).

**25.95 A pure extraction may not acquire a self conjunct.** §12.8b's mapping table listed `self`
among the guard states for which `syncCellLiveGuardRefusal` returns `nil`, and §22.28e (vi) asserted
it. Both are wrong about the shipped code: `syncCellRefusal`'s live arm tests
`st.GuardLive && st.Guard != nil` (`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:305`) over
`GuardLive = guard.PID > 0 && alive(guard.PID)` (`internal/sync_run_state.go:415-417`), which has
**no** `pid != self` term — so a self-recorded guard on cells 2/4/5 refuses today, with the verb's
own sentence, and an extraction returning `nil` there would silently change a shipped answer. The
table gains an explicit self row, the `nil` row is narrowed to absent/dead/`PID <= 0`/unreadable/
symlinked (plus the classifier's own token-mismatch downgrade), and the nil-self assertion is
removed. The self-**excluding** liveness fact still exists and keeps its own home: the controlled
snapshot's `Files.RunGuard.Alive` (`pid > 0 && pid != self && alive(pid)`) and
`ExternalPlanState.LiveForeignOwner()`, which feed `state.files.external_run_guard.alive`, §11.2
cause 3 and `guard.execute_blocked_by: ["live-owner-concurrency"]` — a *foreign*-run question this
feature owns, not a re-decision of the shipped cell refusal. §22.28e (vi) now asserts both facts
against each other over one self-PID fixture, and the recovery arms are restated per cell: the
**cell-4** recovery arm sits below the extraction, so it really does meet only dead, absent or
undecodable guards and its reclaim ladder describes those; the **cell-7** arm has no such
protection, because the shipped switch guards cells 2/4/5 only, and its claim ladder therefore
describes a live guard too (§25.103). The blanket "the recovery arms never meet a live guard" is
**withdrawn**
(§12.3, §12.5 rule 4, §12.8b, §13.2a, §13.6 rule 2c, §17.2, §22.28e, §25.81, §25.103).

**25.96 A residue made in-process carries a live guard, so its recovery test must say which half it
is asserting — and which sentence that half really has.** §22.28a produces its five failure cells by **returning** an error through the §23.1
injected seam, which runs in the harness process; the `.sync-run.lock` inside each measured residue
therefore records that process's own, running PID. §22.28b then asserted that `tws sync <f> --abort`
exits `0` and clears every one of them — which contradicts §12.8's cell-1 self-PID row (fail closed,
exit `1`) and, after §25.95, the live-guard refusal on cells 4 and 5. The criterion is split by
**rule L** of §22.28a: the same-process residue is asserted to **refuse** at exit `1` with nothing
removed, and the clearing outcome is asserted only over a **dead** guard —
either a residue produced by an out-of-process child that has since exited (§23.1 seam 8's
terminating half) or the in-process residue whose guard has been rewritten to a known-dead PID by
seam 7's guard-detaching helper, with every other guard byte asserted unchanged. **The refusing half
is not one sentence, and no text may spell it as one.** A `{sentinel, guard}` or
`{payload, sentinel, guard}` residue is classifier cell 4 or 5, where the *shipped*
`syncCellRefusal` live arm — reproduced by `syncCellLiveGuardRefusal` — answers first, in its
verb-specific spelling, and a self-recorded guard takes that **same** shipped sentence because
`GuardLive` has no self conjunct (§25.95). A `{guard}` residue is classifier **cell 1**, where the
shipped code has **no** live arm at all: it is answered by §12.8's own ladder, whose self-recorded
row is the distinct sentence `sync guard at %s records this process (pid %d); it was not claimed by
this invocation — inspect it and remove it manually` and whose live-foreign row is the shipped
`--abort` sentence. A criterion, test name or comment that asserts "the shipped live-guard sentence"
over the cell-1 residue, or §12.8's self-PID sentence over cells 4/5, is asserting the wrong
sentence and fails §22.28b half 1. Exactly one cell is exempt from the refusing half, and it is exempt by an already-declared rule rather than by convenience: §12.8a's **cell-7**
arm passes `AllowSelfPID: true`, so a `{guard}` residue beside a real `.sync-state.yaml` really is
cleared at exit `0` with a self-recorded guard — the divergence §12.8a declares and §22.28d already
asserts beside a cell-1 fixture that still fails closed. §22.24i (ix-a)'s
named-recovery half and §22.28e's rollback-residue fixture inherit the same split, and outside that
one cell no criterion
anywhere asserts exit `0`, a cleared residue or a successful reclaim over a live or self-recorded
guard (§12.8, §12.8a, §12.8b, §22.24i, §22.28a, §22.28b, §22.28d, §22.28e, §23.1, §23.2). The
operator-facing recovery sentence is untouched and stays true: by the time a human runs
`tws sync <f> --abort`, the process that left the residue has exited, so its guard is dead — the
live/self half exists only because a test can run the recovery while the writer is still alive.

**25.97 A vanished sentinel is absence, not a verdict — and absence is not emptiness.** The
classifier reports cell 4 from a read
that has already happened; §12.8b's interception then performs its **own** fresh `Lstat`/read, so a
concurrent `--abort`, an operator's `rm` or a foreign process can remove `.sync-state.yaml` in
between. That returns `SentinelAbsent`, which round 18 left unhandled: the outcome table had no row
for it, and "every other guarded verdict takes its sentence" would have invented one — a fail-closed
refusal naming a backup that is not there. The interception now **re-classifies exactly once** and
dispatches the ordinary behaviour of whatever the second classification reports. Round 19 then
spelled that dispatch as three fixed absent-state answers, which is the **second** defect and is
withdrawn here: the residue this removal leaves is `{guard}`, so the second classification usually
reports **cell 1 with a live-or-stale run guard**, and cell 1 has an owner — §12.8. The arms are
therefore state-derived, per verb: `--abort` enters §12.8's `case 1:` ladder, where a **self**- or
**live-foreign**-recorded guard fails closed at exit `1` with that arm's own sentence and a provably
**stale** one is released at exit `0` with `Stale sync guard from PID <pid> cleared; no sync state
was present.`; a **plain** run continues as the ordinary no-state run, and where its route claims,
`ClaimSyncRunGuard`'s shipped ladder refuses a live PID (foreign **or** self-recorded, since
`syncProcessAlive` has no self conjunct) and takes a dead one over through its compare-and-swap;
`--continue` keeps the shipped `nothing to continue — no sync in progress` at exit `1` on every
guard state, because §12.8 changes no `--continue`. Only a second classification that finds
**neither** state **nor** guard yields the ordinary absent answers (`Nothing to abort — no sync in
progress.` at exit `0` and its plain twin). The interception never re-enters itself, so no
loop or retry exists; a payload or a real legacy state found by the second read takes that cell's
shipped arm; and every **non**-`ErrNotExist` error keeps failing closed as `unreadable`/`symlink`/
`corrupt`, because "not there" and "could not be read" are different answers. No lock is added and
no ordering between the two reads is claimed — the second read simply decides, which is what an
invocation arriving a moment later would have got. §22.28e (viii) now asserts the dead, live-foreign,
self-recorded and no-guard fixtures separately, and a test asserting the absent answers over a
surviving guard fails it (§12.8, §12.8b, §13.6 rule 2c bindings 2/3a, §22.28e
(viii), §23.1 seam 2a, §23.2).

**25.98 Holder-index applicability is a union of questions, not a row count.** §14.4 rule 2 named
three consumer families and then asserted that "a rows-less document … builds an empty index and
issues zero `worktree list` processes". The two halves disagree for exactly one document: a
rows-less `restoring` checkout continuation, whose entire remaining work **is** the restore and
whose `restore-target-held` question is answered from the index — which, built empty, would have
read as "not held" and let the run walk into a `git checkout` another worktree holds, the precise
failure the fail-closed rule exists to prevent. The rule is restated as a union: an inventory is
built per needed common dir when **any** entry needs a holder fact **or** the fetch family asks
**or** the push/restore family asks, with `restore` contributing its context on every document whose
`restore.applies` is `true` and whose route reaches `restoreOriginal`. Three cells pin it — the
rows-less restoring document builds exactly one, a rows-less document with no restore work builds
none, and a `completed`-stage resume (which asks no holder question despite `applies: true`) builds
none — and §14.4 rule 5's formula and §22.33i (v-d) are corrected to match (§14.4 rules 2/5,
§22.33i (v-d), §23.2, §25.83).

**25.99 External pass 2 switches HEAD, so it re-probes holders at its seam.** §14.4 rule 4 enumerated
the collateral class by argv and then swept external pass-2 rows into the "neither class" list
because their argv carries no `--update-refs` — while §4.2 publishes
`mutation.will_switch_head: true` for exactly those rows, which check the branch out in the
execution context before rebasing it. A foreign worktree (or any of the four `BranchHoldMechanism`
holders) taking that branch between the plan point and the seam is the rank 5.4 condition, and a
stale snapshot would have let the run attempt the switch anyway. The **switch** class is therefore
restated as a published-fact membership test — `mutation.will_switch_head: true` — which covers every
checkout row running a standalone `git checkout` **and** every external pass-2 row; such a row
re-runs `BuildBranchHolderInventory` for its **execution** common dir immediately before the rebase,
and a **foreign** holder that appeared or disappeared is rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` before the
rebase and before the checkout, with the run's own holder still excluded by the canonicalised
self-exclusion. Only `skipped-*` rows, anchor no-ops and **scoped** pass-1 rows remain in neither
class, and no text may claim external pass 2 makes no JIT holder probe (§4.2, §10.3, §11.8,
§14.4 rule 4, §22.33i (v-e), (v-e-1a), §23.2, §25.89).

**25.100 The JIT collateral comparison is over the whole tuple array.** §10.3's outcome row and
§11.8's binding paragraph spelled the refusal as "a ref **enters** known `collateral_refs`, or a
known-unexposed row becomes exposed", which is two cells of a much larger space: a listed ref whose
`sha` moved, a `stack_owned` that flipped, a tuple that was **removed**, and an array that moved
between `null` and known all left the approved plan describing something the executor is no longer
about to do, and all would have passed. The comparison becomes the full canonical
`{repo, ref, sha, stack_owned}` tuple array — the same shape §8.3 binds — plus `collateral_exposed`,
and **any** difference is rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` before any Git mutation. It is declared as
**conservative identity drift**, not as a claim that the listed refs would or would not move: tws
does not reason about whether a changed tuple is benign, because the operator approved an array and
the executor now faces a different one. The narrow spelling is withdrawn everywhere, and §22.33i
(v-e-1) gains added/removed, tip-only-SHA (both directions), `stack_owned`-flip (both directions)
and `null`↔known cells beside an unchanged control that still rebases (§8.3, §10.3, §11.8,
§14.4 rule 4, §22.33i (v-e-1), §23.2).

**25.101 The cell-4 recovery arm is decided by the snapshot, and window 1 is not cell 4.** Ledger
row 17a and §13.6 rule 5's downgrade row described the backup-sentinel residue as "§13.2a crash
windows 1–2", and §23.2 attributed "claim (window 1) or reclaim (window 2)" to the arm. Both
misattribute: window 1 is `{guard}` beside the **untouched real legacy state** — classifier cell 7
on the continuation arm, cell 1 on the fresh route — recovered by §12.8a/§12.8 and by an armed
`--continue` over the intact subject (§22.24i (ix-b) already says so). Only window **2**, and the
`{sentinel, guard}` rollback residue that shares its on-disk shape, is cell 4. The claim/reclaim
choice is likewise not a provenance fact: the arm **reclaims** where the snapshot found a guard and
**claims** where it did not — the same decision for a crash residue and for a rollback residue — and
§22.24j (iii) now asserts it over both provenances (§12.3, §13.2a, §13.6 rule 5 and ledger row 17a,
§22.24i (ix-b), §22.24j (iii), §23.2).

**25.102 The collateral tuple has four inputs, so a seam that refreshes one of them compares three
stale members against one fresh one.** §25.100 made the JIT comparison total over
`{repo, ref, sha, stack_owned}` + `collateral_exposed`, and §25.89 made the seam refresh
`BuildBranchHolderInventory`. Together those still under-specified the measurement: holders answer
only the "minus every ref checked out in any worktree" exclusion, while `ref` and `sha` come from the
repository's local branch inventory and `stack_owned` comes from `stack.yaml`. A run planned at T0
and executing at T1 could therefore be compared against a branch set and an ownership mapping read at
T0 — so a branch created, deleted or moved after the plan, and a `stack.yaml` an operator edited
mid-run, were invisible to the very comparison §25.100 declared total, and cell (2) of §22.33i
(v-e-1) (a `stack_owned` flip driven by editing `stack.yaml`) could not have been observed at all.
Immediately before **any** guarded row whose own published argv can invoke `--update-refs` — external
pass 1 included — the seam therefore re-measures **all four** inputs: the holder inventory for that
row's **execution** canonical common dir; the **complete** local branch ref inventory of that
repository through exactly one `BuildBranchRefInventory` (`internal/stack_status.go:427-447`), i.e.
one `git for-each-ref` process; a **safe reload of the current `stack.yaml`** from which only the
stack-owned membership mapping is rebuilt (a dedicated read-only stack identity probe over
`StackEntry.GitBranch()`, which MUST NOT `TopoSort`, re-select, or change the run's order, universe
or remaining set, so §9.1a rule 3's one-sort count is untouched); and the row's candidate
range/digest. An unreadable `stack.yaml`, an unavailable ref inventory and an unavailable worktree
inventory are each rank 5.9 `probe-failed` **before** any Git mutation — never an empty set read as
"no collateral" — while a **readable** input whose value differs makes the recomputed tuple array
differ, which is rank 9 `revalidation-mismatch` by §25.100's total comparison. Each input is measured
**once per seam** and never shared across seams. The budget follows: a collateral-class seam costs one
further Git process per common dir (the `for-each-ref`), the stack reload costs none, §10.3's per-row
external ceilings become **13** (**11** without the default-branch read) with checkout unchanged at
**8** — checkout never publishes `--update-refs`, so it has no collateral-class row — and §14.4
rule 5's formula gains the same term. Nothing here licenses a prediction: §11.8's upper bound is
unchanged at the seam, and no sentence may claim a listed ref will move or will stay because an
input was refreshed. §22.33i (v-e) counts the two extra measurements per seam and asserts a
switch-only row makes neither; (v-e-1) gains a suppressed-reload cell that misses the `stack_owned`
flip, an unreadable-stack cell and a failed-`for-each-ref` cell, both at rank 5.9
(§10.3, §11.8, §14.4 rules 4–5, §22.33i (v-e), (v-e-1), §23.2, §25.89, §25.99, §25.100).

**25.103 Cell 7 is not pre-handled, so the claim is where its live guard is decided.** §25.95 closed
by stating that "the recovery arms never meet a live guard", which is true of the **cell-4** arm —
it sits below `syncCellLiveGuardRefusal`, which reproduces the shipped live refusal — and false of
the **cell-7** arm. The shipped switch it extracts guards cells **2, 4 and 5 only**
(`internal/cli/sync_modes.go:303-311`); `syncCellRefusal` returns `nil` for cell 7, and the classifier
does not even read the guard there, because `AlwaysReadGuard` is `newMode` and a continuation carries
no trigger (§12.5). An armed `--continue` over `{real .sync-state.yaml, guard}` — the residue §12.8a
exists for — therefore reaches §12.3 step 9, and the authority is `setupGuardedLegacyRunState`'s
step-2 `ClaimSyncRunGuard`. Its answers are the shipped ones, stated here so no arm invents a
sentence: a **live** PID (foreign **or** self-recorded, because `syncProcessAlive` has no self
conjunct) returns `a scoped sync is already running for %q (pid %d, started %s); wait for it or use
--continue/--abort after it exits`; `PID <= 0` returns `sync guard is being initialized or is
invalid; retry or inspect %s`; an undecodable guard returns `invalid sync guard; inspect %s and use
--abort to recover: %w`; a provably **dead** one is reclaimed through the shipped compare-and-swap,
whose `HasSyncRunState` arm cannot fire on a payload-less cell, with `reclaim stale sync guard: %w`
if the swap fails. Every one of them exits `1` marker-free (§6.4 exempts `ClaimSyncRunGuard`), writes
nothing — step 1 is an in-memory read, so there is nothing to roll back — leaves `.sync-state.yaml`
byte-identical and issues no Git mutation. The safety property is unchanged and is **not** replaced
by a pre-check: the `O_EXCL` create stays the mutual-exclusion point, and no read-then-write ladder
is added above it. §22.24i (ix-d) asserts the live-foreign, self-recorded, invalid and dead cells,
and §12.3's `case 7:` comment, its step 9 and its step-4 `external-e4` note no longer imply that a
guard cannot be there (§12.3, §12.5, §12.8a, §13.2a, §22.24i (ix-d), §23.2, §25.95).

**25.104 A nullable join key must be nullable everywhere, and a nullable sort key needs a declared
tie-break.** §4.4a declared `push.targets[].context_id` nullable with the Go field `ContextID
*string`, and §14.1a rule 6 kept the row emitted with `context_id: null` beside the entry's rank 5.1
`repo-unavailable` blocker — while §14.1 called the same member "REQUIRED", `PlanPushContext`
carried it as a `string` whose `""` meant `null`, and §4.8/§8.2 ordered the array by a bare
`(context_id, git_branch)` that says nothing about where a `null` goes. Three spellings of one fact
therefore disagreed, and the one the array is *sorted* by was the ambiguous one: an implementation
could have read "REQUIRED" and dropped the unresolved row, read `""` and collided two unestablished
contexts into one key, or sorted `null` last, first or arbitrarily and still passed every stated
assertion. The resolution keeps the schema and adds no member: `context_id` is **nullable**, the
"REQUIRED" phrasing is **withdrawn**, `""` is **not a context id anywhere** — `PlanPushContext.
ContextID` and `PlanPushRemoteFacts.ContextID` become `*string`, `PlanPushFacts.Remotes` simply has
no entry for a nil-id context, and `PlanPushFacts.Contexts` is ordered nil-first — and the canonical
order becomes `(context_id [null first], git_branch bytewise)`, a **total** order in which a
`null`-id row sorts ahead of every established id and ties break on the branch bytes. The unresolved
row stays total in its other nine members, keeps rule 5a's already-declared
`expectation: unknown` lease with its rank 5.9 `probe-failed` row beside the rank 5.1 row (distinct
facts, both published, `repo-unavailable` winning the §7.2 collapse), costs **zero** probe reads,
and binds a `NULL` TLV member rather than empty `BYTES`, so a run whose push context resolved and
one whose did not can never mint the same token. Nothing else moves: the tuple schema version stays
`0x0004` because no member is added or removed, only the value domain of one already-bound member is
stated honestly (§4.4a, §4.8, §8.2, §14.1, §14.1a rules 2, 2a, 5a, 6, 7, §22.33b, §22.33h (ii)–(v),
§23.2).

**25.105 A stage whose shipped resume gates before it validates is not a validation-only stage.**
§13.3b's `rebased` row said `resumeFromRebased` runs "validation only", and §13.5's projected-gate
list carried the `conflict` arm's `after conflict resolution, …` sentence but not the `rebased`
arm's. The shipped code disagrees on both counts: `resumeFromRebased`
(`internal/checkout_sync.go:941-953`) evaluates `gitIsAncestor(opts.RepoDir, entry.NewBaseSHA,
entry.Branch)` **before** anything else it does for the current row and, on failure, sets
`FailureKind: ancestry`, sets `FailureMsg` to `%s not descended from %s after rebase`, persists the
transaction and returns that sentence. A `--plan --continue` over a `rebased` transaction therefore
promised a resume the executor would refuse, with no blocker and `runnable: true` — the exact
surprise this feature exists to remove. The gate is now projected: **rank 4** `preflight-refused`
(live-Git ancestry for one transaction row, the `switched` HEAD-identity class, not the
recovery-artefact class rank 3 denotes), **document-level** with `entry: null` because §13.3's stage
table publishes **no** row for a `rebased` current index, evaluated through **exactly one**
`merge-base --is-ancestor` process and **zero** at every stage other than `rebased` and `conflict`
(§25.106), with a rank 5.9 `probe-failed`
cell where the probe itself fails, and with **no** write of any kind on the plan route. The
executing guarded twin is untouched — the shipped gate refuses it, marker-free, at exit `1`, having
really persisted `FailureKind: ancestry` and `FailureMsg` with `Stage` still `rebased` — so §13.7
rule 8's mutation exception now has exactly **two** members (the `planned`/`rebasing` active-rebase
gate and this one) and §12.7 preserves both writes rather than undoing them. Rank 4 consequently
carries one postcondition (the external completion gate, one cell) and one precondition (this gate,
checkout-only), which §13.5's five-row table keeps distinct and total against the row's
evidence-only `ancestry` fact; the same `gitIsAncestor` call reached from `processBranch`,
`resumeFromSwitched` or the `conflict` fall-through runs *after* a rebase this invocation performed
and is projected by nobody (§7.1 rank 4, §12.7, §13.3b, §13.5, §13.7 gate e and rule 8a, §22.13d
(b), §23.1 seam 8, §23.2).

**25.106 The `conflict` stage asks the same live-ancestry question, so its probe must be accounted
for rather than assumed away.** §25.105 above closed the `rebased` gate with the accounting "exactly
one `merge-base --is-ancestor` process and **zero** at any other stage", while §13.5 had listed the
`conflict` arm's `after conflict resolution, %s is not descended from base %s` sentence as a bare
rank 3 gate with no predicate, no probe, no entry scope and no probe-failure cell. Both statements
cannot hold: the shipped `conflict` arm (`internal/checkout_sync.go:875-881`) evaluates
`gitIsAncestor(opts.RepoDir, entry.NewBaseSHA, entry.Branch)` itself, immediately below its
rebase-in-progress short-circuit, so projecting its sentence **requires** a probe and the
"zero at any other stage" budget was false for the one stage whose sentence was already listed. An
implementation could have read the old text and issued zero probes (publishing a gate it never
evaluated), two (adding one for the shipped fall-through into `resumeFromRebased`), or hung the
sentence on an `entries[]` row §13.3's stage table never publishes. The resolution adds no kind, no
field and no seam: the `conflict` gate is specified exactly like the `rebased` one but at its own
rank — reached **only** where the short-circuit did not fire, **exactly one** probe over the
persisted `(NewBaseSHA, Branch)` pair with `entry.Base` never re-resolved, rank 3 `state-refused`
document-level (`entry: null`) on `false`, rank 5.9 `probe-failed` on a probe error, and a
satisfied gate that proceeds while the plan performs **none** of the shipped success-side writes
(`PostSHA`, `Stage: rebased`, `SaveCheckoutTransaction`) and issues **no** second probe for the
fall-through. The budget becomes the closed two-cell table of §13.5 rule E — one probe at
`conflict`, one at `rebased`, zero at the other six stages — and §13.7 rule 8a stays at **two**
members, because the `conflict` gate's refusing arms write nothing on either route (§13.3b, §13.5
rule E, §13.7 gate e and rule 8a, §22.13d (b)–(c), §23.2).

**25.107 A whole-plan postcondition that only the future can decide is disclosed, not projected.**
The four ancestry-shaped facts §13.5 called "total" omitted a fifth the shipped executor really
evaluates: `finalizeTransaction` (`internal/checkout_sync.go:1191-1200`) re-checks **every**
`tx.Plan` entry with `gitIsAncestor(opts.RepoDir, pe.NewBaseSHA, pe.Branch)` after `SaveStack` has
written each entry's `LastBaseSHA` and before `tx.Stage = StageRestoring`, and may fail the whole
run with `final ancestry check failed: %s not descendant of %s`. A totality claim that misses a
shipped ancestry refusal is exactly the kind of surprise this feature removes, so the fact is added
— as the table's **fifth** row and as nothing else. It is **not** promoted to a plan preflight or a
JIT input: the drift it catches is a **concurrent ref move that happens after** the plan, the guard
seam and the row's own rebase, which no plan-time or seam-time read can prove, so refusing on it
early would refuse runs that will succeed and would contradict §7.1's rank-4 postcondition rule.
The plan therefore publishes **no** blocker, warning, refusal kind, controlled-path token or new
key for it and its `runnable` is unchanged; the disclosure is prose (§13.5 rule F, §20), which adds
no schema key and no enum member. Its executing behaviour is preserved verbatim on **both** routes:
same position, same sentence, native and marker-free (never a `*PlanGuardRefusalError`, never
`state-preserved: `-prefixed), the transaction and `.checkout-sync.lock` surviving because the
shipped arm writes neither `FailureKind` nor `FailureMsg`, and `stack.yaml` legitimately already
updated — which §12.7 now records as a preserved residue rather than something a cleanup arm may
tidy. The assertion needs **no** new hook site: the shipped `StepHook(StageRebased, …)` fired on the
last index of a ≥2-entry plan can move an earlier entry's branch and return `nil`, which reaches the
finalizer deterministically (§7.1 rank 4, §12.7, §13.5 rules E–F, §17.3, §19.3, §22.13n, §23.1
seam 8, §23.2).

## 26. Final decision register — analysis §19.1–§19.29

| §19 item | Status in analysis | Resolution in this spec | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — where external state is created | open | **Two orderings.** Unguarded new-mode keeps the shipped order `setupSyncRunState` → header → fetch (stage `fetching`) → rebase, byte-, process- and state-order frozen. **Guarded** fresh new-mode runs a controlled-only pipeline: header + validation resolution + payload-free `fetchScopedReposTo(os.Stdout, os.Stderr, …)` (exactly one fetch, whose returned `PlanFetchOutcome` the plan consumes) → plan → guard → claim (`state_version: 3`, written by `setupSyncRunState`'s one new `birth` parameter) → post-claim revalidation → rebase, so a refusal **at or above the guard seam** creates nothing (though its policy fetch already ran), a refusal **below the claim** removes exactly what it created through `rollbackGuardedRunState` with **real** `os.Remove` errors propagated and the measured residue named, and the run's stage history is `initializing` → `rebasing` with `fetching` never written. `tws sync <f> --abort` is made true for every residue, including guard-only cell 1. The guarded legacy route gains the same shape with a `route: legacy` envelope, the guarded **new-mode continuation** gets its own entry point, `handleGuardedScopedSyncContinue`, whose guard seam sits above `ReclaimSyncRunGuard` so a refusal there writes nothing at all, and the guarded **legacy continuation** — `handleGuardedLegacySyncContinue` — covers the v3 envelope cell, the real `.sync-state.yaml` cell 7 and the cell-4 backup-sentinel residue, the middle one writing nothing at or above its guard seam, creating the guarded legacy envelope below it through the four-step, rollback-bearing canonical order of §13.2a — **capture (step 1) → the `O_EXCL` `ClaimSyncRunGuard` (step 2) → the conditional backup sentinel that embeds the replaced document (step 3) → payload (step 4)** — and then entering the shared executor **payload-aware** over that envelope, in `handleSyncContinue`'s own emission order (§12.3, §13.2a, §13.6 rule 2c, §25.46, §25.51, §25.64, §25.65, §25.67, §25.74, §25.76). A continuation that **arms** a limit over a pre-guarded subject persists a `state_version: 3` envelope with an inherited route before its next Git mutation, so the guard survives a re-interruption (§13.2a, §13.6 rule 2b). `tws sync <f> --abort` is true for the legacy-state-plus-guard residue of §12.8a and for the backup-sentinel residue of §12.8b, whose `--continue` **resumes** the interrupted setup instead of refusing it. Checkout lock timing unchanged | §12.2, §12.2c, §12.3, §12.8, §12.8a, §12.8b, §13.2a, §13.6 rules 2a/2b/2c, §17.2, §25.8, §25.9, §25.11, §25.12, §25.46, §25.64, §25.65, §25.67, §25.68, §25.73, §25.74, §25.75 |
| 2 — exit code for a guarded refusal | closed | exit `1`; no exit `2`; consumers branch on document fields | §3.6, §2.22 |
| 3 — fingerprint tuple ratification | closed | tuple schema **stays `0x0004`**; the whitelist and field tables are adopted with exactly one correction — the rendered `workspace.repo_root` is **not** a member, its field id is retired, and workspace identity travels through `mode`/`stable_id` plus the already-bound `context_id`s; successor is `0x0005` and moves as a unit with the assertions | §8.2, §8.3, §25.4 |
| 4 — collateral configuration and loudness | open (both halves) | `collateral-update-refs-config` **warning** only, and only in the `collateral_mechanism: config` cell, which requires `effective_backend == merge`; **no argv override on any guarded run** | §11.8, §25.16 |
| 5 — pin external `--onto` to a SHA | open | **yes, on guarded execution paths only — fresh runs *and* guarded continuations (cells 5, 7 and the cell-4 recovery arm)**; plan displays it; unguarded/no-flag argv frozen; plain rebase unchanged; the guarded/unguarded relation is asserted as a matched pair rather than as byte identity, since the pin is the intended difference | §10.5, §25.72 |
| 6 — `BuildCheckoutPlan` adapter now or later | open | **now**: adapter over the shared planner in this boundary, keeping its shipped `(repoDir, stack, sel)` signature and constructing `RebasePlanLayout{RepoRoot: repoDir}` itself, split into the order-taking `buildCheckoutPlanFrom` body plus that wrapper, which owns the **unguarded** route's `TopoSort`; `ResolveSyncSelection` is split the same way into `ResolveSyncSelectionFromOrder` plus its shipped sorting wrapper, so a controlled route sorts **once** and the selection consumes that order; `ExecutionOrder` takes the precomputed order and never sorts; the unguarded sort counts are declared, not reduced; no conformance-test-and-unify-later | §9.0 rules 2/2a, §9.1a rules 3/3a, §9.2, §9.2a, §25.36 |
| 7 — fix D1 here | open | **yes**: **any** in-stack parent resolves through `parent.GitBranch()` in checkout — the shipped scoped local-only body with its arm conjuncts dropped — with **no** `sameStackRepo` conjunct and no `StackEntry.Repo` consultation; external's same-repo conjunct stays a mirrored D7 divergence; planner and executor change together; **both** changed cells are declared — D1-a (a run that fails today succeeds) and D1-b (a silent destination change where a real Git branch shares the parent's logical name) — in §17.2, §19.4, the CHANGELOG and the test matrix | §9.2, §17.2, §19.4, §22.26, §22.26a, §22.26b, §25.7 |
| 8 — describing a legacy continuation | open | publish the absent context as explicit `null`/`none` values; never omit a key. An **armed** legacy continuation is described by the same producer that executes it: cell 7 dispatches to `handleGuardedLegacySyncContinue`, whose subject is the classifier's already-decoded `state.Legacy`, whose remaining set is the full-stack legacy universe of §13.3, whose prose keeps `handleSyncContinue`'s order and persisted count, and whose executor is entered payload-aware over the envelope its own §13.2a step created, while the flagless resume stays on the shipped handler | §4.1, §12.3, §13.2a, §19.2, §25.51, §25.65, §25.76 |

**All twenty-nine items remain resolved after review round 11.** Rounds 2 and 3 changed *how* several
of them are implemented and declared — §19.1 (guarded ordering, validation resolution, post-claim
cleanup with real removal errors and the guard-only cell-1 `--abort` recovery), §19.7 (both D1 cells
declared), §19.10 (every workflow carries a limit), §19.14 (writer plumbing down to the exec layer
and both plan routes), §19.17 (the frozen command is persisted where the run persists state and is
authoritative afterwards) and §19.27 (the fifth capability gate) — and added the refinements §25.9
through §25.14.

Round 4 changed *how* six of them are implemented and declared, and **opened nothing**:

- **§19.14** — both plan routes are now complete rather than partial. The checkout route
  (§13.7) specifies a fresh **and** a continuation order, projects every gate its executor raises
  above its own fetch (containment, existing transaction, Git operation, dirty tree, detached HEAD,
  HEAD resolution, I14, live lock, I20 and the continuation gates) **before** deciding to fetch, and
  forbids rebuilding the plan on a continuation; the external route (§13.7a) does the same over its
  own ladder and additionally threads the single `resolveSyncPolicy`-owned `changed` map so
  `syncContinueMismatches` is projected rather than re-derived. Prose is now **single-source**: each
  shipped printer's body moves once into a writer-taking twin and the shipped symbol becomes a
  one-line wrapper passing `os.Stdout` — and `os.Stderr` where the shipped body wired a child's
  stderr — so the guarded, unguarded and plan routes cannot drift (§3.6 rule 3).
- **§19.1** — the guarded routes consume the same result-returning fetch helpers with
  `os.Stdout`/`os.Stderr`, so one fetch implementation serves all three routes and the guarded
  document publishes the fetch it really performed.
- **§19.6** — `BuildCheckoutPlan` keeps its shipped signature and builds its own
  `RebasePlanLayout{RepoRoot: repoDir}`; no shared function may require `FeaturePath` or
  `WorktreesRoot` on the checkout arm, which removes the circular reading of §9.0 rule 2.
- **§19.4 / §19.12** — `merge-recreation` and config-enabled collateral now require the effective
  **merge** backend, so an `apply` run keeps a valid candidate bound and an empty known collateral
  set (§25.16).
- **§19.18** — checkout autostash applicability is per continuation stage, because
  `resumeFromSwitched` runs no checkout; tracked dirt with no applicable autostash is rank 5.5 there
  too (§13.3b, §25.15).
- **§19.24** — the `switched` continuation arm gains a guard-introduced rank 4 HEAD-identity
  preflight on the plan and guarded routes, and its `onto` upstream is stated correctly as the
  persisted `LastBaseSHA` cutoff, with the persisted `NewBaseSHA` as destination (§13.3a, §25.17).

It also tightened four cross-cutting contracts: the checkout recovery predicate
`checkoutRecoveryIsNewMode` covering both `AbortCheckoutSync`'s deferred half of I7 and the
continuation gates (§13.6 rule 4c), §11.2 cause 2's membership widened to every pre-fetch gate with
the live-owner tie-break spelled out, the declared hoist of `opts.FeaturePath`/`opts.RepoDir` above
the I19 containment check (§13.7 step 0, §19.4), and the sixth non-behavioural category in the
minimality ledger that classifies it. The token-only guarded-blockers rendering (§6.3), the closed
`push.blocked_by[]`/`restore.blocked_by[]` domains (§7.5), the `guard.evaluation[]` scoping (§4.6),
the `config --show-scope` gate (§16), the file-appropriate documentation gates (§22.33) and the
authoritative validation freeze with no configuration-change mismatch (§15.9) are carried forward
unchanged.

Round 5 changed *how* seven of them are implemented and declared, and **opened nothing**:

- **§19.14 / §19.6** — the checkout plan route now inspects **once**. `CheckoutPlanState` and the
  nil-argument `CheckoutPlanGates` are replaced by `InspectCheckoutPlan` returning one
  `CheckoutPlanInspection` that loads, sorts, resolves, runs I14 and projects every gate a single
  time, and by builders that may only read it —
  `BuildCheckoutRebasePlan(insp, fetched)` / `BuildCheckoutContinuationPlan(insp)` — round 10 adds
  the post-fetch `push PlanPushFacts` parameter to both (§25.45). No double stack
  load, no selection resolved around the fetch, one I14 owner per route in both modes, header and
  fetch both suppressed by any refusing pre-fetch blocker, and rows published exactly where their
  inputs were established (§13.7 rules 1–6, §25.18).
- **§19.14 / §19.22** — the external routes gain a named safe snapshot producer,
  `InspectExternalPlanState`, which always `Lstat`s `.sync-run.lock` (including on a legacy plan,
  where the shipped classifier does not) and travels to the builder as
  `RebasePlanRequest.ExternalState`; no text may treat `SyncExternalState` as that snapshot
  (§12.5, §13.7a rule 6, §25.19).
- **§19.14** — the external plan-only route reads its subject **before** projecting its state
  gates, so a refused document still carries rows wherever the stack was readable, and the
  unreachable deferred-I7 gate is removed rather than kept as dead code. Executing routes keep the
  shipped ladder order (§13.7a, §25.20).
- **§19.4 / §19.12** — `effective_backend` is derived from a seven-row table in which

  intended (§11.7, §11.8, §25.21).
- **§19.24** — the `switched` arm additionally verifies that its **persisted** destination object

  without re-resolving `entry.Base` and without changing the persisted-`LastBaseSHA` upstream
  (§13.3a rule 6, §25.22).
- **§19.15 / §19.8** — `replay.reason` follows one precedence list for every row shape (the
  `unknown`-row sub-enum is withdrawn, and `merge-recreation` is reachable there), and §4.7's

Round 8 changed *how* four of them are implemented and declared, and **opened nothing**:

- **§19.1 / §19.14 — the implicit lease is corrected against Git's own resolution, in the opposite
  direction to round 7.** Git's compare-and-swap mapping **skips** negative fetch refspecs, so a
  branch with a covering positive refspec keeps its remote-tracking destination and its SHA
  expectation; only a missing mapping or an absent/unreadable tracking ref falls back to the null
  OID. §14.2's cell table publishes `expectation: sha` there and marks it
  `expected_sha_freshness: possibly-stale` **even after a successful fetch**, because the negative
  entry is exactly what makes that value unrefreshable. Round 7's `{absent, null, null, fresh}`
  reading is withdrawn as the more dangerous error — it claimed a stricter baseline than Git sends
  — and §22.33f pins the result with three real `--force-with-lease` pushes: matching succeeds,
  stale rejects, null-OID-against-an-existing-ref rejects (§4.4a, §14.2, §25.32).
- **§19.6 / §19.14 / §19.24 — the checkout controlled paths hoist the sort, and the claim about the
  shipped preflight is corrected. (Round 9 corrects this row again, per arm — see below; the
  sentence "the preflight contains no `TopoSort`" is true only of the *visible* call, because
  `ResolveSyncSelection` sorts inside itself, and the new-mode arm therefore moves nothing.)** The
  shipped pre-lock preflight is `LoadStack` →
  `ResolveSyncSelection` → `verifyCheckoutBasesLocally` and contains no visible `TopoSort`; the
  shipped legacy sort
  is inside `BuildCheckoutPlan`, below the lock and the fetch. `--plan` and guarded checkout now
  share one `InspectCheckoutPlan` call that sorts above both (gate g1), so a cyclic stack yields the
  rows-less `stack-unsortable` document at exit `0` on the plan route and its arm's shipped
  refusal at exit `1` on the guarded route — with no
  lock, no fetch and no transaction. The unguarded routes are verbatim
  `lock → optional fetch → BuildCheckoutPlan/TopoSort` (§12.2d, §13.6 rule 8 row 12, §13.7 step 1.3
  and rule 4, §17.2, §19.4 change (d), §22.13l, §25.35).
- **§19.6 — one sort, one order, one signature.** `InspectCheckoutPlan` sorts once and publishes
  `Order []StackEntry`; `ExecutionOrder` takes that precomputed order and MUST NOT sort;
  `BuildCheckoutPlan` becomes the shipped-signature wrapper over the order-taking
  `buildCheckoutPlanFrom`; the external route's step-4 sort travels as `req.Order`. A call counter
  pins one `TopoSort` per **controlled** invocation (§9.1a rules 3–4, §9.2, §22.33g, §25.36).
  *(Round 9 completes this: `ResolveSyncSelection` is split the same way, and the unguarded counts
  are declared rather than claimed to be one — §9.1a rule 3a, §9.2a.)*
- **§19.2 / §19.14 — the request and the document are declared, not described.** §9.1a gives

  member and the twenty-five §4.1 keys as the document struct's own fields, so the source model and

## 27. Definition status and Path B process (non-normative)

This section describes how this artefact moves through tpatch. It adds no requirement, changes no
contract, and nothing in §1–§26 depends on it.

1. **This document is the definition-phase content, and it is complete.** Every §19 item is resolved
   in §26, every refinement is recorded in §25, and there is no "TBD", no open alternative and no
   implementer discretion left anywhere in §1–§26.
2. **Phase state is not definition content.** `status.json` reading `state: analyzed`, `spec.md`
   being untracked, and the absence of a `chore(tpatch)` commit are **not** gaps in this
   specification and are not review blockers against it. Path B advances the phase **after** the
   definition is approved, in this order: stage the artefact and record its checksum, run
   `tpatch define --manual` (the coding agent is the provider, per `docs/engineering-workflow.md`
   step 5), then commit and push the tpatch metadata as its own `chore(tpatch)` commit, separate
   from any production change (`.tpatch/steering/local.md`).
3. **Exploration is the next phase, not an input to this one.** `exploration.md` is produced by
   `tpatch explore` **after** `define` (`defined → tpatch explore → defined`, steering "Phase
   Ordering"); its absence now is expected. §21's two soft-parent registrations and
   `tpatch feature deps --validate-all` run after `define` and again after `explore`, exactly as
   §21 already says.
4. **`status.json`'s `compatibility` field is lifecycle/release metadata, not a specification
   choice.** The compatibility contract of this feature is stated normatively in §17 (what is
   frozen, what may change and on which path) and in §13.6 rule 5 (the fail-closed downgrade); the
   field is set when the feature lands and is released, following the release cadence of
   `docs/engineering-workflow.md`. Editing it is not part of approving this definition.
5. **This feature is not split, and the recovery arms are the reason it must not be.** §12.8
   (guard-only cell 1), §12.8a (cell 7) and §12.8b (cell 4) are not independent conveniences: each
   recovers a residue whose existence, shape and fail-closed guarantees are created by the
   `state_version: 3` guarded state envelope of §13.6 — the backup sentinel of rule 2c, the claim
   ordering of §13.2a and the downgrade refusal of rule 5. Landing the envelope without the recovery
   arms would ship a state an operator cannot clear; landing the arms without the envelope would
   recover a document nothing writes. They share one set of writers, one classifier, one guard
   ladder and one set of goldens, so they are **one logical tpatch feature per implementation
   boundary** (`AGENTS.md`), landed as one traceable feature commit through `tpatch land`.
